notes: From “I Can” to “I Already Am”
A Change of Mindset (Part 3)
I have been crucified with Christ
It is no longer I who live
But Christ lives in me (Galatians 2:20)
• Theme of the lesson: trade “I can” and “I will” for “I already am”.
• Key verse Galatians 2:20 — read the full verse aloud once first.
• Note on the subtitle: this is the third lesson in the “A Change of Mindset” series.
• Open warmly, and first invite the brothers and sisters to be quiet for a minute.
The war ended long ago
Hiroo Onoda hid in the jungle
And fought on for twenty-nine years
Because he didn’t believe the war was over
Are you still fighting a finished war?
• History: Japanese second lieutenant Hiroo Onoda — the war ended in 1945, but he fought on in Lubang Island, the Philippines, until 1974.
• Set beside John 19:30, “It is finished” — the war ended two thousand years ago.
• Ask: lately, has your most common feeling been lightness or weariness?
• Bring in the lesson’s introduction: we get stuck not because we don’t try hard, but because our mindset hasn’t changed.
Key verse and background
Galatians — Paul, around AD 48
Judaizers demanded circumcision
The gospel swapped for “I must do more”
Paul set a boundary stone for the gospel
• Author Paul; possibly his earliest letter, AD 48–49, after the first missionary journey.
• Recipients: the churches of Galatia — Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, Derbe.
• Background: Judaizers required Gentile believers to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses.
• Context: Paul opposed Peter to his face in Antioch (Galatians 2:11–14); 2:15–21 is the theological summing-up.
• Stress: Galatians 2:20 is not a devotional nugget but a boundary stone guarding the freedom of the gospel.
Where faith begins
Not justified by the works of the law
But through faith in Jesus Christ (Galatians 2:16)
Not how much I have done
But whether I believe in Jesus
• Galatians 2:16 says “not by the works of the law” three times and points to faith three times in one sentence.
• The original: “justify”, dikaioō, is a courtroom term — to declare righteous, not to make better.
• Scripture interpreting Scripture: Ephesians 2:8–9; Galatians 3:1–3, “Having begun in the Spirit, are you now completed in the flesh?”
• Illustration: an adopted child doesn’t have to wash the dishes every day to earn his place on the family register.
• Supporting witness from psychology: Albert Ellis founded REBT in 1955, observing that people whip themselves with “musts”.
The faith of “I already am”
I have been crucified with Christ
Perfect tense, passive voice
Already done — and not by me
Jesus crucified my old self for me
• Greek synestaurōmai, perfect tense, passive voice: already done, still in force, not done by me.
• Romans 6:6, “knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him” — knowing comes first, then victory.
• Romans 6:11, “consider yourselves … dead”: logizesthe is an accounting term — reckon the account this way.
• Supporting witness from psychology: Bluma Zeigarnik (1927) — unfinished tasks occupy the mind.
• 321: the grammar of pride is “I will” (five “I will”s in Isaiah 14:13–14); the grammar of humility is “I already am”.
Three declarations of faith
I have been crucified with Christ
It is no longer I who live
But Christ lives in me
A choice of faith, a mindset turned around
• Invite everyone to read these three sentences together — this is the mindset turned around.
• Not “I must die” but “I have already died”; not “I must live out Christ” but “Christ lives in me”.
• Answer the misunderstanding: the flesh remains, but the old self’s identity has ended and sin is no longer master (Romans 6:14).
• 321: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering the limitless and living out the limitless.
How a mindset changes
Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation
Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication
When you fall, choose “I already am” again
A mindset repeated becomes life
• The lesson’s four steps: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation; the 321 eight stages add Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
• Revelation comes from the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 1:17) — the Three Foundations: the Holy Spirit is my guide.
• Repentance, metanoia, has at its root a change of mind — the essence of repentance is a change of mindset.
• Scientific witness: Donald Hebb, The Organization of Behavior (1949) — neurons that fire together wire together.
• Carol Dweck’s mindset research: the mindset changes first, then behaviour.
Measuring your faith
“I can / I will”: struggle, suppress, exhaustion
“I already am”: no more wrestling with sin
The key isn’t refusing sin
But turning to the finished salvation
• Faith is not measured amid the sound of praise; it is measured under temptation.
• Supporting witness from psychology: Daniel Wegner’s 1987 white bear experiment — suppression rebounds.
• Colossians 2:23: severity to the body is “not of any value against the indulgence of the flesh”.
• History: the 1863 Emancipation Proclamation, yet Texas only learned on 19 June 1865 — free, yet still slaves.
• 321: the focus is Jesus — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances.
The key to victory
The victory that has overcome the world:
your faith (1 John 5:4)
Not by trying harder
But by believing more
• 1 John 5:4–5; nikaō, to overcome, in the past tense — the victory is settled.
• Colossians 1:13: “delivered” and “translated” are both completed actions.
• Illustration: someone struggling in water sinks; relaxing and trusting buoyancy, they float (adult density about 0.95–0.99).
• History: Martin Luther’s 1545 preface on being set free through Romans 1:17; Hudson Taylor’s “exchanged life” in 1869.
• 321: let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.
Putting it into practice
1. Discern the state of your faith
2. Replace “I must try harder” with “I already am”
3. Practise the choice of faith daily
Stop, declare, turn
• Practice one: today, notice whether your reaction is “I can”, “I will” or “I already am”.
• Practice two: when struggling, don’t rely on willpower; declare “I have been crucified with Christ”.
• Practice three: practise deliberately every day; when you fall, turn back at once, until it becomes habit and life.
• Three actions: stop, declare the verse, turn to Jesus.
• The 920 practice: live out selflessness before every “2” and bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23).
Closing and call
When the mindset changes, the life changes
When the life changes, daily living changes
Lay down “I can” and “I will”
Enter the faith of “I already am”
• Echo the lesson’s closing words and the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry.

• 1 Corinthians 15:57, “But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.”
• The call: let Jesus be King — I step down, he takes the throne, and all the glory goes to him.

I choose to believe what you have completed
Jesus, be King in my life
All glory to the Lord Jesus

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Our theme today is: from “I can” to “I already am.” This is the third lesson in the series “A Change of Mindset.” Our key verse is Galatians 2:20: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” Please notice: what Paul says is not “I will,” nor “I can,” but “I already am.”

Brothers and sisters, first let me tell you a true story. Hiroo Onoda, a second lieutenant in the Japanese army, was sent to Lubang Island in the Philippines during the Second World War. The war ended in 1945, but he didn’t believe it; he hid in the jungle and kept fighting. For how long? Twenty-nine years. Only in 1974, when his former commanding officer went in person to tell him, “The war is over,” did he come out. Brothers and sisters, he lacked neither courage nor effort; what he lacked was believing. Are we, too, still fighting a war that ended long ago?

Let’s look at the background. Galatians was written by Paul, very possibly his earliest letter, around AD 48. After he left, some people came into the churches saying: believing in Jesus is good, but you also have to be circumcised and keep the law. It sounds very devout, but it is deadly, because it quietly swaps the gospel from “Christ has already accomplished it” to “I still have to do something more.” Paul was outraged. He wrote chapter 2, verse 20, setting up a boundary stone for the freedom of the gospel.

Our first point: where faith begins is not works but believing. Galatians 2:16 says, “a man is not justified by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ.” In one sentence Paul says “not by the works of the law” three times, and three times he points to faith. He is driving in a stake. Brothers and sisters, our relationship with God is not built on “how much I have done” but on “whether I believe in Jesus.” A child adopted into a family doesn’t have to wash the dishes every day to earn his place on the family register. He washes the dishes because he already is a child of the family.

Our second point: the faith of “I already am.” “I have been crucified with Christ” — in Greek this is a perfect tense in the passive voice. The perfect tense means it is already done, and still in force today. The passive voice means it was not done by me. Brothers and sisters, the old self was not crucified by us; Jesus has already crucified it on our behalf. Romans 6:6 says, “knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him.” Notice: “knowing.” The first step to victory is not doing but knowing.

So the starting point for living out selflessness is not effort but three declarations of faith. The first: I have been crucified with Christ. The second: it is no longer I who live. The third: but Christ lives in me. Brothers and sisters, do you hear the difference? It isn’t that I must die, but that I have already died; it isn’t that I must live out Christ, but that Christ will live in me. The first is a burden; the second is rest. Someone asks: if the old self has already been crucified, why do I still lose my temper? Brothers and sisters, Scripture doesn’t say we no longer have weakness; it says sin is no longer master. Romans 6:14 says, “For sin will not have dominion over you.” It may knock at the door; it cannot give orders.

Our third point: a change of mindset is a process. The lesson says: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation. The 3-2-1 vision adds four more steps: Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. When you first hear it, it is only information; when the Holy Spirit shines his light, it becomes revelation; when you accept it inwardly, that is conviction; and then it must be put into practice in daily living. What if you fall? Repent once more and choose “I already am” afresh. In 1949 the neuropsychologist Donald Hebb proposed that neurons that fire together wire together. Repeated practice really does carve a new path inside us.

Our fourth point: measuring your faith. When temptation comes, it shows. If it is “I can” and “I will,” you will struggle, strive and suppress, find it exhausting, and still be swayed by the world. In 1987 the psychologist Daniel Wegner carried out the white bear experiment: people were told not to think of a white bear, and they ended up thinking of it even more. Colossians 2:23 says severity to the body is “not of any value against the indulgence of the flesh.” Brothers and sisters, the key is not “refusing sin” but turning to the salvation Jesus has already completed.

Our fifth point: the key to victory is not striving but believing. 1 John 5:4 says, “This is the victory that has overcome the world: your faith.” Not our effort, not our perseverance — our faith. When someone falls into water, the more they thrash, the more they sink; if they relax and lie back, the water holds them up. Brothers and sisters, the water is holding you up all the time, and grace is holding you up all the time. Colossians 1:13 says he “delivered us out of the power of darkness, and translated us into the Kingdom of the Son of his love.” It is all already accomplished.

Next come this week’s practices — three things. First, discern the state of your faith: when you meet difficulty today, ask yourself — was I just living by “I can,” “I will” or “I already am”? Second, replace “I must try harder” with “I already am”: when you are struggling, don’t wrestle; do three things — stop, declare, turn. Stop; declare, “I have been crucified with Christ”; then turn your eyes to Jesus. Third, practise every day: when you fall, turn back at once, and let it become habit and life.

Brothers and sisters, the lesson’s closing words put it beautifully: when the mindset changes, the life changes; when the life changes, daily living changes. This is exactly the fivefold change the 3-2-1 vision speaks of: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. This morning the Lord Jesus himself walks into your jungle and says to you: child, it is finished. The war is over. You can come out now. Let us lay down “I can” and “I will,” enter into the faith of “I already am,” let Jesus be King, and give all the glory to him.

Let us pray together. Lord, I no longer rely on my own effort; I choose to believe in the salvation you have already completed. I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. May your Holy Spirit carry these words from our heads into our hearts, and make them our daily living today. Reign as King in our lives, and may all the glory go to you. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. May the Lord bless and keep every brother and sister, so that today you live in the identity of those who have already overcome.

Brothers and sisters, good morning. Our theme today is from “I can” to “I already am,” the third lesson in the series “A Change of Mindset.” Our key verse is Galatians 2:20: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” Notice the verb Paul uses. He did not say “I will,” nor “I can.” What he said is — “I already am.”

Before we begin, please answer one question honestly: over this past year, what has been your most common feeling in your faith — lightness or weariness? I know a sister who has been a believer for twenty-two years. Every day she gets up at five to read the Bible and pray, and she serves in every part of her church. Yet one day she wept and said, “I’m so tired. I feel as if I’m climbing a mountain that never ends.” Brothers and sisters, it isn’t that we haven’t tried hard; we have tried too hard. The lesson puts it precisely: we get stuck not because we don’t try hard, but because our mindset has not changed. When the mindset is wrong, effort becomes a burden; when the mindset is right, life becomes light.

Let me tell you a true story from history. Hiroo Onoda, a second lieutenant in the Japanese army, was sent to Lubang Island in the Philippines. In 1945 the Second World War ended, but he didn’t believe it, so he hid in the jungle and kept fighting. For how long? Twenty-nine years. Only in 1974, when his former commanding officer flew there in person to relieve him of his mission, did he hand over his rusted sword. Brothers and sisters, the war had long been over, but because he didn’t believe it, he fought on for another twenty-nine years. Two thousand years ago the Lord Jesus cried out on the cross, “It is finished!” The war is over. Yet we are still in the jungle, wrestling every day with an old self that has already been crucified. Why? Because our mindset is still stuck at “I can” and “I will.”

First, the background. The author of Galatians is the apostle Paul; it may well be his earliest letter, written around AD 48 or 49, after his first missionary journey. It went to the churches of the Galatian region: Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe. After Paul left, a group of Judaizers came in and said: it’s good that you believe in Jesus, but you must also be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. That sounds very devout, but it is deadly — it quietly swaps the gospel from “Christ has already accomplished it” to “I still have to do something more.” Paul was outraged and wrote, “I marvel that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ.” Galatians 2:20 is the boundary stone he set up for the freedom of the gospel.

Our first point: where faith begins is not works but believing. Galatians 2:16 says, “a man is not justified by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ.” In one sentence, three times “not by the works of the law,” and three times faith. Paul isn’t being wordy; he is driving in a stake. The Greek word for “justify” is a courtroom term, meaning to declare righteous, not to make a person over. So justification is God’s verdict, not our report card. And he says no flesh will be justified by the works of the law — not that most people can’t manage it, but that not a single person can.

Someone will ask: so do works not matter? Of course they matter. But notice the order: works are the fruit of faith, not its root. Fruit grows on the tree; the tree does not grow on the fruit. Paul says, “Having begun in the Spirit, are you now completed in the flesh?” The way you came in is the way you must walk on. A child adopted into a family doesn’t have to wash the dishes every day to earn his place on the family register. In 1955 the psychologist Albert Ellis founded Rational Emotive Behaviour Therapy; he found that much of people’s anxiety comes not from events but from the absolute commands they lay on themselves: I must succeed, I mustn’t fail. Brothers and sisters, if selflessness has to be achieved by the strength of the self-centred life, it is nothing but legalism with a new programme.

Our second point: the faith of “I already am” is where selflessness begins. “I have been crucified with Christ” — in Greek it is a perfect tense in the passive voice. The perfect tense says: it is already done, and still in force today. The passive voice says: this was not something I did. Had it been active, I would have to find a way every day to nail myself up there — an endless self-torment. But it is passive: the old self was not crucified by me; Jesus has already crucified it on my behalf. Romans 6:6 says, “knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him.” Notice the word “knowing.” The first step to victory is not doing but knowing.

So the starting point for living out selflessness is not effort but a choice of faith, and it has three sentences. The first: I have been crucified with Christ. The second: it is no longer I who live. The third: but Christ lives in me. Shall we read them softly together once? Do you hear the difference? It isn’t that I must die, but that I have already died; it isn’t that I must live out Christ, but that Christ will live in me. The first is a burden; the second is rest. The 3-2-1 vision says: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering the limitless and living out the limitless. An empty cup is not empty for the sake of being empty; it is empty in order to be filled.

Someone asks: if the old self has already been crucified, why do I still lose my temper? Scripture doesn’t say we no longer have weakness; it says the power of sin has been broken. Romans 6:11 says, “Thus consider yourselves also to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord.” The word “consider” in Greek is an accounting term, meaning to reckon the account this way. God has already entered it this way; we must bring our ledger into line with his. When the books are right, daily living will come right. The next verses say, “For sin will not have dominion over you.” It may knock at the door; it cannot give orders.

Our third point: a change of mindset is a process. The lesson gives us four steps: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation. When you first hear “I already am,” it is only information, like an unopened letter; information cannot change people — otherwise libraries would long ago have become temples. When the Holy Spirit shines his light, information becomes revelation — and that is the third of the Three Foundations: the Holy Spirit is my guide. When something inside you truly yields, that is conviction. Then it must be put into practice in daily living. Two people both get up early to pray: one to earn God’s pleasure, the other because God is already pleased with him. On the outside they look the same; on the inside they are utterly different.

The 3-2-1 vision adds four more steps: Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Evaluation is praying like David: “Search me, God, and know my heart.” Accusation makes people hide; searching draws them near. Correction is confessing and turning back; the Greek word for repentance has at its root “a change of mind” — so the very essence of repentance is a change of mindset. Repetition is doing it again and again. In 1949 the neuropsychologist Donald Hebb proposed that neurons that fire together wire together. An old mindset is an old road walked for decades; a new mindset begins as a narrow track, but every time you walk it, it becomes a little clearer. Finally, Multiplication is passing it on to others — that is the 235 relationships of the 3-2-1 vision.

Our fourth point: how do we measure our faith? Ordinarily you can’t see it; the moment temptation comes, it is exposed. The faith of “I can” and “I will” has three marks: we struggle, strive and suppress; we find it exhausting; we are still swayed by the world. You clench your teeth so as not to look; you clench your fists so as not to speak; inside you are playing tug-of-war with yourself. On the surface you win a round, but inside you are already worn out. And the more you suppress it, the bigger the thing grows in your heart. Brothers and sisters, how many years have you lived like this?

This isn’t just a feeling; experiments confirm it. In 1987 the psychologist Daniel Wegner and his colleagues carried out the white bear experiment: people were asked not to think of a white bear for five minutes, and they ended up thinking of it more — and once the ban was lifted, they thought of it even more often. Scripture said it long ago: “These things indeed appear like wisdom in self-imposed worship, humility, and severity to the body; but aren’t of any value against the indulgence of the flesh.” The key is not “refusing sin” but turning to the salvation Jesus has already completed. With refusing sin, the focus is still on sin; with turning to Jesus, the focus is on Christ. What did Joseph do? “He left his garment in her hand, and ran outside.” He didn’t debate; he ran. The 3-2-1 vision says: the focus is Jesus — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances.

Let me tell another true story from history. On 1 January 1863, Lincoln’s Emancipation Proclamation took effect; in law, those slaves were already free. But the news was slow to reach Texas. Not until 19 June 1865, when General Granger publicly read out the order in Galveston, did the slaves of Texas learn that they had long been free. For two and a half years they were free men in law and still slaves in daily living, only because they didn’t know. Galatians 5:1 says, “Stand firm therefore in the liberty by which Christ has made us free.” In 1967 Seligman and Maier at the University of Pennsylvania put forward “learned helplessness”: after repeated failure, even when the door is opened, they no longer try. This morning the Lord Jesus walks into your jungle and says to you: child, the war is over. The door is open.

Our fifth point: the key to victory is not striving but believing. 1 John 5:4 says, “This is the victory that has overcome the world: your faith.” Not our effort, not our perseverance — our faith. “Has overcome” is in the past tense; the victory is already settled. The next verse says, “Who is he who overcomes the world, but he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?” The list of overcomers is not ranked by merit; it is drawn up by faith. Colossians 1:13 says he “delivered us out of the power of darkness, and translated us into the Kingdom of the Son of his love.” Delivered, translated — both already completed. Your citizenship now is not in the kingdom of darkness but in the kingdom of light.

Let me use a picture. When someone falls into water, the more they thrash, the more they sink; if they relax and lie back, the water holds them up. There’s a reason for this: the average density of an adult is slightly less than fresh water, so when relaxed with the lungs full of air a person can float, but struggling breaks the balance. Brothers and sisters, the water is holding you up all the time, and grace is holding you up all the time; the question is whether you are willing to believe. The Lord Jesus said, “He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit.” A branch doesn’t have to grit its teeth; it only has to stay connected. In 1545 Martin Luther recalled that as a young man he had hated “the righteousness of God,” but later understood it was the righteousness God gives, received by faith — and at that moment he felt himself altogether born again. The Reformation did not begin with a movement; it began with one man’s mindset being turned around.

Next come this week’s practices. Practice one: discern the state of your faith. Today, when you face difficulty or temptation, notice your reaction — is it “I can,” “I will” or “I already am”? Face the true condition of your faith honestly. Practice two: replace “I must try harder” with “I already am.” When you find yourself struggling, don’t fight with willpower any more; do three things — stop, declare, turn. Stop; declare, “I have been crucified with Christ”; then turn your eyes to Jesus. Please learn Galatians 2:20 by heart, because when temptation strikes it gives you only three seconds, and you won’t have time to look it up on your phone.

Practice three: practise the choice of faith every day. Deliberately practise the faith of “I already am”; even when you fall, turn back at once, so that this faith becomes habit and life. I especially want to point out three of the eight stages: Evaluation, Correction and Repetition. Most people who fail don’t fail because they refuse to put things into practice; they fail because after they fall, they never come back. Turning back is not starting to earn all over again; it is coming back again to “I already am.” I suggest you work in forty-day cycles; after forty days, take someone else through the same forty days — and that is the eighth stage, Multiplication.

Let us put today’s message back into the 3-2-1 vision. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — on the cross he said, “It is finished”; the Bible is my standard — when my feelings say, “You’re not enough yet,” the Bible says, “I have been crucified with Christ”; the Holy Spirit is my guide — he turns information into revelation. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — in someone who still says “I can,” the one sitting on the throne is really himself; let Jesus receive all the glory — since the victory is his accomplishment, the glory belongs wholly to him. The Goal: establish God’s system. Isaiah records five “I will”s in the heart of the fallen one. The grammar of pride is “I will”; the grammar of humility is “I already am.” So humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan; pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. And there is the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry — life first, then relationships, then ministry.

Brothers and sisters, this lesson today has really said only one thing: exchange “I can” and “I will” for “I already am.” The lesson’s closing words say: when the mindset changes, the life changes; when the life changes, daily living changes. This is not a slogan; it is a spiritual law, because your life will never rise above your mindset. Let me ask you one last time: in your jungle, is there a war that should have ended long ago? Is there a door that has already been opened, yet you refuse to walk out through it? Today the Lord Jesus himself walks into your jungle and says: child, it is finished. You can come out now. “But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.” He has already fought this battle to the end. All we need to do is believe, then walk out, and hand over that rusted sword.

Let us pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you. We confess that we have lived by “I can” for too long, and held ourselves up with “I will” for too long; we thought loving you meant trying harder, and the harder we tried, the further we got from rest. Forgive us for turning your grace into our project. This morning, by faith, we receive what you have already accomplished: I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. May the Holy Spirit carry these words from our heads into our hearts — from information into revelation, from revelation into conviction, and from conviction into our daily living. Help us, before everyone we meet today, to live out a selfless life and bear the fruit of the Spirit; no longer to wrestle with sin, but simply to turn to you. Reign as King in our lives, and may all the glory go to you. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. May the Lord bless and keep every brother and sister, so that today you live in the identity of those who have already overcome.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: One Sentence Can Turn a Whole Life Around
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Before we begin this morning’s reading, I want to ask you to be still for thirty seconds and answer one question in your heart: over this past year, what is the sentence you have said to yourself most often?

Some people say most often, “How have I failed again?” Some say, “I have to try harder.” Some say, “I can’t do it.” And some say, “I’ll deal with it once I’m a bit better.” These sentences sound very honest, very humble. But look closely and you’ll find they all share one subject — I. I fail, I try, I can’t, I get better. In the whole script of our life, the lead role is always played by “I.”

I once walked alongside a brother. He had believed in the Lord for more than ten years. He knew his Bible well and served faithfully, yet he was living in deep weariness. He told me, “Pastor, every morning when I get up, I first have to fight a battle with myself. I have to deal with my temper, my greed, my laziness, my envy. I’m like a man with a broom, sweeping every day in a house that will never be clean.” When I’d heard him out, I asked him one thing: “Brother, have you ever considered that the Lord Jesus finished this battle for you two thousand years ago?” He froze. “I know that,” he said. “Of course I know Jesus died for me.” I said, “You know it, but you don’t live this way. Your knowledge has stopped in your head. It hasn’t yet become your mindset.”

Brothers and sisters, that is exactly what we are going to talk about today. This is the fourth session in our series on the change of mindset. In the three sessions before it, we saw one thing again and again: change the mindset and you change the life, and change the life and you change the daily living. Today we want to follow that road to its deepest point — when the mindset changes, what changes is not only our thinking; the whole way our life operates is turned upside down.

The lesson puts it beautifully: “I have been crucified with Christ” is not a slogan but a truth that brings real change. There is a key word here, and I want you to remember it, because it is today’s key — “already.” Not “I will be,” not “I hope to be,” not “I’m trying hard to become,” but “I already have been.” Scripture speaks in the language of something completed, because this was accomplished on the cross. We are not striving for an identity we don’t yet have; we are believing a fact that is already ours.

When we truly choose to believe “I already have been,” life no longer stays stuck in struggle and effort; it enters a completely new way of living — no longer I, but Christ. This is the beginning of selflessness, and the starting point of a victorious life.

I love one illustration. A man bought a brand-new car, but he kept pushing it. He pushed until he was drenched in sweat, until his back ached. Every day he pushed it three kilometres to work, and he told people, “Driving is exhausting.” One day someone beside him asked, “Why don’t you start the engine?” He said, “The engine? I thought that was just for decoration.” Brothers and sisters, many Christians are just like that. The greatest power in the universe lives within us — the risen Christ — yet we are still pushing our life along with the strength of our own flesh. This morning, let’s learn together how to start the engine.

In the 321 vision there is a saying that captures this vividly: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of every problem. And selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the limitless and living out the limitless — “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. Today’s lesson is the entrance to the road of selflessness.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: How Galatians 2:20 Came to Be Written
sections.html:
To truly understand “no longer I,” we first have to go back to the scene where these words were spoken.

The author of Galatians is the apostle Paul. As to when it was written, evangelical scholars generally hold one of two views. If “Galatia” refers to the churches of South Galatia (Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe — the churches Paul founded on his first missionary journey), it was written around AD 48–49, possibly Paul’s earliest letter, before the Jerusalem Council. If it refers to North Galatia, it dates to around AD 53–55. Whichever view we take, one thing is clear: this letter was written in great haste and with great weight, because the very foundation of the gospel was being shaken.

What was happening? A group of people known as the “Judaizers” had come into the Galatian churches, teaching: believing in Jesus is good, but it isn’t enough; if Gentiles are to become God’s people for real, they must be circumcised and must keep the law of Moses. In other words, on top of “justification by faith” they added “plus works.” It sounds very devout, but it is deadly. Because the moment you add anything at all to the gospel, the focus shifts from Christ back to ourselves — Have I done it? Am I good enough? Am I keeping it well?

Paul was furious. In this letter he doesn’t begin, as he usually does, by commending the church he is writing to. He says straight out, “I marvel that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ to a different ‘good news’” (Galatians 1:6). Then he spends two chapters on his own testimony: his gospel was not received from man but came by revelation from Jesus Christ. He also tells how, in Antioch, he opposed Cephas (that is, Peter) to his face, because Peter, afraid of the circumcision party, had drawn back and separated himself from the Gentile believers.

Galatians 2:20 is the concluding sentence of that whole argument. Paul first says, “For I, through the law, died to the law, that I might live to God” (Galatians 2:19). Then comes the declaration that has shaken the church through every age: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.”

Notice that these words were not originally a quiet devotional meditation; they were a banner raised in the middle of a theological war. Paul is saying: you want me to become a child of God by relying on the law, on circumcision, on my own effort? No need. The “I” that wanted to rely on itself is already dead — it has already been nailed to the cross. The one who lives now is Christ.

Let’s also look at the force of the original. “I have been crucified with Christ” — the Greek uses the perfect tense (συνεσταύρωμαι). The perfect tense means an action completed in the past that brings an effect continuing into the present. It is like someone who has had a heart transplant: the operation was completed in the past, but the new heart is still beating today. So Paul isn’t saying, “Every day I try hard to nail myself up there.” He is saying, “I have already been nailed there, and that is still in effect today.”

Another key word is “live.” “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” — here “in me” (ἐν ἐμοί) tells us that the life of Christ is at work inside this person that I am. He isn’t standing beside me cheering me on; he has moved in and become the source of my life.

The third key word is in the second half of the verse: “That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God.” The original’s “by faith” shows that the one and only channel by which we draw on this life is faith. Christ has already moved in, but whether we live by that fact each day depends on whether we believe it.

So the whole verse has three layers. The first is the fact — I have been crucified with Christ. The second is the identity — it is no longer I who live. The third is the method — I live by faith in the Son of God. Today’s five key points unfold step by step along these three layers.

One more piece of background is worth mentioning. In Roman times the cross was no ornament. It was the most shameful, most brutal instrument of execution, reserved for slaves, rebels and the lowest criminals. Roman citizens were, in principle, exempt from it. So when Paul said, “I have been crucified with Christ,” it would have grated on first-century ears — it was the same as saying: by the world’s system of values, I have been sentenced to death; I am out of the game. And the paradox is this: it was precisely this sentence of being “out” that opened up the freest, most powerful life of all.

sections.heading: 3. Choose “I Already Have Been,” and Life Changes Naturally
sections.html:
The lesson’s first key point says this: when we choose to believe “I have been crucified with Christ,” the standard by which we live changes.

No longer “How do I get better?” or “How do I overcome?” but “It is no longer I who live” and “Christ lives in me.” This is a change of identity, and it is also a change in the way we live. We no longer strain to be justified by the law; we live in grace by faith.

As Scripture says, “Thus consider yourselves also to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 6:11).

Brothers and sisters, notice the most important word in this verse: “consider.” In the original it is a bookkeeping term (λογίζεσθε), meaning “to enter it in the account,” “to reckon it at this figure.” This is the language of accounting. An accountant doesn’t keep the books by feel; he records the facts. On the cross God has already settled the account, and now he says to us: keep your books according to this fact — reckon yourself dead to sin and alive to God.

There is an order here, and it’s crucial — don’t get it backwards. It isn’t that I first feel I’m dead and then believe it. It’s that I first believe this is the fact, and then my feelings slowly catch up. Fact first, faith in the middle, feelings last. So much of the chaos in life comes from turning that order upside down: we let our feelings decide whether we believe, and let our feelings decide whether God loves us.

There’s a very fitting example. After a war had ended, the defeated nation had signed its surrender, and the war was legally over. But deep in the jungle there were soldiers who didn’t know. They went on fighting, went on hiding, went on with the battle for years. Their suffering was real, but their war no longer existed. What they lacked was not courage but information. Brothers and sisters, Satan’s greatest trick is to make people who have already overcome go on living by the identity of the defeated. He cannot change the fact of the cross; all he can do is deceive you into not keeping your books by the facts.

Psychology offers us good corroborating evidence here. In the 1960s Aaron T. Beck (1921–2021), a psychiatrist at the University of Pennsylvania, developed cognitive behavioural therapy. His central discovery was that our emotions and behaviour are not determined directly by events, but by our “cognitions” of those events and our “automatic thoughts.” Change the core beliefs, and emotions and behaviour change with them. This echoes Scripture exactly: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind” (Romans 12:2). Only Scripture goes further than psychology — psychology helps us replace mistaken thoughts, but the gospel replaces the whole “I.”

Brain science encourages us too. The research of Eric Kandel, winner of the 2000 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, showed that learning and memory change the synaptic connections between neurons — in other words, the brain is plastic. Eleanor Maguire’s team at University College London published a study in 2000 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, finding that London taxi drivers, after years of memorising a complex road network, had greater grey-matter volume in the posterior hippocampus than a control group. Brothers and sisters, if even memorising roads can change the structure of a person’s brain, how could the life of someone who keeps his books every day by “I have been crucified with Christ” possibly stay unchanged?

In the 321 vision, this is the starting point of the five-fold change: mindset → life → daily living → relationships → ministry. Mindset is the first domino. Many people try to start changing from “daily living,” so they draw up a pile of plans and make a pile of resolutions, and they can’t keep them going for even three months. They pushed the wrong domino. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change the daily living. If you take away only one thing this morning, take this: stop asking, “How do I get better?” and start saying, “I already have been.”

When the mindset changes, our feelings, attitudes and reactions all begin to change. This isn’t self-hypnosis; it’s living according to the facts God has spoken.

sections.heading: 4. Gaining Christ: Finding Your True Self
sections.html:
The lesson’s second key point says: “No longer I, but Christ” is not losing yourself; it is finding your true self.

We need to pay special attention to this, because many people are frightened when they hear the word selflessness. They think Christianity wants to wipe out our personality and turn us into soulless tools. Not at all. The 321 vision says it plainly: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the limitless and living out the limitless.

Let me use an illustration. Leave a drop of water on a table, and within an hour it has dried up. Put that same drop into the ocean, and it will never dry up. What did it lose? It lost the fragility of existing on its own. What did it gain? It gained the vastness of the whole ocean. That is selflessness. Not being swallowed up, but being enlarged.

When we are selfless, Christ becomes our everything: his life becomes my life; his wisdom becomes my wisdom; his power becomes my power.

This is what Ephesians says: “and what is the exceeding greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to that working of the strength of his might which he worked in Christ, when he raised him from the dead and made him to sit at his right hand in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 1:19–20).

Brothers and sisters, look carefully at what Paul uses to measure the size of this power. He doesn’t say “as great as a mighty wind,” or “as great as the ocean waves.” He says: the measure of this power is the very might and strength that raised Jesus from the dead and seated him at God’s right hand in the heavens. In other words, the power God measures out to us who believe is “resurrection-grade” power. This is one of the boldest sentences in the whole Bible. Here Paul piles up four words for power one after another (δύναμις power, ἐνέργεια working, κράτος might, ἰσχύς strength), as though language were no longer enough and he had to heap every word he had on top of each other.

Why, then, do we so often not feel it? Because we are still living on the budget of “I.” If a man has ten million in the bank but thinks he only has a thousand, he’ll still live like a poor man. What we lack is not power; what we lack is the right mindset about that power.

We are no longer limited by our own limitations, because the “self” has been crucified. When we face weakness, we no longer say, “I can’t do it.” Instead we declare: I have been crucified with Christ; the one who lives now is Christ.

Someone may ask, “So am I allowed to admit I’m weak?” Of course — and you should. Paul himself says, “He has said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.’ Most gladly therefore I will rather glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may rest on me” (2 Corinthians 12:9). Brothers and sisters, where is the difference? “I can’t do it” is a full stop: once you’ve said it, you stay right there. “I can’t, but Christ in me can” is a comma: once you’ve said it, you keep going. The first makes us smaller; the second lets us be filled.

In the nineteenth century Hudson Taylor (1832–1905), founder of the China Inland Mission, went through a season of deep spiritual dryness in mid-life. He found that the harder he pursued holiness, the more he felt himself failing. In 1869, in a letter to his sister, he described the light he had received: he had finally seen that it was not for him to strive harder to lay hold of Christ, but that Christ already lived in him, united with him. His son and daughter-in-law later called this “the exchanged life” in their book Hudson Taylor’s Spiritual Secret. From then on his service was no longer a matter of grimly holding on, but of overflowing. Brothers and sisters, what we need today is exactly this discovery.

Self-determination theory in psychology offers further corroboration. Research put forward since the 1980s by Edward Deci and Richard Ryan of the University of Rochester shows that a person’s truly lasting motivation comes from intrinsic motivation, not from outside pressure, rewards and punishments. Whatever we force ourselves through with “I absolutely must get this done” won’t last; only what wells up naturally from within can go the distance. The gospel moves our motivation from the outside to the inside — from law to life.

This is what 321 means when it says Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. When the focus is right, we stop asking, “How much do I have?” and start asking, “How much does he have?” That brings tremendous release and hope.

sections.heading: 5. True Satisfaction: Not Living for Ourselves
sections.html:
The lesson’s third key point says: when it is “no longer I,” the focus of our daily living changes as well. We no longer live for ourselves; we live for Christ.

We no longer ask, “What do I want?” but “What is the Lord’s heart in this?” A life like that may look as though it has lost its freedom, but in fact it has entered true freedom.

Why? Because if we live for ourselves, we will end up in nothing but emptiness: “‘Vanity of vanities,’ says the Preacher; ‘Vanity of vanities, all is vanity’” (Ecclesiastes 1:2).

Brothers and sisters, the Hebrew word for “vanity” in this verse is הֶבֶל (hevel), whose root meaning is “breath, vapour, mist.” Breathe out on a cold morning and you can see a little white cloud; reach out to grab it and there is nothing to hold. When Solomon uses this word, he isn’t saying life has no value. He’s saying: apart from God, nothing under the sun can be held on to. He goes on: “I have seen all the works that are done under the sun; and behold, all is vanity and a chasing after wind” (Ecclesiastes 1:14). “Chasing after wind” — what a vivid picture. Someone who lives for himself spends his whole life chasing a gust of wind.

Solomon is the person best qualified to say this. He had wisdom, wealth, great building works, parks and gardens, men and women singers, every kind of pleasure. In Ecclesiastes 2 he tried them all one by one, and his conclusion was: chasing wind. Very few people in this world have ever taken “living for yourself” as far as he did, and very few have told us the outcome as honestly as he did.

What alternative does Scripture give us? “He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again” (2 Corinthians 5:15). Notice the logic of this verse: Christ died for me, therefore I no longer live for myself. It is a response of love, not moral blackmail.

Here I need to draw a very important distinction. “Not living for yourself” does not mean “not taking care of yourself,” and it doesn’t mean becoming someone with no boundaries who lets others use them up. Jesus himself withdrew into the wilderness to pray, and went up the mountain to rest. “Not living for yourself” means this: my life no longer has me at its centre. Change the centre of the circle, and every radius changes with it.

On this point, modern psychology has, surprisingly, come down on the Bible’s side. In 2008 Elizabeth Dunn, Lara Aknin and Michael Norton published a study in Science, finding that people who spent money on others felt happier than people who spent the same money on themselves. The Harvard Study of Adult Development, which began following its participants in 1938, is one of the longest studies of adult life ever conducted. Its current director, Robert Waldinger, points out that over the long run, the biggest factor in keeping people healthy and happy is not wealth, not fame, but good relationships.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the order 321 teaches: life first, then relationships, then ministry; people matter more than tasks, relationships matter more than things. And the priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Someone who lives for himself will always turn that order upside down — he chases things first, then people, and only last of all thinks of God. The result: the task gets done, the people are lost, and God is far away.

At the opening of his Confessions, the church father Augustine wrote a line that has been repeated for over a thousand years: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” This is not a deduction of psychology; it is the personal confession of a prodigal who has come home.

So what does a person who lives for the Lord gain? The lesson puts it well: the Lord’s satisfaction is my satisfaction; the Lord’s joy is my joy. Jesus himself lived this way: “Jesus said to them, ‘My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work’” (John 4:34). Brothers and sisters, have you noticed that Jesus calls doing the Father’s will his “food”? Not his job, not his duty — his nourishment. When someone truly reaches this place, obedience is no longer pressure; it is delight.

The psalmist says too: “You will show me the path of life. In your presence is fullness of joy. In your right hand there are pleasures forever more” (Psalm 16:11). True satisfaction is not found in “getting what I want,” but in being “in his presence.” This is the true meaning of life.

This is also the shift of perspective that 321 talks about: from the human to the divine; from the earthly to the heavenly; from the temporary to the eternal; from the worldly to the godly. Once our perspective shifts, our whole definition of what is “worth it” shifts too. We used to ask, “What will I get out of doing this?” Now we ask, “What glory will the Lord’s name receive if I do this?”

sections.heading: 6. Living Out Christ: The Most Powerful Witness
sections.html:
The lesson’s fourth key point says: when Christ lives himself out through us, people will see Jesus. This doesn’t depend on eloquence; it depends on life.

Jesus said, “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself” (John 12:32).

The context of this verse is precious. Some Greeks had come up to the feast, and they said to Philip, “Sir, we want to see Jesus” (John 12:21). Philip went and told Andrew, and the two of them went together and told Jesus. Jesus’ answer was unusual. He didn’t go straight out to meet them. Instead he said, “The time has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.” Then he spoke these words: “Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). Only then did he say, “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.” And John adds an explanation: “But he said this, signifying by what kind of death he should die” (John 12:33).

Brothers and sisters, look at the sequence: someone wants to see Jesus → a grain of wheat must die → if I am lifted up, I will draw all people. So the key to people seeing Jesus is “dying” and “being lifted up.” And this sequence is our sequence too. When the “I” falls into the ground and dies, Christ is lifted up in me; when Christ is lifted up, people are drawn.

We so often get the direction wrong. We work hard to lift up the “I” — to lift up my eloquence, my knowledge, my achievements, how dramatic my testimony is — and what people end up seeing is us, not Jesus. John the Baptist had the right attitude: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

The lesson gives a wonderful example: Peter and John in the early church were unschooled men, yet when people saw them, they recognised that they had been with Jesus. This is how Scripture records it: “Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and had perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marveled. They recognized that they had been with Jesus” (Acts 4:13).

Notice that act of “recognising.” The members of the Council weren’t listening to how many verses they could recite; they “recognised” the likeness of Jesus in them. What did that look like? It was the boldness and composure of men who, even under threat, could still say, “for we can’t help telling the things which we saw and heard” (Acts 4:20). Brothers and sisters, people may doubt your arguments, but it’s very hard for them to doubt your life.

Brain science offers an interesting piece of corroboration. In the 1990s Giacomo Rizzolatti’s team at the University of Parma discovered mirror neurons in the brains of macaque monkeys — when a monkey watches another perform an action, the neurons in its own brain responsible for that action fire as well. Later research has linked this to imitation and empathy in human beings. In 1977 Albert Bandura (1925–2021) of Stanford University put forward social learning theory, showing that a great deal of human behaviour is learned by observing role models, not by being lectured. Brothers and sisters, when God made us, he placed “seeing, then learning” inside us. So the most effective way the gospel has ever been passed on is not by debate, but through a life that can be seen.

This is the first of 321’s Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model. And when Christ lives himself out through us, we too become role models others can see — not in our own likeness, but in the likeness of Christ. This is also the spirit of the 920 practice: everyone connected to us is our “2,” and before them we practise living out the selfless “0,” bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). Brothers and sisters, your colleague doesn’t read the Bible every day, but he reads you every day. That is the most powerful gospel there is.

sections.heading: 7. Faith Plus Obedience: Letting the Light Shine Out
sections.html:
The lesson’s fifth key point says: with faith alone and no action, people cannot see Jesus; but when faith is joined with obedience, life begins to shine.

Jesus said, “Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16).

Brothers and sisters, pay special attention to the second half of this verse. When it’s quoted, people often stop at “good works,” but the Chinese Union Version goes on with the most crucial line of all: “and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” The purpose of shining is not to make people see us, but to make people give the glory to God. This is the second of 321’s Two Core Values: let Jesus receive all the glory. If people see our good works and end up praising us, the light is shining in the wrong direction.

James says, “Even so faith, if it has no works, is dead in itself” (James 2:17). Faith and obedience are not two things; they are two sides of one thing. Real faith always walks out into action. A faith that never walks out isn’t faith — it’s an opinion.

The lesson reminds us: many people work hard at fighting the darkness, and the more they fight it, the more exhausted they become. In fact the way is very simple — you don’t need to chase the darkness away; you only need to shine.

That statement holds up completely in physics. Darkness is not a substance; darkness is the absence of light. You can’t carry a bucket of darkness and pour it into a bright room, but you can carry a candle into a dark room. The speed of light is 299,792,458 metres per second — the fixed value by which the International System of Units defines it. The instant you switch on a lamp, the darkness in the room has no “time to escape.” It simply ceases to exist.

Scripture begins exactly this way: “God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light” (Genesis 1:3). God didn’t deal with the darkness first; he simply said, Let there be light. John says too: “This is the message which we have heard from him and announce to you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all” (1 John 1:5). Jesus said, “I am the light of the world. He who follows me will not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8:12). And to us he says, “You are the light of the world. A city located on a hill can’t be hidden” (Matthew 5:14).

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to this order: Jesus is the light, and we are the light. Our light is reflected light, like the moon’s. The moon gives off no light of its own; it simply doesn’t block the sun. So the secret of our shining is not burning ourselves brighter, but not standing in Christ’s way.

Nature gives us another wonderful example. A firefly’s bioluminescence is a “cold light” that gives off almost no heat, and it converts energy with remarkable efficiency, far beyond a traditional incandescent bulb. One tiny firefly needs no blazing fire to be seen on a summer night. Brothers and sisters, you don’t need to become a sun. You only need to glow quietly in the corner where you are.

So how do we actually do it? The key lies in the word “obedience.” Obedience is the step that puts faith into action. In the 321 vision this is called “Implementation” — the fourth of the eight stages of changing our mindset. Many people get stuck at the third stage, “Conviction,” and go no further; they feel they already understand it all. But understanding the truth doesn’t mean the life has changed.

Phillippa Lally’s team at University College London published a study in 2010 in the European Journal of Social Psychology, finding that for a new behaviour to become an automatic habit, participants needed sixty-six days on average, with individual differences ranging from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days. That gives us two reminders. First, don’t assume that if you’ve obeyed for three days and felt nothing, you’ve failed. Second, don’t assume that once you’ve heard a message, your life will change automatically. You have to repeat it, and keep at it.

When we live out Christ, darkness naturally retreats. It isn’t that we drive the darkness away; it’s that the light of Christ shines out from within us.

sections.heading: 8. Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set today’s five key points back into the 321 framework and look at them once more.

The Three Foundations. Jesus is my role model — he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7); this is the most perfect demonstration of “no longer I.” The Bible is my standard — we keep our books according to Romans 6:11, not according to our feelings. The Holy Spirit is my guide — Christ living in me is accomplished through the Holy Spirit who dwells within us.

The Two Core Values. Let Jesus be King — the positive way of saying “no longer I” is “let Christ reign as King.” There is only one throne: if he isn’t sitting on it, I am. Let Jesus receive all the glory — which is why the purpose of our shining is that people may give the glory to the Father in heaven (Matthew 5:16).

The Goal: establish God’s system. Only a selfless person can work together with others; only a company of selfless people together can establish God’s system. When self-centred people gather, all they do is compete with one another: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

Here I want to say a little more clearly what the “self” is. 321 says: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. So “no longer I” is not self-belittling; it is returning to our originally intended position. A soldier returning to his post hasn’t failed; everyone is simply in their proper place. Once a person is willing to let God be God, he can at last be at peace being human. What a tremendous release that is.

Look again at the five-fold change: mindset → life → daily living → relationships → ministry. Today’s first key point is “mindset”; the second is “life” — Christ becomes my life; the third is “daily living” — no longer living for ourselves; the fourth is “relationships” — people recognise Jesus in us; the fifth is “ministry” — faith plus obedience, and the light shines out. Brothers and sisters, do you see it? The five key points of this lesson are precisely 321’s five-fold change, in exactly the same order. That’s no coincidence; it is the order Scripture itself has always had.

Then there are the 235 relationships. Become a “2” with a selfless person — do you have a spiritual companion beside you, someone with whom you can speak the truth to each other? Build your “3” — do you have spiritual parents, and are you walking alongside spiritual children? Become part of a “5” — are you working together with brothers and sisters of the fivefold ministry, as a team of spiritual comrades? Brothers and sisters, if “no longer I” stays only in private meditation, it will slowly dry up; put it into relationships, and it comes alive.

Finally, the Path of Serving: Spirit → Understanding → Life → Service → God. The Holy Spirit is my guide (Spirit), the Bible is my standard (Understanding), Jesus is my role model (Life), let Jesus be King (Service), let Jesus receive all the glory (God). Today’s lesson is really a walk through all five steps.

And there’s one more 321 reminder that fits today perfectly: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. For “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

sections.heading: 9. Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. We’ll keep all three, and deepen them with the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — so that they truly take root.

Practice 1: Live by your new identity

Remind yourself every day, “It is no longer I who live,” and in every decision learn to respond from the standpoint of “Christ lives in me.”

Information: Copy Galatians 2:20 and Romans 6:11 onto a card and put it somewhere you’re sure to see it every day — beside the mirror, in the car, as your phone wallpaper.

Revelation: Be still for three minutes each morning and ask the Holy Spirit to turn this verse from knowledge into sight. Pray, “Lord, let me truly see today that the ‘I’ who wanted to rely on myself is already dead.”

Conviction: Say it out loud to yourself. Not self-hypnosis, but keeping the books according to God’s word: “I have been crucified with Christ. This is a fact, not a feeling.”

Implementation: Choose one very concrete situation. For example, the moment today when someone makes you angry, pause for three seconds and say in your heart, “It is no longer I who live.” Only then open your mouth.

Evaluation: In the evening, take thirty seconds to look back — how many times today did I react out of “I”? How many times did I let Christ react?

Correction: Identify the time of day, or the kind of person, where you are most likely to give ground, and prepare especially for it tomorrow.

Repetition: Keep it up for at least sixty-six days. Remember, forming a habit takes sixty-six days on average.

Multiplication: Find a brother or sister, share your experience with them, and invite them to practise with you.

Practice 2: Turn from satisfying yourself to satisfying the Lord

In everyday choices, deliberately ask, “Is this what I want, or what pleases the Lord?” Practise finding your satisfaction in the Lord’s heart.

Information: Memorise 2 Corinthians 5:15 and John 4:34.

Revelation: Ask the Lord to show you where the centre of your life’s circle is right now. Be honest with this one; don’t rush to give a spiritual answer.

Conviction: Admit that “living for myself is chasing wind.” This isn’t low self-esteem; it’s waking up.

Implementation: Each day, pick one small decision and deliberately ask that question: “Is this what I want, or what pleases the Lord?” Start with small things — how will I use my time today? Should I say this or not? How will I spend this money?

Evaluation: At the end of the week, notice which kinds of things you find hardest to let go of: is it time? Money? Face?

Correction: Take the hardest of these on its own before the Lord in prayer, and ask him to reign as King in that very thing.

Repetition: Let this question become a reflex.

Multiplication: Share your week’s practice with one another in your small group, and let this question become the common language of the fellowship.

Practice 3: Bear witness to Jesus with your life

Don’t only share the gospel with your mouth; live out Christ in your daily living, so that people see Jesus in your reactions, your attitudes and your love.

Information: Memorise the whole of Matthew 5:16, especially its last line: and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

Revelation: Ask the Lord to show you which fruit of Christ the three people around you who don’t yet believe most need to see in you.

Conviction: Believe that the witness of a life is more powerful than eloquence; believe the law of “the grain of wheat.”

Implementation: This week, do one practical thing for each of those three people — a phone call, a meal, a helping hand, an apology.

Evaluation: Did they come to know a little more of Jesus because of it? When I did it, was my heart set on my own image, or on the Lord’s name?

Correction: If your motives weren’t pure, there’s no need to condemn yourself. Simply return to your originally intended position and set your focus right again.

Repetition: Put these three people on your prayer list and keep bringing them before the Lord over the long haul.

Multiplication: When one day they come to believe in the Lord, take them along to do the same for three others. That is spiritual multiplication.

A Gentle Reminder

It isn’t about trying hard to shine; it’s about letting Christ live himself out through you.

sections.heading: 10. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, we are nearly at the end. Let’s walk today’s road once more.

Once the mindset changes, life begins to turn around. From “I’m trying hard” into “the Lord is alive”; from “living for myself” into “living for the Lord.” When we live like this, the light shines out naturally, and revival begins with us.

I want to say one thing in particular: revival does not begin with a meeting; revival begins with a person — one person who truly believes “I already have been.” It has been this way in every generation. When one person gives up the throne, God’s power has a channel.

So this morning I want to invite you to make a decision that is very simple, yet very deep. Not a decision to try harder, but a decision to believe. Not a decision to do more, but a decision to step aside.

Please answer three questions in your heart:

First, in what area am I still saying, “How do I get better?” Exchange it for “I already have been.”

Second, who is at the centre of my life’s circle right now? Give that place back to the Lord.

Third, who around me is waiting to see Jesus in me? Hold his or her name in your heart.

May we enter together into this kind of daily living: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. May we no longer be the one who sweeps every day and never gets the house clean, but the one who switches on the light. For the one we believe in is Jesus, “who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame” (Hebrews 12:2). He has already walked this road to the end for us.

No longer I, but Christ. May these words today be not just our slogan, but our daily living.

keyVerses: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)
declarations: Lord, I choose to believe: I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me! Let my life be your witness, so that people see you in me!
practices: Turn from satisfying yourself to satisfying the Lord
Bear witness to Jesus with your life
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

Thank you that on the cross you have already put to death the old self that wanted to rely on itself. Lord, I confess that I still often live by my old identity, struggling every day in my own strength. This morning I choose to believe the fact you have spoken: I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.

Lord, please take back the throne. One by one I place into your hands my plans, my wants, my face, my fears. Holy Spirit, guide me, so that I rely on the heart and on you, not on the brain and on myself. Let your resurrection power work within me, so that I no longer say, “I can’t do it,” but say, “Christ in me can.”

And make my life a lamp — not so that people will see me, but so that they will give the glory to you. Let the people around me recognise, from my reactions, my attitudes and my love, that I have been with Jesus.
Reign as King in my home, reign as King in my workplace, reign as King in my heart. May all the glory be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “Thus consider yourselves also to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord.” (Romans 6:11) In your life right now, what specific situation makes it hardest for you to “consider yourself dead”? If you kept your books today by “I already have been,” how would your reactions be different?

“Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 5:16) Name one person who is watching your daily living. What one concrete thing could you do this week so that what he or she sees in you is not you, but Jesus?
l102.title: No Longer I
l102.subtitle: A Change of Mindset (Part 4)
l102.partTitle: Unit 7 · The Journey to Selflessness — Denying of Self

blog.title: No Longer I

blocks.x: The Sentence You Say to Yourself Most Is Shaping Your Life
Over this past year, what is the sentence you have said to yourself most often?
“How have I failed again?” “I have to try harder.” “I can’t do it.” “I’ll deal with it once I’m a bit better.”
These sentences sound very honest, very humble. But look closely and you’ll find they all share one subject — I. In the whole script of our life, the lead role is always played by “I.”

I once walked alongside a brother. He had believed in the Lord for more than ten years and served faithfully, yet he was living in deep weariness. He told me, “Every morning when I get up, I first have to fight a battle with myself. I’m like a man with a broom, sweeping every day in a house that will never be clean.” I asked him, “Did you know the Lord Jesus finished this battle for you two thousand years ago?” “I know that,” he said. I said, “You know it, but you don’t live this way.”
The key is not “I will” but “I already have been”

Paul spoke words that have shaken the church through every age: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20).
Notice those words: I have been.

Not “I will be,” not “I hope to be,” but “I already have been.” The Greek uses the perfect tense — an action completed in the past that brings an effect continuing into the present. It is like someone who has had a heart transplant: the operation was completed in the past, but the new heart is still beating today.

That is why Paul says in Romans 6:11 that we are to “consider” ourselves dead to sin but alive to God in Christ Jesus. In the original, “consider” is a bookkeeping term. An accountant doesn’t keep the books by feel; he records the facts. On the cross God has already settled the account; all we have to do is keep our books according to that fact.
Whatever you do, don’t get the order backwards: fact first, faith in the middle, feelings last.

Here is a very fitting picture: a war had long since ended and the surrender had been signed, yet deep in the jungle there were soldiers who didn’t know, and they went on fighting for years. Their suffering was real, but their war no longer existed. What they lacked was not courage but information. Satan cannot change the fact of the cross; all he can do is get you to stop keeping your books by the facts.
You Don’t Need to Chase the Darkness Away — Just Shine

When the mindset changes, the focus changes. We used to ask, “What do I want?” Now we ask, “What is the Lord’s heart in this?” We used to work hard at fighting the darkness, and the more we fought it, the more exhausted we became. Now we discover the way is astonishingly simple — you don’t need to chase the darkness away; you only need to shine.

That holds up completely in physics. Darkness is not a substance; darkness is simply the absence of light. You can’t carry a bucket of darkness and pour it into a bright room, but you can carry a candle into a dark room.
Jesus said, “Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16).

Notice that last line. The purpose of shining is not to make people see us, but to make people give the glory to God. Our light is reflected light, like the moon’s — the moon gives off no light of its own; it simply doesn’t block the sun. So the secret of our shining is not burning ourselves brighter, but not standing in Christ’s way.

The early church is the best example. Peter and John were unschooled, ordinary men, yet the members of the Council recognised that they had been with Jesus (Acts 4:13). Your colleague may not read the Bible, but he reads you every day.

So how can you begin today? First, before every decision, say in your heart, “It is no longer I who live.” Second, in the small choices of everyday life, deliberately ask, “Is this what I want, or what pleases the Lord?” Third, do one practical thing for each of three people around you who don’t yet believe in the Lord.

Don’t give up because you’ve felt nothing after three days. A 2010 study by Phillippa Lally’s team at University College London found that for a new behaviour to become an automatic habit takes sixty-six days on average.
Once the mindset changes, life begins to turn around. Revival does not begin with a meeting; revival begins with a person — one person who truly believes “I already have been.”
It isn’t about trying hard to shine; it’s about letting Christ live himself out through you.
Reflection Question
In your life right now, in what area are you still saying, “How do I get better?” If today you exchanged it for “I have been crucified with Christ,” how would your reactions be different?
