blog.title: Why Are Those Thirty Metres So Far?

blocks.x: One sentence, one narrow lane — and seeing which system you’re living in

Two cars meet in a narrow lane. Forward, neither can get through; backward, one of them would only have to reverse thirty metres. Neither driver budges. They lean on their horns and glare at each other. Ten minutes pass, a long line of cars builds up behind them, and everyone ends up late together.

If just one of them were willing to reverse first, it would all be sorted in thirty seconds. But those thirty metres feel longer than three kilometres — because it isn’t a question of distance. It’s a question of “who bows his head first.”
It Isn’t the Thing That Makes You Suffer

Last night her husband said only one sentence: “You really haven’t thought this through.” It was no big thing, but that sentence was like a small thorn lodged in her heart, and all night long she couldn’t pull it out.

We often think it’s the “thing” that makes us suffer. It isn’t. If that very same sentence had come from an older person you deeply respected, you might simply smile and say, “Thank you for the reminder.” The same sentence, falling into different hearts, bears completely different fruit.
What truly sets the course of our lives has never been the size of the matter. It is the “system” we use to face the matter.
There’s a very simple test: is my life growing more joyful, or more painful? Is my service growing lighter, or more exhausting?

Live in the system of the self-centred life, and the more you serve, the more tired you get; the more you do, the more you compare; and you grow ever drier. Live in the system of selflessness, and the more you serve, the more joyful you become; the more you live, the freer you are; and your life grows ever richer.

The Sea of Galilee and the Dead Sea are both fed by the Jordan River. The Sea of Galilee has an outlet; its water flows on downstream, so it has fish and life. The Dead Sea only takes in and never gives out; its salt content runs above thirty per cent, and almost nothing can live in it. A life that only wants to be loved and won’t go and love will in the end become a Dead Sea, however much truth it soaks up.
Pride Clings; Humility Lets Go
The nature of pride is clinging to self: clinging to our rights, clinging to face, clinging to our own ideas. The result is strained relationships, inner pressure and a life gone dry.

Pride often isn’t swaggering at all; it’s quiet — it’s the insistence that “I can’t give way here,” the injured “Why should I be the one to apologise first?” What pride does best is dress itself up as principle.
The nature of humility is letting go of self: letting go of our rights, letting go of face, letting go of control. The result is restored relationships, a heart set free and a life that grows.

Scripture’s fullest picture of humility is the Lord Jesus himself: “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.” (Philippians 2:6–7) He was entitled, and yet he did not cling. That is humility at its deepest: being entitled, and not clinging.
So humility isn’t weakness. When someone who has nothing lets go, that’s having no choice; when someone who has everything lets go, that is humility.
Three Sentences You Can Say Today
Humility isn’t abstract; it is three very concrete sentences.
The first: I will listen to you. Set aside your own opinion, and let God speak to you through people.
The second: I will take care of you. Move from “You must love me” to “I will love you.”
The third: I will change myself to fit you. Stop demanding that others change, and adjust yourself first.

When we choose like this, we enter a cycle: we humble ourselves, and God gives grace; with grace we have more strength; and the stronger we become, the more we know that strength isn’t our own, so we grow humbler still. On the other hand, pride is resisted by God; being resisted, we struggle all the more; and the more we struggle, the prouder we become.
“For ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’” (1 Peter 5:5)
Some people find life growing lighter the longer they live, while for others it grows harder and harder. The difference isn’t ability; it is choice.
Humility is not just a virtue; it is a way of life. When you let go of yourself, Jesus begins to live himself out in you.

Reflection: In the relationship that is tightest in your heart today, what are you clinging to — your rights, face, or your own ideas? What would happen if, today, you were the first to give up those thirty metres?

brief12.title: Choose Humility
notes: A Change of Choices (Part 4): Humility and Pride
God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble
(1 Peter 5:5)
Key points:
1. After greeting everyone, announce the lesson: A Change of Choices (Part 4): Humility and Pride.

2. Theme verse, 1 Peter 5:5: “Likewise, you younger ones, be subject to the elder. Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility, to subject yourselves to one another; for ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’”
3. State the lesson’s main thread: what truly sets the course of our lives isn’t the size of the matter, but the system behind it.
4. Keep the tone warm and suited to the early morning; address everyone as “brothers and sisters.”

brief12.title: Not the Size of the Matter
notes: The same sentence, falling into different hearts
bears completely different fruit
What sets a life’s course isn’t the matter
but the system behind it
Key points:
1. Illustration 1: the sister lying awake before dawn — one sentence from her husband, “You really haven’t thought this through,” stung her all night.
2. Contrast: if the same sentence had come from an older person she respected, she would simply say, “Thank you for the reminder.”
3. Illustration 2: two cars in a narrow lane; neither will reverse thirty metres, and the whole road ends up late.
4. Key sentence: it isn’t the situation that makes you suffer; it’s which system you face the situation with.

brief12.title: Clothed with Humility
notes: All of you clothe yourselves with humility
to subject yourselves to one another (1 Peter 5:5)
Clothe: tie on a servant’s apron
Resist: God draws up his ranks against him
Key points:
1. The author is the apostle Peter, with Silvanus as scribe (1 Peter 5:12), around AD 62–64, around the time of Nero’s persecution.
2. The recipients are “living as foreigners in the Dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1 Peter 1:1) — people with no standing and no one to back them.
3. Original language: “clothe” (ἐγκομβόομαι) appears only here in the New Testament and means to tie on a servant’s apron; it echoes John 13:4, where the Lord wrapped a towel around his waist.
4. Original language: “resists” (ἀντιτάσσομαι) is a military term, to draw up in battle array — pride places God on the opposite side.
5. Source: quoted from Proverbs 3:34; James 4:6 quotes the same verse.

brief12.title: Judging the System by Its Results
notes: Self-centred: more service, more tired, more comparing
ever drier
Selfless: more service, more joy, more freedom
a life ever richer
Key points:
1. The lesson’s two test questions: is life growing more joyful or more painful? Is service growing lighter or more exhausting?
2. Every good tree produces good fruit (Matthew 7:17) — fruit doesn’t lie.
3. “The more we serve, the more tired we get”: the Lord’s burden is light (Matthew 11:30); the heavy yoke is one that “self” has added.
4. Scientific illustration: the Dead Sea only takes in, its salt content above thirty per cent, with almost no life; the Sea of Galilee has an outlet, and so has life.
5. Psychology: June Price Tangney (2000) — humility is not low self-esteem but “a relative lack of focus on the self.”

brief12.title: The Nature of Pride: Clinging to Self
notes: Clinging to rights, clinging to face
clinging to our own ideas
Result: strained relationships, inner pressure
a life gone dry
Key points:
1. Pride isn’t necessarily swaggering; often it’s quiet — “I can’t give way here,” “Why should I be the one to apologise first?”
2. What pride does best is dress itself up as principle.
3. Isaiah 14:13–14: five “I will”s in two verses; Genesis 3:5, “like God.”
4. 321: pride is leaving our originally intended position and grasping power, wanting to take God’s place.
5. Psychology: of John Gottman’s “Four Horsemen,” the strongest predictor of a marriage breaking down is “contempt” — contempt is the face pride wears in a relationship.

brief12.title: The Nature of Humility: Letting Go of Self
notes: Letting go of rights, letting go of face
letting go of control
Result: restored relationships, a heart set free
a life that grows
Key points:
1. Humility isn’t putting yourself down; it is unclenching your hand. The three things let go are exactly the three that pride clings to most tightly.
2. Philippians 2:5–8: “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant”; “emptied” (κενόω) means to pour out until empty.
3. Definition: humility is being entitled, and not clinging. John 13:3–4 — it was because the Lord knew all things were in his hands that he bent down.
4. 321: humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.
5. Research: Jim Collins, Good to Great, the “Level 5 leader” — personal humility combined with professional will.

brief12.title: Environment Shapes Life
notes: Proud environment: performance, comparison, being seen
Result: the selfless life is choked
Humble environment: hiddenness, helping others succeed, the Lord seen
Result: selflessness grows naturally
Key points:
1. Life is shaped not only by the individual but also by the surrounding culture; family, small group, workplace and church are all soil.
2. A proud environment: the disciples argued on the way about who was greatest (Mark 9:34); the Lord turned the ranking table upside down (Mark 9:35).
3. Psychology: Twenge and Campbell, The Narcissism Epidemic (2009) — American college students’ narcissism scores rising since the 1980s.
4. A humble environment: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30); “in honor preferring one another” (Romans 12:10).
5. Nature: coast redwoods grow over a hundred metres tall with roots only two or three metres deep, standing because their roots lock together in a grove — this is 321’s 235 relationships.

brief12.title: Three Exercises in Humility
notes: I will listen to you
I will take care of you
I will change myself to fit you
From “You must love me” to “I will love you”
Key points:
1. Three sentences short enough to memorise and usable this very morning.
2. I will listen to you: “swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (James 1:19); Carl Rogers’s “active listening” (1957).
3. I will take care of you: Emmons and McCullough’s gratitude study (2003) — those who see what they have received have something to give (1 Corinthians 4:7).
4. I will change myself: “I have become all things to all men” (1 Corinthians 9:22); Galatians 2:20.
5. 321: these three sentences are the most concrete operating manual for the 920 practice.

brief12.title: The Cycle of Grace
notes: Humility → God gives grace → more strength → more humility
Pride → God resists → more struggle → more pride
The difference isn’t ability, but choice
Whoever humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 14:11)
Key points:
1. Both cycles gather speed: humility grows lighter the further you go; pride grows harder.
2. “But he gives more grace” (James 4:6) — grace isn’t rationed out in fixed portions.
3. Picture: a cup set upside down in the rain — not too little rain, but the mouth facing the wrong way; science: air flows from high pressure to low pressure.
4. Negative examples: Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 4:30, 37) and Herod, who “didn’t give God the glory” (Acts 12:23).
5. “That he may exalt you in due time” (1 Peter 5:6) — a position God sets you in, God himself will hold you up in.

Build a humble environment
Deepen with the eight stages of changing our mindset
Key points:
1. Keep the three exercises exactly as in the lesson, in the same order.
2. Deepen with the eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
3. Practical tip: before reacting, count three seconds silently and ask, “What am I clinging to right now?”
4. Environment tip: this week, publicly give the glory to the Lord, publicly praise someone unnoticed, and publicly admit one weakness of your own.

choosing growth, choosing revival
Let go of self, and Jesus lives in you
Let Jesus be King and receive all the glory

2. Choosing humility = choosing grace, growth and revival; the first condition for revival is “humble themselves” (2 Chronicles 7:14).
3. “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).
4. Three questions for the call: is there a name that makes you tense? Something you can’t let go of? Is your service exhausted?
5. Point to 321’s Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

so that others see you in me

4. Definition: humility is being entitled, and not clinging; John 13:3–4 — knowing all things were in his hands, he bent down.
5. Correct the misunderstanding: humility isn’t weakness; real humility is something only a person with power can do.

brief21.title: The Results of Humility
notes: Restored relationships, a heart set free, a life that grows
Learn from me, and you will find rest for your souls
(Matthew 11:29)
Humility draws out humility, and both sides win
Key points:
1. The lesson’s three results: restored relationships, a heart set free, a life that grows.
2. Matthew 11:29: the Lord didn’t say “learn my power”; he said “learn from me.”
3. Research: Jim Collins, Good to Great, the “Level 5 leader” — personal humility combined with professional will.
4. 321: humility draws out humility, and both sides win; tie back to the narrow lane — if one car backs up, the whole road comes alive.

brief21.title: A Proud Environment
notes: Stressing performance, comparison, being seen
People want a name, want to prove themselves
The disciples argued on the way about who was greatest
(Mark 9:34)
Key points:
1. Life is shaped not only by the individual but also by the surrounding culture; family, small group, workplace and church are all soil.
2. Three marks of a proud environment: stressing performance, comparison and being seen; the problem isn’t these three but the “stressing.”
3. Scripture: the Lord out in front speaking of the cross, the disciples behind arguing about who was greatest (Mark 9:34–35).
4. Psychology: Twenge and Campbell, The Narcissism Epidemic (2009) — American college students’ narcissism scores rising since the 1980s.
5. Warning: Matthew 6:1 — don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them.

brief21.title: A Humble Environment
notes: Stressing hiddenness and helping one another succeed
Stressing letting Jesus be seen
He must increase, but I must decrease (John 3:30)
Result: selflessness grows naturally
Key points:
1. Three marks of a humble environment: stressing hiddenness, helping one another succeed, letting Jesus be seen.
2. “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30); “in honor preferring one another” (Romans 12:10).
3. Nature: coast redwoods grow over a hundred metres tall with roots only two or three metres deep, standing for a thousand years because their roots lock together in a grove.
4. 321: this is the 235 relationships — 2 spiritual companions, 3 spiritual parents and children, 5 a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.
5. The result is that selflessness grows naturally; our responsibility is to provide the soil, and the growing is God’s work (1 Corinthians 3:6).

brief21.title: Exercise 1: I Will Listen to You
notes: Set aside your own opinion and listen to others
Swift to hear, slow to speak (James 1:19)
Let God speak to you through people
920: living out the “0” with every “2”
Key points:
1. The lesson’s words: this isn’t having no mind of your own; it is letting God speak to you through people.
2. “He who answers before he hears, that is folly and shame to him” (Proverbs 18:13).
3. Psychology: Rogers and Farson’s “active listening” (1957) — when people are truly understood, their defences come down, and only then is change possible.
4. Reminder: God often speaks through the very person we least want to hear.
5. 321: the 920 practice — everyone we’re in relationship with is our “2”; live out the “0” with them and bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23).

brief21.title: Exercise 2: I Will Take Care of You
notes: Stop waiting for others to meet my needs
From “You must love me” to “I will love you”
The Lord tied on a towel and washed the disciples’ feet
You also ought to wash one another’s feet (John 13:14)
Key points:
1. The lesson’s words: move from “You must love me” to “I will love you.”
2. The difference between demanding and giving: no person can fill the hole in another’s heart; that is God’s place.
3. “We love him, because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19).
4. Illustration: that night, the one who would betray him and the one who would deny him both sat at the table, and still he tied on the towel and washed their feet.
5. Psychology: Emmons and McCullough’s gratitude study (2003) — those who see what they have received are more willing to help others (1 Corinthians 4:7).

brief21.title: Exercise 3: I Will Change Myself
notes: Stop demanding others change; adjust yourself first
I have become all things to all men
(1 Corinthians 9:22)
No longer I, but Christ lives in me
Key points:
1. This is the hardest of the three sentences, because it touches who I am.
2. Our inborn logic says the problem is the other person; the line most heard in counselling is “Please talk some sense into him.”
3. Paul had theology, vision and authority, yet chose to change himself to fit people (1 Corinthians 9:22).
4. Galatians 2:20: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite.
5. Psychology: Carol Dweck, Mindset (2006) — the fixed mindset protects “me,” the growth mindset cares about growth; this matches 321’s fivefold change.

brief21.title: The Cycle of Grace
notes: Humility → God gives grace → more strength → more humility
Pride → God resists → more struggle → more pride
The difference isn’t ability, but choice
Whoever humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 14:11)
Key points:
1. Both cycles gather speed, which is why some find life growing lighter and others harder.
2. “But he gives more grace” (James 4:6) — grace isn’t rationed out in fixed portions.
3. Picture: a cup set upside down in the rain — not too little rain, but the mouth facing the wrong way; science: air flows from high pressure to low pressure.
4. Negative examples: Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 4:30, 37); Herod, who “didn’t give God the glory” (Acts 12:23).
5. “That he may exalt you in due time” (1 Peter 5:6); the “Therefore” of Philippians 2:8–9.

brief21.title: Practice for Daily Living (1)
notes: Examine how I react
Today, am I clinging to self or letting go?
Deliberately practise the three sentences
I will listen to you, take care of you, change myself
Key points:
1. Exercise 1, exactly as in the lesson: today, in conflict or under pressure, am I clinging to self or choosing to let go of self?
2. Practical tip: before reacting, count three seconds silently and ask, “What am I clinging to right now?”; review for three minutes before bed.
3. Exercise 2: practise one of the three sentences each day in turn, for a full three weeks.
4. Tip: the name the Holy Spirit brings to mind is usually the one you least want to mention.

brief21.title: Practice for Daily Living (2)
notes: Build a humble environment
Let Jesus be seen, not make people famous
Eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction
Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication
Key points:
1. Exercise 3: deliberately cultivate a culture of “letting Jesus be seen” rather than making people famous.
2. Three concrete things: publicly give the glory to the Lord, publicly praise someone unnoticed, publicly admit one weakness of your own.
3. Walk briefly through the eight stages, stressing Repetition and Multiplication — a change of mindset isn’t a single flash of insight but is formed through repeated practice.
4. Encouragement: the temperature of a room changes as soon as one person opens a window.

brief21.title: Summary of the 3-2-1 Vision
notes: Three Foundations: Jesus, the Bible, the Holy Spirit
Two Core Values: King, all the glory
The Goal: establish God’s system
Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan
Key points:
1. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.
2. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory; the Goal: establish God’s system.
3. The old self is self-centred, the new self is selfless; humility overcomes pride, selflessness overcomes Satan (James 4:7 — first submit to God, then resist the devil).
4. The fivefold change and the four shifts of viewpoint: from man’s to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly.
5. Life first, then relationships, then ministry; the focus is Jesus — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances.

brief21.title: Response Prayer and Blessing
notes: Lord, I choose humility
letting go of myself, returning to my originally intended position
letting Jesus be King
so that others see you in me
Key points:
1. First lead the congregation in the lesson’s declaration of faith, slowly and clearly.
2. Response prayer: confess the self, ask for a humble heart, ask to build an environment where Jesus is seen.
3. Cast all our worries on God (1 Peter 5:7), and ask the Lord to bring us into the cycle of grace.
4. After the blessing, pause in silence and let the Holy Spirit work; close by pointing again to: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come together to the fourth lesson of “A Change of Choices,” and our title is: Choose Humility. Our theme verse is 1 Peter 5:5: “Likewise, you younger ones, be subject to the elder. Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility, to subject yourselves to one another; for ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’” Brothers and sisters, we make choices every day. But what truly sets the course of our lives isn’t the size of the matter; it is the system behind it.

Let me start with a morning. It isn’t light yet, and a sister lies awake in bed. Last night her husband said only one sentence: “You really haven’t thought this through.” It was no big thing, but that sentence was like a small thorn, and all night long she couldn’t pull it out. Dawn comes, and she is more tired than when she went to bed. Brothers and sisters, we often think it’s the thing that makes us suffer. It isn’t. If that very same sentence had come from an older person she deeply respected, she might simply have smiled and said, “Thank you for the reminder.” The same sentence, falling into different hearts, bears completely different fruit.

This letter was written by the apostle Peter, to believers scattered far and wide, living as foreigners. They had no standing and no one to back them. Peter didn’t teach them to fight for status; instead he told them to “clothe yourselves with humility.” Brothers and sisters, this word “clothe” appears only once in the whole New Testament, and it means to tie on a servant’s apron and fasten it tight. Peter must have remembered that night when the Lord wrapped a towel around his waist and washed the disciples’ feet. And the word “resists” is a military term, meaning to draw up in battle array against someone. The proud place God on the opposite side.

The lesson gives us a very practical test. First question: is my life growing more joyful, or more painful? Second question: is my service growing lighter, or more exhausting? Brothers and sisters, fruit doesn’t lie. Live in the system of the self-centred life, and the more you serve, the more tired you get; the more you do, the more you compare; and you grow ever drier. Live in the system of selflessness, and the more you serve, the more joyful you become; the more you live, the freer you are; and your life grows ever richer. The Dead Sea only takes in and never gives out, so it is dead; the Sea of Galilee has an outlet, so it has life.

The most direct expression of the self-centred life is pride. What is the nature of pride? Clinging to self: clinging to our rights, clinging to face, clinging to our own ideas. Brothers and sisters, pride isn’t necessarily swaggering. Very often pride is quiet. It’s the insistence that “I can’t give way here,” the injured “Why should I be the one to apologise first?” And the result? Strained relationships, inner pressure and a life gone dry. The psychologist John Gottman found that the strongest predictor of a marriage breaking down isn’t arguing; it’s “contempt.” Contempt is the face pride wears in a relationship.

The most direct expression of selflessness is humility. What is the nature of humility? Letting go of self: letting go of our rights, letting go of face, letting go of control. Brothers and sisters, humility isn’t putting yourself down; humility is unclenching your hand. Scripture’s fullest picture of humility is the Lord Jesus: “who, existing in the form of God … emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” (Philippians 2:6–7) He was entitled, and yet he did not cling. And the result? Restored relationships, a heart set free and a life that grows.

Our life is shaped not only by us as individuals but also by our environment. A proud environment stresses performance, stresses comparison, stresses being seen. There, people want to make a name for themselves and want to prove themselves, and the selfless life is choked to death. A humble environment stresses hiddenness, stresses helping one another succeed, stresses letting Jesus be seen. There, selflessness grows naturally. Brothers and sisters, the coast redwood grows over a hundred metres tall, yet its roots are only two or three metres deep. How does it stay standing? Because its roots and the roots beside it lock into one another.

Humility isn’t abstract; it is three very concrete sentences. The first: I will listen to you. Set aside your own opinion, and let God speak to you through people. The second: I will take care of you. Move from “You must love me” to “I will love you.” Brothers and sisters, most of the pain in relationships comes from that one sentence: “You should love me, and you don’t.” The third: I will change myself to fit you. Stop demanding that others change, and adjust yourself first. Paul says, “I have become all things to all men.” These three sentences are the most practical lesson in the 920 practice.

When we choose humility, we enter a cycle: we humble ourselves, and God gives grace; with grace we have more strength; and the stronger we become, the more we know that strength isn’t our own, so we grow humbler still. But when we choose pride, God resists us; being resisted, we struggle all the more; and the more we struggle, the prouder we become. Brothers and sisters, grace is like water, and water flows to the lowest place. Some people find life growing lighter the longer they live, while for others it grows harder and harder; the difference isn’t ability, but choice. The Lord said, “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”

Today we have three exercises. First, examine how I react: today, in conflict or under pressure, am I clinging to self, or choosing to let go of self? Before you react, count three seconds silently and ask yourself one question: what am I clinging to right now? Second, deliberately practise the three sentences: I will listen to you, I will take care of you, I will change myself. Third, build a humble environment: this week, publicly give the glory to the Lord, publicly praise someone who has gone unnoticed, and publicly admit one weakness of your own.

Brothers and sisters, humility is not just a virtue; it is the way of life. When you choose humility, you are choosing grace, choosing growth, choosing revival. And when you let go of yourself, Jesus begins to live himself out in you. This morning, is there a name in your heart that makes you tense up the moment you think of it? Today the Lord says to you: let Jesus be King. Not so that you win — so that Jesus reigns as King. This morning, is there something in your heart you can’t let go of? The Lord says: lay down your rights and return to your originally intended position. Let man be man and let God be God.

Let’s declare together: Lord, I choose humility, letting go of myself and returning to my originally intended position, letting Jesus be King, so that my life is lived in your grace, and others see you in me! Dear Lord, forgive our pride and give us a humble heart, so that this very day we can say those three sentences. We are willing to humble ourselves under your mighty hand and cast all our worries on you. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen. May the Lord’s grace and loving kindness be with us all today.

Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come together to the fourth lesson of “A Change of Choices,” and our title is: Choose Humility. Our theme verses are 1 Peter 5:5–6: “Likewise, you younger ones, be subject to the elder. Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility, to subject yourselves to one another; for ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’ Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time.” Brothers and sisters, we make choices every day. But what truly sets the course of our lives isn’t the size of the matter; it is the system behind it. Today we’ll look at five things: judging the system by its results, the nature of humility and pride, how our environment shapes our life, three practices of humility, and the cycle of grace that humility brings.

Let me start with a morning. It isn’t light yet, and a sister lies awake in bed. Last night her husband said just one sentence: “You really haven’t thought this through.” Just one sentence. Dinner was finished, the lights were off, but that sentence was like a small thorn lodged in her heart, and all night long she couldn’t pull it out. Dawn comes, and she is more tired than when she went to bed. Brothers and sisters, we often think it’s the “thing” that makes us suffer. It isn’t. If that very same sentence had come from an older person she deeply respected, she might simply have smiled and said, “Thank you for the reminder.” The same sentence, falling into different hearts, bears completely different fruit. Let me ask you: is there a sentence from last night still stuck in your heart?

Here’s another picture. Two cars meet in a narrow lane. Forward, neither can get through; backward, one of them would only have to reverse thirty metres. But neither driver budges. They lean on their horns and glare at each other. Ten minutes pass, a long line of cars builds up behind them, and everyone ends up late together. If just one of them were willing to reverse first, it would all be sorted in thirty seconds. But to the self-centred, those thirty metres feel longer than three kilometres — because it isn’t a question of distance. It’s a question of “who bows his head first.” Brothers and sisters, God’s principle has never changed: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” Not “dislikes” — “resists.”

The author of this letter is the apostle Peter, with Silvanus as his scribe, written around AD 62 to 64, right around the time Nero turned on the church. It was addressed to the believers living as foreigners in the Dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia. “Living as foreigners” means no roots, no standing, no one to back them. In that culture, Peter didn’t teach them to fight for status; instead he told them to “clothe yourselves with humility.” Brothers and sisters, this word “clothe” appears only this once in the whole New Testament, and it means to tie on the apron worn by servants and fasten it tight. Peter must have remembered that night — the Lord wrapped a towel around his waist and washed the disciples’ feet. That night Peter even said, “You will never wash my feet!” Thirty years had passed, and that towel was still in his memory. And “resists” is a military term, meaning to draw up in battle array against someone.

The lesson opens by giving us a very practical test. It doesn’t ask how many years we’ve been reading the Bible; it asks only two questions. First question: is my life right now growing more joyful, or more painful? Second question: is my service growing lighter, or more exhausting? Brothers and sisters, these two questions are short, but they are honest, because results speak. The Lord Jesus said, “By their fruits you will know them.” Fruit doesn’t lie. Get the system right and the fruit comes right of its own accord; get the system wrong and no amount of effort will produce good fruit. That is why the lesson says: this isn’t an outward problem; it’s the system inside.

Living in the system of the self-centred life produces three fruits: the more we serve, the more tired we get; the more we do, the more we compare; and we grow ever drier. Why do we get more tired the more we serve? The Lord said, my yoke is easy, and my burden is light. So who put that heavy yoke on us? “Self” did. Of course we get tired when we serve carrying “self,” because we’re doing two jobs at once: serving others with one hand and protecting ourselves with the other. Why do we compare more the more we do? Because win, and you fear being overtaken; lose, and you fear being seen; win or lose, you aren’t free. On the other hand, living in the system of selflessness, the more we serve, the more joyful we become; the more we live, the freer we are; and our life grows ever richer. Paul says, though I was free from all, I brought myself under bondage to all. Brothers and sisters, only a free person can willingly be a servant.

Speaking of growing dry, I think of a fact of geography. The Sea of Galilee and the Dead Sea are both fed by the Jordan River — the same water. But the Sea of Galilee has an outlet; its water flows on downstream, so it has fish, fishing boats and life. The Dead Sea only takes in and never gives out; its salt content runs above thirty per cent, and almost nothing can live in it. Brothers and sisters, that is geography — and it is also a portrait of the spiritual life. A life that only takes in and never gives out, that only wants to be loved and won’t go and love, will in the end become a Dead Sea, however much truth it soaks up. Today, are you a Sea of Galilee, or a Dead Sea?

The most direct expression of the self-centred life is pride. What is the nature of pride? The lesson uses a very precise verb: clinging to self. Clinging to our rights, clinging to face, clinging to our own ideas. Brothers and sisters, notice that pride isn’t necessarily swaggering. Very often pride is quiet. It’s the insistence that “I can’t give way here,” the injured “Why should I be the one to apologise first?”, the certainty that “this is a matter of principle.” What pride does best is dress itself up as principle. Isaiah 14 records the words of the fallen one: I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne, I will make myself like the Most High. In just two verses there are five “I will”s. The core grammar of pride is “I will.”

What is the result of clinging to self? The lesson says: strained relationships, inner pressure and a life gone dry. For decades the psychologist John Gottman studied how couples interact, and he identified four of the most dangerous signs: criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling; and the strongest predictor of a marriage breaking down is “contempt.” Brothers and sisters, contempt is the face pride wears in a relationship — I am above you, I look down on you. Then there’s inner pressure: try clenching your fist tightly for ten minutes and your hand will ache; clinging to face is the same, only the ache is in the heart, and the tighter you cling, the more you fear losing it. In 321 we say: pride is leaving our originally intended position and grasping power, wanting to take God’s place; pride provokes pride, and both sides lose.

The most direct expression of selflessness is humility. What is the nature of humility? Letting go of self: letting go of our rights, letting go of face, letting go of control. Brothers and sisters, these three are exactly the three things pride clings to most tightly. Humility isn’t putting yourself down; humility is unclenching your hand. Scripture’s fullest picture of humility is the Lord Jesus: “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” “Emptied himself” means poured out until empty. He did not give up his divinity; what he laid aside were the rights, the glory and the honour that were his by right. He was entitled, and yet he did not cling. So the deepest definition of humility is this: being entitled, and not clinging. Some people think humility is weakness — not so. When someone who has nothing lets go, that’s having no choice; when someone who has everything lets go, that is humility.

What is the result of letting go of self? The lesson says: restored relationships, a heart set free and a life that grows. Restored relationships, because humility draws out humility — in that narrow lane, if just one car is willing to back up, the whole road comes alive. A heart set free, because the Lord said, “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.” The Lord didn’t say “learn my power”; he said “learn from me.” A life that grows — even management research has discovered this: in Good to Great, Jim Collins studied companies with lasting excellence and found that their leaders had a paradoxical blend: personal humility combined with professional will.

Our life is shaped not only by us as individuals but also by the culture around us. Brothers and sisters, the family is soil, the small group is soil, the workplace is soil, and the church is soil too. A proud environment has three marks: it stresses performance, it stresses comparison, it stresses being seen. The problem isn’t these three things; it lies in the word “stresses.” In that air, people want to make a name for themselves, people want to prove themselves, and people won’t let go. Scripture gives an example: the Lord out in front speaking of the cross, the disciples behind him arguing about who was greatest. How did the Lord respond? “If any man wants to be first, he shall be last of all, and servant of all.” The Lord turned the whole ranking table upside down. And the most frightening result is this: the selfless life is choked to death.

A humble environment also has three marks: it stresses hiddenness, it stresses helping one another succeed, and it stresses letting Jesus be seen. John the Baptist spoke words every servant of God should remember: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” Paul says, “in honor preferring one another.” Brothers and sisters, I think of an example from nature. The coast redwoods of North America are the tallest trees on earth, able to grow beyond a hundred metres, yet their roots are shallow, often only two or three metres deep. How do they stay standing? Because redwoods grow in groves, and underground their roots intertwine and lock into one another. A lone redwood topples easily, but a grove of redwoods can stand for a thousand years. That is 321’s 235 relationships: we don’t stand by our own strength; we stand within relationships that hold on to one another.

Humility isn’t abstract; it is three very concrete sentences. The first: I will listen to you. Set aside your own opinion and be willing to listen to others. Brothers and sisters, many people don’t listen — not because they didn’t hear, but because “I already know the answer.” James says, be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger; human nature runs exactly the other way. In 1957 the psychologist Carl Rogers put forward “active listening,” and found that when someone is truly understood, their defences come down of their own accord, and only then does change become possible. Going deeper, the lesson says: let God speak to you through people. God often doesn’t speak in thunder; he speaks through the very person we least want to hear.

The second: I will take care of you. Stop waiting for others to meet my needs, and reach out to care for others. Move from “You must love me” to “I will love you.” Brothers and sisters, the vast majority of the pain in relationships comes from the same sentence pattern: “You should love me, and you don’t.” But people are limited; no person can fill the bottomless pit in another person’s heart — that is God’s place. “We love him, because he first loved us.” That night, the one who would betray him sat at the table, and the one who would deny him sat at the table too. He had every reason to say, “You love me first.” Instead he got up, tied on the towel, washed their feet and said, “You also ought to wash one another’s feet.”

The third: I will change myself to fit you. Stop demanding that others change, and adjust yourself first. Brothers and sisters, this one is the hardest, because it touches who I am. Our inborn logic says: the problem is the other person. The sentence most often heard in counselling is “Please talk some sense into him”; very few say, “Please tell me how I should change.” What did Paul do? “I have become all things to all men, that I may by all means save some.” Someone will ask: then won’t I lose myself? Yes — and that is exactly the point: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite.

When we choose humility, we enter a cycle: we humble ourselves, and God gives grace; with grace we have more strength; and the stronger we become, the more we know that strength isn’t our own, so we grow humbler still. But when we choose pride, God resists us; being resisted, we struggle all the more; and the more we struggle, the prouder we become. Brothers and sisters, grace is like water, and water flows to the lowest place. A person who exalts himself is like a cup set upside down in the rain — it isn’t that there’s too little rain; the mouth of the cup is facing the wrong way. Nebuchadnezzar said, “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built … by the might of my power?” and the words were still in his mouth when judgement fell. Herod didn’t give God the glory, and he was struck down on the spot. But the Lord said, “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” The difference isn’t ability, but choice.

Today we have three exercises. First, examine how I react: today, in conflict or under pressure, am I clinging to self, or choosing to let go of self? Before you react, count three seconds silently and ask yourself one question: what am I clinging to right now? Before bed, spend three minutes looking back: how many times did I cling today, and how many times did I let go? Second, deliberately practise the three sentences: I will listen to you, I will take care of you, I will change myself — one sentence a day, for a full three weeks. Brothers and sisters, the name the Holy Spirit brings to mind is usually the one you least want to mention.

Third, build a humble environment. In your family, small group and church, deliberately cultivate a culture of “letting Jesus be seen” rather than making people famous. This week, please do three things: first, publicly give the glory to the Lord, changing “what I did” into “what the Lord did”; second, publicly praise someone who has gone unnoticed; third, publicly admit one weakness of your own. We deepen this using the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Brothers and sisters, a change of mindset isn’t a single flash of insight; it is formed through repeated practice. The temperature of a room changes as soon as one person opens a window.

Let’s set today’s lesson back into the picture of 321. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal: establish God’s system. The old self is self-centred, the new self is selfless; humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. Why? Because every work of Satan has to plug into the socket called “self”; if that “self” has already been crucified with Christ, he has nothing to get a grip on. The fivefold change is mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Life first, then relationships, then ministry. The focus is Jesus — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances.

Brothers and sisters, humility is not just a virtue; it is the way of life. Let’s declare together: Lord, I choose humility, letting go of myself and returning to my originally intended position, letting Jesus be King, so that my life is lived in your grace, and others see you in me! Dear Lord Jesus, though you existed in the form of God, you emptied yourself and took the form of a servant. Forgive our pride and give us a humble heart, so that this very day we can say those three sentences. Use us to build an environment in our families, small groups and churches where Jesus is seen. We are willing to humble ourselves under your mighty hand and cast all our worries on you. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen. May the Lord’s grace and loving kindness be with us all today. Let Jesus be King. Let Jesus receive all the glory.

sections.heading: Introduction: The Same on the Outside, Utterly Different Within
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, peace be with you this morning. Let’s begin by asking you to picture a scene in your heart: two people, on the same morning, doing the same thing.

The first gets up at six, opens the Bible, reads three chapters, writes some notes, prays for ten minutes and heads off to work. The whole thing takes twenty-five minutes — not a minute more, not a minute less.

The second also gets up at six and reads the same three chapters. But when he comes to one sentence he stops, reads it again, bows his head and says, “Lord, are these words for me?” He is quiet for a while, and his eyes grow wet. When he leaves the house, he is seven minutes later than he planned.

From the outside, these two people are doing the same thing — their devotions. Same time, same passage, same posture. And yet, brothers and sisters, the lives those two mornings produce are completely different.

Why? Because the first person is “completing” his devotions, while the second is “meeting” God. The first relies on his own discipline; the second relies on the guidance of the Holy Spirit.

That is the question this lesson takes up today. We often think the key to the spiritual life lies in “how well we do” — did we finish our Bible reading, did we pray enough, did our service go off well? But Scripture wants to tell us something more fundamental: the real key isn’t what you do, but whom you rely on to do it.

The same sermon can be preached relying on the manuscript, or relying on the Holy Spirit. The same decision can be made relying on experience, or relying on the Holy Spirit. On the outside they look exactly alike, but the outcome in a person’s life is worlds apart.

This is the watershed between the self-centred life and selflessness. Self-centred people put themselves at the centre and rely in everything on their own cleverness, experience, ability and methods. Selfless people put Jesus on the throne, and in everything they seek the Holy Spirit’s guidance, obey the Holy Spirit’s promptings and rely on the Holy Spirit’s power.

On the 321 road, what trips us up most easily is often not some obvious sin but a kind of “relying on ourselves” that looks very devout. We go on serving, go on reading the Bible, go on attending meetings — but the Holy Spirit has already been ushered off to one side.

Brothers and sisters, this morning let’s honestly ask ourselves one question together: the things I did this week — whom did I actually rely on to do them?

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Three Books, One Shared Cry
sections.html: Today’s three key passages come from three entirely different eras, three different authors and three different situations. Yet they all raise the same cry.

sections.heading: 1. Proverbs 3: A Father’s First Lesson to His Son
sections.html:
The bulk of Proverbs comes from the hand of King Solomon. Solomon reigned over Israel from roughly 970 to 930 BC and is the king Scripture renowned for his wisdom. Proverbs 25:1 also tells us that some of these proverbs were later the ones “which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied out” — which shows that Proverbs is a collection of wisdom gathered and edited over a long period.

Chapters 1 to 9 of Proverbs have a very distinctive form: they are a father’s long exhortation to his son, with the call “My son, listen” sounding again and again. So Proverbs 3:5–6 is not an abstract maxim. It is an old father with his hands on his child’s shoulders, saying: you’ll learn a great many skills in life, but remember this — don’t lean on your own understanding.

It’s worth pondering that these words come from Solomon, the man with the best claim of anyone to lean on his own understanding. And the failure of his later years became a witness from the other side: 1 Kings 11 records that when he was old, his heart turned away from Yahweh. Having wisdom is not the same as having a refuge; gifts are not the same as life.

A few key words in the original are worth noting. “Trust” is the Hebrew בָּטַח (batach), whose basic meaning is “to lie down at ease, to put your whole weight on something, to entrust yourself without any guard”. It doesn’t picture lightly steadying yourself on a railing with two fingers; it pictures lying full length on a bed. “Lean” is a different word, שָׁעַן (sha’an), meaning “to rest your body against something, to prop yourself on it” — it too puts the weight down, only in the wrong place. “Understanding” is בִּינָה (binah), meaning “discernment, insight, seeing how things work”. So what this verse really says is: my child, put the whole weight of who you are on Yahweh, not on your own skill at reading situations.

sections.heading: 2. Galatians 3: A Heartbreaking Question
sections.html:
Galatians was written by the apostle Paul. As to its date, scholars who hold the “South Galatian” view place it after the first missionary journey and before the Jerusalem Council, around AD 48–49; those who hold the “North Galatian” view put it at around AD 53–57. Whichever date you take, the situation is clear: a group of Judaising teachers had come into the churches of Galatia and were telling these Gentile believers that simply believing in Jesus wasn’t enough — they also had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses in order to be complete.

Paul wrote this letter in a state of deep agitation; of all his letters to churches, it is the only one that doesn’t open by giving thanks to God. In 3:1 he says, “Foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you not to obey the truth, before whose eyes Jesus Christ was openly portrayed among you as crucified?” Then in 3:2 he asks, “Did you receive the Spirit by the works of the law, or by hearing of faith?” And only then comes today’s key verse, 3:3: “Having begun in the Spirit, are you now completed in the flesh?”

The word for “begun” is ἐνάρχομαι (enarchomai), meaning “to start, to make a beginning”; “completed” is ἐπιτελέω (epiteleō), meaning “to finish, to reach the end”. Paul’s question paints a deeply ironic picture: your spiritual life was begun by the Holy Spirit — do you now mean to finish it off in your own flesh? It’s like someone flying across the Pacific who, halfway over, says, “I’ll swim the rest of the way myself.”

Notice this: the Galatians hadn’t left the church, hadn’t gone off to worship idols, hadn’t fallen into gross moral sin. They simply wanted to be “a bit more complete”, to add a little of their own effort on top of grace. Yet Paul calls this “foolish”, and in 5:4 he even says they have “fallen away from grace”. That reminds us that relying on ourselves doesn’t necessarily wear the face of self-indulgence. More often it wears the face of “pursuing spiritual growth”.

sections.heading: 3. Romans 8: The Charter of the Holy Spirit
sections.html:
Romans was written around AD 57, while Paul was in Corinth. Many commentators call Romans 8 one of the summits of the whole Bible. It moves from the struggle of chapter 7 — “desire is present with me, but I don’t find it doing that which is good” — to the release of chapter 8 — “There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus” — and the turning point in between is the Holy Spirit. In this one chapter alone, the word “Spirit” appears around twenty times.

Romans 8:13 says, “For if you live after the flesh, you must die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live.” Notice that Paul doesn’t say, “Try a little harder and put your evil deeds to death.” He says to put them to death “by the Spirit”. In putting evil deeds to death, we have to act, but the power doesn’t come from us. Verse 14 follows straight on: “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God.” The word for “led”, ἄγω (agō), is in the passive voice here, describing a person who is being led, being drawn along. The mark of a child of God isn’t “I’m good at walking” but “I’m willing to be led.”

Three books, three eras, one shared cry: don’t rely on yourself; rely on the Spirit of God.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: Two Kinds of Reliance, Two Kinds of Outcome
sections.html:
Right at the outset the lesson spreads out the whole map: when you trace every choice in life back to its root, there are only two kinds of reliance, and these two lead to two entirely different outcomes.

Relying on Self: The System of the Self-Centred Life

People who rely on themselves lean on four things: experience, ability, methods and control.

None of these four is bad in itself. Experience is a gift from God; ability is a gift from God; methods are the distilled fruit of wisdom. The problem isn’t in “having” them but in “relying” on them. When I put my whole weight on them, they turn from tools into idols.

Jeremiah 17:5–6 speaks very severely: “Yahweh says: ‘Cursed is the man who trusts in man, relies on strength of flesh, and whose heart departs from Yahweh. For he will be like a bush in the desert, and will not see when good comes, but will inhabit the parched places in the wilderness, an uninhabited salt land.’” Notice the image — a bush in the desert. It isn’t dead. It’s still alive, still green; but it lives on salt land, so it never grows tall and never bears fruit. How many Christians are in just that condition: not dead, but not growing either.

The lesson lists the four results of relying on ourselves with great precision: pressure, exhaustion, dryness and finally spiritual death.

These four are a downhill road. First comes pressure — because I have to carry every outcome myself. Then exhaustion — because my strength is limited and the needs are limitless. Then dryness — not just a lack of strength, but a heart that has lost its savour. Finally, spiritual death — not the loss of salvation, but the loss of living fellowship with God; the person is still there, but the spirit has gone stiff.

Psychology describes this downhill road precisely. From 1981 onwards, the social psychologist Christina Maslach of the University of California, Berkeley developed the Maslach Burnout Inventory, which identifies three core dimensions of burnout: emotional exhaustion, depersonalisation (coldness and cynicism towards people) and a reduced sense of personal accomplishment. In 2019 the World Health Organization formally listed burnout in the eleventh revision of the International Classification of Diseases as an occupational phenomenon resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed. Brothers and sisters, these three dimensions follow almost the same track as the exhaustion, dryness and spiritual death the lesson describes. Scripture simply traces it deeper: the root of burnout is often a heart that has moved God out of the way and is carrying everything alone.

Relying on the Holy Spirit: The System of Selflessness

People who rely on the Holy Spirit do four things: they seek his guidance, obey his promptings, rely on his power and entrust him with sovereignty.

These four correspond exactly to the Three Foundations and the Two Core Values of 321: seeking guidance — the Holy Spirit is my guide; obeying promptings — the Bible is my standard; relying on power — Jesus is my role model; entrusting sovereignty — let Jesus be King.

Jesus himself is the perfect demonstration. John 5:19: “Most certainly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing. For whatever things he does, these the Son also does likewise.” Brothers and sisters, the Son of God on earth said, “I can do nothing of myself.” If even the Lord Jesus chose not to rely on himself, what makes us think we can?

The four results of relying on the Holy Spirit: peace, joy, lightness and a life that grows.

Galatians 5:22–23: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.” Notice that Paul speaks of “fruit”, not “products”. Products have to be manufactured; fruit only needs connection. A branch doesn’t have to grit its teeth to produce grapes; it only has to stay on the vine.

In Matthew 11:29–30 Jesus says, “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” The word for “easy” is χρηστός (chrēstos), meaning “well-suited, well-fitting”. Carpenters in those days would measure an ox’s neck to make its yoke, so that it wouldn’t chafe. The Lord’s yoke is light not because there’s no work, but because that yoke has been made to measure for you — and a yoke is made for two: at the other end, the Lord carries it with you.

A Real-Life Contrast: The Sea of Galilee and the Dead Sea

Israel has two lakes that drink from the same river, the Jordan. In the north, the Sea of Galilee has water flowing in and flowing out; there are fish in it, and the disciples cast their nets there. In the south, the Dead Sea only takes in and never gives out, so its salt keeps concentrating. Today its salinity is around thirty per cent, nearly ten times that of ordinary seawater, and apart from a few salt-loving microbes, no fish can survive in it — which is why it is called the “Dead” Sea. The same source of water — so why is one alive and the other dead? There’s only one difference: whether or not the water flows on.

People who rely on themselves are like the Dead Sea — only interested in absorbing, accumulating and controlling, wanting to grip everything in their hands, so the more they hoard, the saltier and deader they become. People who rely on the Holy Spirit are like the Sea of Galilee — grace flows in from God and flows out again through me, so within there is always life.

Applying the 321 Vision: The Key Isn’t What You Do, but Whom You Rely On

The lesson sums up this point in one sentence: “The key isn’t what you do, but whom you rely on.”

That sentence is the very starting point of the fivefold change. 321 says: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. What this lesson sets out to change is the mindset at the very headwaters — turning “I must get this done well” into “I will let the Holy Spirit do it.”

Our perspective must shift along with it. From man’s perspective, the most capable person wins; from God’s perspective, the one willing to rely on him wins. From an earthly perspective, busyness is fruitfulness; from a heavenly perspective, being connected to the Lord is what counts as fruitfulness.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: The Greatest Danger — Once We Can Do It, We Stop Relying
sections.html:
The lesson says something very sharp: “The most dangerous thing isn’t not knowing how — it’s ‘knowing how’.” Brothers and sisters, that sentence deserves to be copied onto the flyleaf of your Bible.

A Curve Everyone Has Travelled

The lesson traces the path very clearly: at first we don’t know how, so we rely on God; once we become skilled, we start relying on ourselves.

Do you remember the first time you led a small group? You couldn’t sleep the night before, and you prayed over and over: Lord, I don’t know how to do this; please help me. And that time it went with surprising power. Three years later, with the same small group, you spend five minutes thinking through the plan in the car on the way, walk in and get started — and you speak far more smoothly than you did three years ago. But that prayer, “Lord, I don’t know how,” has disappeared.

The curve of rising skill and the curve of falling reliance often cross. That is exactly the situation of Galatians 3:3.

Why the Brain Works This Way

Science offers a fascinating piece of corroboration. The MIT neuroscientist Ann Graybiel and her team have long studied the role of the brain’s basal ganglia in forming habits. They found that a sequence of actions that at first requires step-by-step thought is, after repeated practice, “packaged” by the brain into a single chunk: once triggered, it runs to completion automatically, with almost no conscious monitoring. Research by the psychologists Sian Beilock and Thomas Carr (2001) also shows that highly skilled people, after performing the actions they are best at, often can’t say what steps they just went through — what is called “expertise-induced amnesia”.

This is a wonderful part of how God made us — otherwise just walking and driving every day would wear us out. But once this design is carried over into the spiritual life, a danger appears: prayer, Bible reading and service can also be “packaged” into automatic routines. The hands are moving, the mouth is speaking, and the heart can be entirely absent.

Isaiah 29:13 pointed this out long ago: “Because this people draws near with their mouth and honors me with their lips, but they have removed their heart far from me.” Brothers and sisters, what the spiritual life should fear most isn’t being out of practice; it’s being “too familiar”. Too familiar, and you don’t have to think; no need to think, no need to ask; no need to ask, no need to rely.

Three Places Where Things Most Easily Go Wrong

The lesson singles out three conditions: when we’ve served a long time, when we’ve gained a lot of experience, and when our skills have become second nature.

Then we begin to say three things: it’s fine without praying; it’s fine without seeking; it’s fine without waiting.

No one would ever say these sentences out loud, yet they are an honest record of our diaries. When you find the time spent doing growing longer and the time spent waiting growing shorter; when you find yourself saying “I don’t know” less and less; when your first thought in a difficulty is “I’ll find a way” rather than “Lord, how do you see this?” — brothers and sisters, the alarm bell is already ringing.

Scripture has a heartbreaking example. In Joshua 9, the Gibeonites came with mouldy bread and split wineskins to deceive Israel. Joshua 9:14 records the reason for Israel’s failure: “The men sampled their provisions, and didn’t ask counsel from Yahweh’s mouth.” It wasn’t that their judgement was poor; it was that, that one time, they didn’t ask. Fresh from the great victory at Jericho, that was precisely when they least felt the need to ask.

The Result: The More We Do, the More Tired and Empty We Become

The lesson says: the more we do, the more tired we get, the emptier we become, the less life there is.

That is the very portrait of the church in Ephesus. The Lord commended their toil, their perseverance and their ability to discern false teaching, and then said, “But I have this against you, that you left your first love” (Revelation 2:4). Full marks for ministry; a failing grade for love.

321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. When ministry runs ahead of life, ministry begins to devour people. It isn’t ministry that crushes you; it’s “doing ministry by relying on yourself” that crushes you.

Applying the 321 Vision: Selflessness Overcomes Satan

Why is “once we can do it, we stop relying” so dangerous? Because its root is pride.

321 puts it penetratingly: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place. When I stop relying on the Holy Spirit because “I know how now”, I am doing God’s work while sitting in God’s seat. Isaiah 14:13–14 records what Satan said in his heart: “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! … I will make myself like the Most High!” Those “I will”s are the template of the self-centred life.

That is why 321 says: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. The way to deal with “once we can do it, we stop relying” isn’t to do a little less. It is, in every single thing “I’m best at”, to deliberately return to our originally intended position and say once again, “Lord, without you I can do nothing.”

sections.heading: Key Point 3: The Real Cause of Spiritual Dryness
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, if I asked you, “Why have you been so dry spiritually lately?”, the lesson has already listed the three answers we most often give: too busy, too tired, bad circumstances.

All three answers sound reasonable, and they’re often true. But the lesson tells us that none of them is the real cause. There is only one real cause: we have left the system of relying on the Holy Spirit.

The Difference Between the Disease and the Symptoms

Too busy, too tired, bad circumstances — these are symptoms, not the disease.

When a person relies on the Holy Spirit, he can be busy and still have peace; when a person relies on himself, he can be idle and still dry up. On Mount Carmel, in a single day, Elijah took on four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and then ran ahead of Ahab’s chariot — busy to the utmost, yet full of power. But one threatening message from Jezebel, and he fled into the wilderness, sat down under a broom tree and asked to die. The same man, the same God — what changed was where his eyes were fixed.

Jeremiah 2:13 says, “For my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the spring of living waters, and cut out cisterns for themselves: broken cisterns that can’t hold water.” Look carefully at the order: first they forsook the spring, and then they went to cut out cisterns. A spring takes no effort; it wells up on its own. A cistern takes effort, and it cracks. People who rely on themselves are forever cutting out cisterns, and the harder they dig, the more it proves how far they are from the spring.

Symptom 1: Devotions Become a Duty

The lesson’s first example pierces many hearts: Bible reading becomes a task, prayer becomes a formality, and the result is that the more devotions we do, the less we want to do them.

That is a vitally important observation. If our devotions are an encounter with God, how could anyone want to see him less the more they meet him? Unless it isn’t an encounter at all, but just getting the job done.

Psychology offers some corroboration here. Self-determination theory, developed from the 1980s by the University of Rochester psychologists Edward Deci and Richard Ryan, distinguishes between autonomous motivation and controlled motivation. When an activity springs from inner meaning and free choice, people show lasting engagement and vitality; once it is taken over by external rules, evaluation or pressure, intrinsic motivation is eroded and engagement actually drops. Turning “I want to” into “I have to” is the quickest way to put out a fire.

Brothers and sisters, this is the double edge of a Bible-reading plan. The plan itself is good; it is a tool. But when the plan becomes the master, Bible reading shifts from “What does the Lord want to say to me today?” to “How many chapters am I behind today?” How many chapters you’re behind can be counted; what the Lord says cannot. And our nature always prefers what can be counted — because that is what I can control.

In 1 Samuel 15:22, Samuel says to Saul, “To obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.” Saul’s sacrifice was real, the sheep were real, the outward show of piety was real; the problem was that he hadn’t listened. In sacrifice, I bring something to God; in obedience, I hand myself over to God. The first I can do by relying on myself; the second is impossible without relying on the Holy Spirit.

So the way to restore our devotions isn’t to step up the reading plan; it is to return to encounter. Psalm 46:10 says, “Be still, and know that I am God.” First be still, and then you will know. People who cannot stop will never meet God.

Symptom 2: Service Loses Its Joy — a Fish Out of Water

The lesson’s second example uses a wonderfully vivid image: doing a great deal without any life is like a fish out of water. The best fish food in the world won’t help, because the environment is wrong.

Scientifically, the image is spot on. A fish out of water dies, not because there’s no oxygen in the air — the air actually holds far more oxygen than water does. It dies because in water its gill filaments are held open by buoyancy, keeping up an enormous surface for exchange; once out of the water, the filaments stick together and collapse, the surface area plummets, and even surrounded by oxygen-rich air it can’t get oxygen into its blood. The oxygen is right there beside it, yet it suffocates.

Brothers and sisters, a servant of God who has left the Holy Spirit doesn’t dry up for lack of resources. He is surrounded by sermons, courses, materials and applause — resources galore. He dries up because he has left the environment in which grace can be absorbed.

Jesus said the same thing even more directly. John 15:5: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” The word for “remains” is μένω (menō), meaning “to settle down, to stay, not to move out”. The Lord doesn’t ask the branches to strive to bear fruit; he only asks them to stay on the vine. Take a branch that has been cut off from the vine, plant it in the richest soil, tie the loveliest grapes onto it — it is still withered. Brothers and sisters, have you ever tried “tying on grapes” in your service? Fruit on the outside, no sap within.

Jeremiah 17:7–8 gives us the positive picture: “Blessed is the man who trusts in Yahweh, and whose confidence is in Yahweh. For he will be as a tree planted by the waters, who spreads out its roots by the river, and will not fear when heat comes, but its leaf will be green, and will not be concerned in the year of drought. It won’t cease from yielding fruit.” This tree meets the same heat and the same year of drought; the difference is that its roots are set down beside the water. In the same drought year, the bush on the salt land withers, while the tree by the water never stops bearing fruit.

So, brothers and sisters, let’s stop blaming our dryness on our circumstances. The problem isn’t the drought year; the problem is where the roots are set.

Applying the 321 Vision: Life First, Then Relationships, Then Ministry

Here the 321 order shows how wise it is: life first, then relationships, then ministry. The priority of relationships is just as clear: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things.

Spiritual dryness is almost always the result of the order being turned upside down — things running ahead of people, and people running ahead of God. When the day comes that you find there’s no sap left in your heart, it’s usually not because you’ve done too much, but because you’ve given the first-place seat to what belongs fourth.

321 also says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. Proverbs 4:23 says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” When all that’s left of our service is the brain, troubles pile up; when our service returns to the heart, joy comes back.

sections.heading: Key Point 4: The Key to Preaching and Serving
sections.html:
Here the lesson turns its lens on the most spiritual arena of all — preaching. For the place Satan most loves to hide is often the holiest place.

Materials Aren’t the Problem; Reliance Is

The lesson is very balanced: “The materials themselves aren’t the problem. The key is this — are you relying on the materials, or letting the Holy Spirit use them?”

We need to hear this clearly: 321 never tells anyone to despise preparation. The Bible is my standard, and that requires us to study it diligently. Getting up to speak without preparing isn’t spiritual; it’s lazy. And calling laziness “leaving it to the Holy Spirit” is an affront to the Holy Spirit.

The real difference isn’t whether there’s a sermon manuscript, but in whose hands the manuscript lies. The rod in Moses’ hand was an ordinary shepherd’s staff. Held in a man’s hand, it was only wood; stretched out at God’s command, it parted the Red Sea. The rod didn’t change; whose command it obeyed was the key.

Relying on the Manuscript: Content, but No Life

We’ve all heard that kind of message: neatly structured, richly referenced, perfectly timed — and when it’s over, nothing has happened. We’ve all heard the other kind too: the speaker may even stumble over his words, but one sentence flies into your heart like an arrow, and you weep all the way home.

1 Corinthians 2:4–5: “My speech and my preaching were not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, that your faith wouldn’t stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God.” Paul didn’t want people to admire him; he wanted their faith “not to stand in the wisdom of men”. A message that relies on self, even when it succeeds, only brings people to the preacher; a message that relies on the Holy Spirit brings people to God.

This is exactly the Two Core Values of 321: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. The deepest battle in the pulpit has never been over content; it has always been over who gets the glory.

The nineteenth-century missionary Hudson Taylor is generally credited with saying, “God’s work done in God’s way will never lack God’s supply.” The weight falls on the middle phrase — in God’s way. The same work of God, done in man’s way, has to be propped up by man’s strength; only when it’s done in God’s way does it have God’s supply.

Relying on the Holy Spirit: Life, Power, and Hearts Touched

The lesson says the results of relying on the Holy Spirit are three: life, power, and the ability to touch people’s hearts. And the reason comes down to one sentence: “because the Holy Spirit knows what people really need.”

When we prepare, we are facing “a general congregation”. The Holy Spirit is facing the sister who had a row with her husband just this morning, the brother who got his medical results yesterday, the young person who has already decided this will be the last time he comes. However good our materials, they can only reach “people in general”; the Holy Spirit can reach “that one”.

1 Corinthians 2:10 says, “But to us, God revealed them through the Spirit. For the Spirit searches all things, yes, the deep things of God.”

And in 2 Corinthians 3:5 Paul says, “Not that we are sufficient of ourselves, to account anything as from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God.”

Brothers and sisters, this section isn’t only for preachers. An email you write at work, a sentence you say to your child at home, a message you reply to in a group chat — each one can be done relying on your materials or relying on the Holy Spirit. You can rely on your arguments to win against your child, or you can rely on the Holy Spirit to speak into your child’s heart. With the first you’ll win, but both of you will lose; only the second brings life.

321 says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. That holds true in the pulpit, and it holds just as true at the dinner table.

Applying the 321 Vision: Let the Holy Spirit Use the Five Loaves and Two Fish in Your Hands

The five loaves and two fish in a boy’s hands could never have fed five thousand people. But placed in Jesus’ hands — given thanks for and broken — there was more than enough.

Your sermon notes, your professional expertise, your experience — these are your five loaves and two fish. 321 doesn’t tell you to throw them away; it tells you to hand them over. Handing them over is letting Jesus be King; being broken is selflessness; and when twelve baskets are left over, giving the glory to the Lord is letting Jesus receive all the glory.

sections.heading: Key Point 5: Relying on the Holy Spirit as a Practical Way of Life
sections.html:
Someone may say: relying on the Holy Spirit sounds beautiful, but it’s too abstract. What exactly am I supposed to do?

The lesson answers without hesitation: “Relying on the Holy Spirit isn’t abstract; it is a concrete way of living.” Then it gives us five very workable sentences.

Three “Firsts”: Pray First, Seek First, Wait First

One: before making a decision, pray first.

Two: before acting, seek first.

Three: before speaking, wait first.

Brothers and sisters, notice what these three sentences have in common: each contains the word “first”. The line between relying on the Holy Spirit and relying on ourselves is often only a few seconds wide — those few seconds before you press “send”, those few seconds before you open your mouth.

James 1:19 says, “So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger.” The order of swift and slow is the spiritual order.

In 2 Samuel 5, David twice faced the same Philistine army. The first time he inquired of Yahweh, God said, “Go up,” and he won. The second time — same enemy, same place — he inquired again, but God’s answer was different: “You shall not go up. Circle around behind them, and attack them in front of the mulberry trees” (2 Samuel 5:23). Had David relied the second time on his experience from the first, he would not have won. God’s leading is living; it can’t be copied and pasted.

Two “Don’ts”: Don’t Rush to React, Don’t Rely on Feelings

Four: don’t rush to react; ask the Holy Spirit first.

Five: don’t rely on feelings; rely on guidance.
