script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come together to Lesson 109 of Morning Devotion 321, and our title is “Caring About Every Single Choice.”
Our key verse is John 15:19: “If you were of the world, the world would love its own. But because you are not of the world, since I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you.”
Brothers and sisters, picture a plane flying from Taoyuan to Los Angeles. At take-off its nose is pointing just one degree off course, and sitting in the cabin you feel nothing at all.
But one degree off over ten thousand kilometres puts you 175 kilometres off course — not landing at the other end of the runway, but landing in another city.

We often think life is decided by the “big decisions.” But the lesson says: what truly sets the course of our life is not one major choice, but the choices we make every day and every moment. Every thought, every reaction, every decision is quietly establishing a “system.”
So please remember this sentence: it’s not about what kind of life you’re living, but about what kind of system you’re establishing.
This verse comes from the Lord Jesus’ farewell words before he went to the cross.
The word “world” here is the Greek kosmos. It doesn’t mean the mountains, rivers and land, but an operating system that is hostile to God and centred on man.
Yet the Lord did not tell us to run away. That same night he prayed: “I pray not that you would take them from the world, but that you would keep them from the evil one” (John 17:15).
This is our situation: in the world, yet not of the world. Daniel is the best example — in Babylon, yet not of Babylon.
The lesson asks a question that cuts to the heart: are you living in the world’s “environment,” or in the world’s “system”?
The environment is your outward situation; the system is what’s running on the inside. God has never promised to move us out of our environment; what he wants to do is move us out of the system.

On the day the decree came down, the Bible says Daniel knelt before God three times a day, “as he did before” (Daniel 6:10). Listen to those words: as he did before. He could stay unchanged on the day of the lions’ den because he hadn’t changed on any of the days in the decades before.
So the key is not where you are, but how you choose.

The lesson says: God’s system does not appear naturally. Brothers and sisters, weeds grow by themselves, but wheat has to be sown. The worldly system forms automatically; God’s system has to be established deliberately.
How is it established? Not by one big decision, but by every small choice.

Every day you are choosing: will I be humble? Will I lay myself down? Will I obey the Holy Spirit? Will I trust God? Will I love? These choices are so small you don’t even feel you’re making a choice. But the Lord said: “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much” (Luke 16:10).

When you choose humility rather than insisting on your own way, rely on the Holy Spirit rather than yourself, live by faith rather than by sight, and choose love rather than hate, you are doing one thing: establishing God’s system.

These choices are small — so small you’ve forgotten them by evening. But the result of their accumulation is a changed life, changed relationships, a changed spiritual condition — and in the end, Christ lived out.

Let’s do the sums: improve by one per cent a day, and after a year it’s thirty-seven times greater; decline by one per cent a day, and only a thirtieth is left. The same 365 days, and a gap of more than a thousandfold. This is the compound interest of choice.
Conversely, when you choose pride, choose to rely on yourself, choose to go by your feelings, choose to hold a grudge, you are also establishing a system — the worldly system.

The lesson says the results of this system are: the more you live, the more tired you get; the more you serve, the drier you become; the harder you try, the more powerless you feel. Brothers and sisters, have you had days like that? You still go to the meetings, still take on the ministry, yet inside you feel as though you’ve been drained dry.

It’s because your life is not in the right environment. Like a fish out of water — however hard it tries, it cannot live. There is actually more oxygen on the bank than in the water; the fish doesn’t die from a lack of oxygen, it dies from leaving the water.
The Lord said: “Apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).
The lesson says: the starting point of revival is not behaviour but mindset. Mindset determines choices, choices establish a system, and the system shapes a life.

Paul says: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind” (Romans 12:2). This word “transformed,” in the original, is the very word used for a caterpillar becoming a butterfly.
When you truly believe “it is no longer I who live,” you will no longer feed the “self.” The “self” needs to eat, and every time you argue your own case, you feed it a mouthful.
When you truly believe “Christ lives in me,” you will naturally depend on God, obey God and live out God. So the real key isn’t effort; it’s what you believe.
There is one phenomenon that is truly heartbreaking: many people know about selflessness, yet they can’t live it out.
Why? Because the mindset is still stuck in the “head.” Hebrews says the word they heard wasn’t mixed with faith (Hebrews 4:2).

Real change comes in four steps: Information is hearing it; Revelation is the Holy Spirit opening it up so it drops into your heart; Conviction is your whole being yielding; Implementation is really doing it.
When “I already” moves from knowledge to revelation, your choices will change, and your life will change.

The lesson gives us three practices. First, notice your everyday choices. Set three reminders on your phone, and when one goes off, stop for thirty seconds and ask yourself: in the past hour, have I been living in the self-centred life, or in selflessness?
Second, deliberately make the right choice. When your emotions rise, don’t open your mouth straight away; say silently in your heart: “Lord, in this matter I let you be King.”

Third, let mindset become action. Every morning, declare aloud: “I have been crucified with Christ.” In the evening, write down one choice that was different because of it. Then drive it deep with the eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

The lesson leaves us a short reminder: you are not shaped by your circumstances; you are shaped by your “choices.” Most of our circumstances we cannot change, but the choice is always in our hands. Daniel couldn’t change Babylon, but he could decide what he ate, and he could decide which way his window faced.
One choice — you can’t see the difference; a hundred choices — they decide your direction. Brothers and sisters, the best time to correct your course is always now.
Your first thought this morning, that phone call at noon, that message tonight — in every small choice, choose Jesus.
Let’s declare together: Lord, in every choice I am willing to choose you, to establish God’s system, and to let Christ live out his life in me!

Let’s pray together. Lord Jesus, thank you for choosing us out of the world. Forgive us for so often comforting ourselves with big decisions while indulging ourselves in the small choices of every day. Enlighten the eyes of our hearts, so that in every thought and every decision we choose you. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
May each of you be like branches joined to the vine, no longer dry, but bearing much fruit. Let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

The Lord said: “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much” (Luke 16:10).

First, choose humility rather than insisting on your own way. “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6). 321 says: pride is leaving our originally intended position and grasping power; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position. So when you choose not to fight over that one remark, you haven’t lost; you have returned to your originally intended position.
Second, choose to rely on the Holy Spirit rather than on yourself. “‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says Yahweh of Armies” (Zechariah 4:6).

Third, choose to live by faith rather than by sight (2 Corinthians 5:7). The twelve spies saw the same land of Canaan; ten said, “We can’t go up,” two said, “Let’s go up at once.” What they saw was the same; what they chose was different — and the outcome differed by forty years.
Fourth, choose love rather than hate. “Love your enemies, … and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you” (Matthew 5:44).

The lesson says these choices look very small, yet the result of long-term accumulation is a changed life, changed relationships, a changed spiritual condition — and in the end, Christ lived out. Let’s do the sums: improve by just one per cent a day, and after a year it’s 37.8 times greater; decline by just one per cent a day, and only a thirtieth is left. The same 365 days, and a gap of more than a thousandfold. This is the compound interest of choice.

The British apologist C. S. Lewis wrote in “Mere Christianity” that every time you make a choice, you are turning the central part of you, the part that chooses, into something a little different from what it was before; and all the innumerable choices of a lifetime are slowly turning that central thing either into a heavenly creature or into a hellish creature. Brothers and sisters, no choice is neutral; every choice is carving you.

The lesson’s fourth key point is the reverse side of the same truth. When you choose pride, choose to rely on yourself, choose to go by your feelings, choose to hold a grudge, you are also establishing a system: the worldly system.

The lesson doesn’t say “you have sinned”; it says “you are establishing a system.” James describes the process as if in slow motion: “Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death” (James 1:15). The system is that production line.

Paul says: “Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath, and don’t give place to the devil” (Ephesians 4:26–27). “Place” in the original simply means “a place.” Every time we hold a grudge, we clear a little plot of ground in our heart for the enemy; clear enough of it, and he moves in to live there.
The lesson names three results of this system: the more you live, the more tired you get; the more you serve, the drier you become; the harder you try, the more powerless you feel.
Brothers and sisters, please ask yourself honestly: have you had days like that? You still go to the meetings, still take on the ministry, yet inside you feel as though you’ve been drained dry.

The lesson names the reason: because your life is not in the right environment. Like a fish out of water — however hard it tries, it cannot live. The moment a fish leaves the water, its gill filaments stick together and collapse.
Listen carefully: there is actually more oxygen on the bank than in the water. The fish doesn’t die from a lack of oxygen; it dies from leaving the water.

The Lord said: “Apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). This verse comes just before our key verse. The order can’t be reversed: first remain in the Lord, and the line appears of its own accord.

The lesson’s fifth key point answers exactly this: the starting point of revival is not behaviour but mindset. Mindset, choices, system, life — notice where this chain begins: not with effort, but with mindset.

Paul says: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind” (Romans 12:2). The Greek word for “transformed” is the very word used for a caterpillar becoming a butterfly. It isn’t about training a caterpillar to be a slightly faster caterpillar; it’s about letting it become a butterfly from the inside.

In the 1960s the University of Pennsylvania psychiatrist Aaron T. Beck discovered that what shapes our emotions and behaviour is often not the event itself but the automatic thoughts we have about it. Psychology says “change your thinking”; the Bible says “the renewing of your mind”; 321 says “change the mindset and you change the life.”
Which mindset needs renewing? The lesson points to two sentences. The first: “It is no longer I who live.” When you believe this, you will no longer feed the “self.”

Brothers and sisters, the “self” needs to eat. Every time you argue your own case, you feed it a mouthful; every time you feed on other people’s opinions of you, you feed it a big mouthful. The most effective way to deal with the “self” is not to fight it every day, but to stop feeding it.

The second sentence: “but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). When you believe this, you will naturally depend on God, obey God and live out God. Notice the word “naturally” — not “strive to,” but “naturally.”
So the lesson concludes: the real key isn’t effort; it’s what you believe.
The lesson’s last key point describes a truly heartbreaking phenomenon: many people know about selflessness, yet they can’t live it out.

Brothers and sisters, does that describe you? We can talk about it, we can teach it, we can even lead others through it. But we get home, one remark goes wrong, and that “self” is instantly back on its feet.
Why? The lesson’s answer is a single sentence: the mindset is still stuck in the “head.”
Hebrews diagnosed this sickness long ago: “but the word they heard didn’t profit them, because it wasn’t mixed with faith by those who heard” (Hebrews 4:2).
So how does real change happen? The lesson gives four steps: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation.

Revelation is the Holy Spirit opening up that knowledge and letting it drop from your head into your heart; Paul prays for “the eyes of your hearts enlightened” (Ephesians 1:18). Revelation isn’t your head knowing one more fact; it’s your heart seeing one more glimpse of God. Conviction is your whole being yielding; Implementation is really doing it. When “I have been crucified with Christ” moves from knowledge to revelation, your choices will change.

Repeated practice really does change people. In 2000, Eleanor Maguire’s team at University College London found that London taxi drivers, who must memorise tens of thousands of the city’s streets, had markedly greater grey-matter volume in the rear part of the hippocampus than the control group — and the longer they had been driving, the more pronounced the difference.
The lesson gives us three practices. First, notice your everyday choices: pay attention to your reactions in daily life — are they self-centred or selfless?

Today, set three reminders on your phone — morning, noon and evening. When one goes off, stop for thirty seconds and ask yourself: “In the past hour, have I been living in the self-centred life, or in selflessness?” You can also use David’s prayer: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts” (Psalm 139:23).

Second, deliberately make the right choice: in conflict, under pressure and amid strong emotions, practise choosing humility, faith and love. An instinctive reaction is the fastest, but often the oldest. Look at the Lord’s own choice: he “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7). Practise one very simple thing: the moment your emotions rise, don’t open your mouth yet; say silently in your heart, “Lord, in this matter I let you be King.”
Third, let mindset become action. Don’t stop at “I know”; live out “I already” in practice every day.
Be clear on the difference between three sentences: “I will” means I haven’t done it yet; “I can” means I do it in my own strength; “I already” means Christ has already accomplished it.
Every morning, declare aloud once: “I have been crucified with Christ.” Every night before bed, write down one choice you made today that was different because of it.
Then drive it deep with the eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
Remember that number: a new habit takes an average of sixty-six days to become automatic, so don’t give up on day five.
Brothers and sisters, the Three Foundations are three questions we ask at every choice: What would the Lord do? What does God’s word say? What is the Holy Spirit saying in my heart right now?

The Two Core Values are the criteria for every choice: this time, do “I” have the final say, or does the Lord? When it’s done, will people see me, or him? And the Goal is the direction of every choice we make: establish God’s system.

In our relationships we practise 920: everyone we relate to is our “2,” and before them we live out selflessness and bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23). Patience only grows when someone provokes you — that hardest-to-get-along-with “2” is the training ground God has given you. We also practise 235: walking with selfless people and building spiritual parents and children and teams of spiritual comrades.
The lesson leaves us a short but weighty reminder: you are not shaped by your circumstances; you are shaped by your “choices.”

Most of our circumstances we cannot change, but the choice is always in our hands. Daniel couldn’t change Babylon, but he could decide what he ate; he couldn’t change that decree, but he could decide which way his window faced. Moses said: “I have set before you life and death, the blessing and the curse. Therefore choose life” (Deuteronomy 30:19).

The lesson’s closing words say: life isn’t changed overnight; it is shaped through countless choices. One choice — you can’t see the difference; a hundred choices — they decide your direction. Our repetition isn’t held up by sheer willpower; it is the natural fruit of a branch joined to the vine.

So this morning I’m not calling you to make some earth-shaking big decision; I’m calling you back to today. Your very first thought this morning: will you choose to complain, or to give thanks? That phone call at noon: will you choose to argue, or humility? That message tonight: will you choose to hold a grudge, or to love? The great revival won’t suddenly drop out of the sky; it grows out of thousands upon thousands of small choices.
Let’s declare it together, out loud: Lord, in every choice I am willing to choose you, to establish God’s system, and to let Christ live out his life in me!

Let’s pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, thank you that you did not move us out of the world, yet you chose us out of the world. Forgive us for comforting ourselves with big decisions while indulging ourselves in the small choices of every day. Give us the spirit of wisdom and revelation, and enlighten the eyes of our hearts.

Lord, help us to choose you in every thought, every reaction and every decision; make us like Daniel, in Babylon yet not of Babylon; like branches joined to the vine, no longer dry, but bearing much fruit.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
May God bless you, brothers and sisters. Let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: You Are Not Just Living Your Life — You Are Establishing a System
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Before we come to today’s lesson, I’d like you to picture a very ordinary scene.

On a mountainside there is a slope covered in wild grass. The first person walks across it, and the grass is pressed down only a little; the next day it springs back up, and there is no trace left at all. A second person crosses the same way, then a third, a tenth, a hundredth. Six months later a faint pale line appears on the slope; a year later that pale line has become a firm little path; three years later, whoever comes that way doesn’t have to think at all — their feet simply take them onto that path.

Brothers and sisters, let me ask you: on what day was that path made?

On no day at all. Nobody held a meeting and decided to build a path there. Nobody drew up plans. Nobody turned a single spadeful of earth. That path was made by countless footsteps passing over it.

That is the first thing today’s lesson wants to say to us.

We often think of a “system” as something very large, as though only churches, nations and institutions deserve to be called systems. A system sounds remote — someone else’s business, the business of the people on the platform, the kind of thing that only comes about through endless meetings and pages of regulations.

But the lesson takes that misunderstanding apart right at the start. It says that, in fact, the way you live each day, your habits in making decisions, your attitude in responding to things — these are establishing a system.

Listen carefully to those three phrases.

First, the way you live each day. What is the first thing you do when you wake up in the morning? Where do you put your time? Where does your money flow?

Second, your habits in making decisions. When you stand at a fork in the road, do you first ask, “Do I like it?” or do you first ask, “Lord, what do you want me to do?”

Third, your attitude in responding to things. When someone bumps into you, what is the very first reaction that comes out of you?

Brothers and sisters, these three are the feet that cross that grassy slope, one pair after another. Every time you walk it, you press the path a little deeper. Walk it long enough and the path is no longer only your path; it becomes the path of the people in your home, the path of the people you serve, even the path of the next generation.

So the lesson says: this system affects not only you; it affects your family, your church, even a whole generation.

That is why today’s lesson is called “Care About Every Choice.” Not only the few big choices — whether to change jobs, whether to buy a house, whether to emigrate — but every choice: including the sentence you said to your spouse this morning, including the message you just sent in the group chat, including how you are going to respond in a moment to that person who makes you uncomfortable.

Because the kingdom of God has never been established from the big things down; it is established from the small things up. The Lord Jesus said, “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much.” (Luke 16:10)

Today we are going to walk six stretches of road with the lesson. First, a system begins with the individual, but it doesn’t stop with the individual. Second, a wrong choice brings the fall of a whole system. Third, two kinds of wisdom establish two kinds of system. Fourth, the way you lead determines the system you establish. Fifth, don’t bring the world’s system into God’s kingdom. Sixth, the key to establishing God’s system is 321.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background
sections.html:
Today’s lesson draws on two key passages: one is a negative warning, the other a positive standard. Let’s first get the background of these two passages clear, so that the rest of the road is firm underfoot.

(1) 1 Samuel 8: The Day a Nation Changed Its System

First and 2 Samuel were originally a single book, called “Samuel” in the Hebrew Bible. Jewish tradition holds that its material came from the hands of the prophet Samuel, the prophet Nathan and the seer Gad (see 1 Chronicles 29:29). The book records Israel’s crucial turning point, from the age of the judges into the age of the kingdom, roughly between 1100 and 1010 BC; the events of chapter 8 are generally dated around 1050 BC, at Ramah, Samuel’s home town.

Before that, Israel was a theocracy. They had no king, because Yahweh was their King. When the people fell into danger, God raised up judges to rescue them. This system had something very distinctive about it: it had no visible centre of power. All its reliance rested on the God who could not be seen, yet was truly present.

But Samuel had grown old. He appointed his two sons as judges in Beersheba, yet they “didn’t walk in his ways, but turned away after dishonest gain, took bribes, and perverted justice” (1 Samuel 8:3). So the elders of Israel gathered, came to Samuel at Ramah, and made a request. That request is the verse our lesson quotes today.

(2) James 3: Two Kinds of Wisdom in One Church

The James who wrote the letter of James is not either of the two Jameses among the twelve apostles, but the Lord Jesus’ brother in the flesh (Matthew 13:55; Galatians 1:19). The risen Lord appeared to him (1 Corinthians 15:7), and he later became a leader of the church in Jerusalem, one of those Paul calls the “pillars” of the church (Galatians 2:9).

The letter was written roughly between AD 45 and 49, and may well be the earliest book of the New Testament. It is addressed to “the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion” (James 1:1) — Jewish Christians scattered abroad by persecution.

The first half of James 3 is about the tongue; the second half is about wisdom. Why put the two together? Because the church of that day had problems: some were jostling to be teachers (James 3:1), some were biting one another with their tongues, and there were even “wars and fightings” in the church (James 4:1). James did not begin by revising the structure; he went first to the source of wisdom. He asks, “Who is wise and understanding among you? Let him show by his good conduct that his deeds are done in gentleness of wisdom.” (James 3:13)

Brothers and sisters, notice that order. Whatever wisdom people use, that is the system they establish. First Samuel 8 shows us how one wrong choice can tear down a system; James 3 shows us how two kinds of wisdom grow two utterly different environments.

sections.heading: 3. A System Begins with the Individual, but Doesn’t Stop There
sections.html:
The lesson says that systems exist on different levels: the individual, the family, the church, the nation.

These four levels are really like four concentric circles, one ring enclosing the next. The psychologist Urie Bronfenbrenner, in The Ecology of Human Development, published in 1979, put forward his well-known “ecological systems theory.” He pointed out that a person’s growth never happens in a vacuum; it is shaped by environment upon environment, layer upon layer — innermost the family and close relationships, further out school and community, further out still culture and institutions. His conclusion was this: if you want to understand a person, you have to understand the layers of systems that person lives in.

The Bible said this thousands of years before the theory. When God saves a person, he never thinks only of that one person. God said to Abraham, “All the families of the earth will be blessed through you.” (Genesis 12:3) When God spoke to Noah, he saved Noah “with all of your household” (Genesis 7:1). In the New Testament, the Philippian jailer asked Paul in the middle of the night, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” And the answer was, “Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your household.” (Acts 16:30-31)

The lesson goes on to state a principle of influence: the larger the system, the greater the influence.

It uses a lovely comparison: a fish in a fish tank, and a fish in the ocean.

This comparison is not just a literary flourish; there is something behind it. In ichthyology there is a class of fish known as “indeterminate growers” — goldfish and koi, for example. They keep growing all their lives, and how fast and how far they grow is heavily affected by the size of the body of water, its quality and its dissolved oxygen. The very same koi, kept in a small tank in the living room, may spend its whole life at little more than ten centimetres; put it in a spacious pond and it can grow to sixty or seventy centimetres.

The same water, the same fish — but a different environment, and a different scale of life.

Brothers and sisters, please take this to heart: the size of the system you place yourself in is the size your life will grow to. Some people’s spiritual horizon, all their lives, is no bigger than their own little fish tank — my needs, my grievances, my plans, my face. Others live in the ocean of God’s kingdom — God’s heart, God’s household, God’s kingdom. They are equally born again and saved, yet the scale of their lives is worlds apart.

Yet the lesson immediately pulls us back to the most crucial point: everything begins with “the individual.”

This is what 321 means by “life first, then relationships, then ministry.” It is true that the larger the system, the greater its influence; but a system is not built from the large down to the small; it grows from the small up to the large. The kingdom of God is not an organisation dropped from the sky. The Lord Jesus said it is like a mustard seed, “which indeed is smaller than all seeds. But when it is grown, it is greater than the herbs” (Matthew 13:32).

So the lesson puts it very directly: if individuals have not established God’s system, families cannot be healthy, churches cannot be united, and the kingdom cannot be revived.

The psalmist said it long ago: “Unless Yahweh builds the house, they who build it labor in vain. Unless Yahweh watches over the city, the watchman guards it in vain.” (Psalm 127:1)

Notice the words “in vain.” They don’t mean “builds more slowly,” nor “builds less well”; they mean “labours for nothing.” A person can be extremely hard-working, extremely self-sacrificing, extremely gifted — and yet be building a house God never asked them to build. Brothers and sisters, how much that deserves our quiet reflection.

In pastoral ministry I often meet brothers and sisters like this. There was one sister who had a part in every ministry in the church, large or small — Sunday school, welcoming, visitation, the kitchen; she never missed a thing. But one day she said to me through her tears, “Pastor, at church I’m the busiest person there; at home I’m the biggest stranger. My children have to book an appointment to talk to me.”

It wasn’t that she didn’t love the Lord; she loved him dearly. She had simply got the order of the system the wrong way round — she started building from the outermost ring and never built the innermost one first.

The Lord Jesus said, “But seek first God’s Kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.” (Matthew 6:33) Those words “seek first” are precisely about order.

Brothers and sisters, please don’t get the order wrong. It is not “once the church is healthy, I’ll be healthy,” but “once I am healthy, the church can become healthy.” It is not “wait for my family to change first,” but “I change first, and then my family will change.” The Goal of 321 is to establish God’s system, and in that Goal, the first brick is always laid on you yourself.

sections.heading: 4. A Wrong Choice Brings the Fall of a Whole System
sections.html:
“They said to him, ‘Behold, you are old, and your sons don’t walk in your ways. Now make us a king to judge us like all the nations.’” (1 Samuel 8:5)

Brothers and sisters, notice that on the surface this sounds entirely reasonable. Samuel was old — that was a fact. His sons were corrupt — that too was a fact. What the elders put forward was a proposal grounded in reality, one that looked very responsible.

But how did God see it?

“Yahweh said to Samuel, ‘Listen to the voice of the people in all that they tell you; for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me as the king over them.’” (1 Samuel 8:7)

With a single sentence God peels away the outward reasons and exposes the real problem underneath. The word “rejected” is the Hebrew מָאַס (ma’as), meaning to refuse, to cast away, to regard as useless. The people were not adjusting a structure; they were casting away their King.

So the lesson rightly asks: what was Israel’s problem?

First, they were not content to have God as King. Second, they wanted to be like the world.

“Like all the nations” — that short phrase is the key to the whole passage. Later the people said it again, even more bluntly: “No; but we will have a king over us, that we also may be like all the nations, and that our king may judge us, and go out before us, and fight our battles.” (1 Samuel 8:19-20)

What they wanted was not a better leader; what they wanted was “something visible to lean on.” What they wanted was not justice; what they wanted was “to be like everyone else.”

Psychology calls this force conformity. In 1951 the psychologist Solomon Asch ran a famous series of experiments at Swarthmore College. Participants were asked to judge which of three lines was the same length as a standard line. The answer was obvious; a person answering alone almost never got it wrong. But when everyone else in the room — all of them, in fact, the experimenter’s confederates — unanimously gave a plainly wrong answer, about three-quarters of the real participants conformed at least once; overall, in roughly a third of the critical trials, participants went along with the wrong answer.

Brothers and sisters, think about it: if people will give an answer against their own judgement about something as simple as the length of a line, just because of other people — how much more about something invisible like “shall we let God be King?”

The pressure to be “like all the nations” has been blowing from 1050 BC right down to today.

The lesson says this was a “choice.” But the result of that choice was a shift from the rule of God to the rule of man, from God’s system to the Worldly system.

This is exactly the change of perspective 321 speaks of — only running in reverse. 321 calls us to turn from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. What Israel did that day was those four turns in the opposite direction: they exchanged God’s for man’s, the heavenly for the earthly, the eternal for the temporary, the godly for the worldly.

Samuel spelled out the consequences to them one by one: the king would take their sons for his chariots and to be his horsemen; he would take their daughters to be perfumers, cooks and bakers; he would take the best of their fields, vineyards and olive groves; he would take a tenth of their grain and of their vineyards; and in the end, “you will be his servants” (1 Samuel 8:11-17).

Did the people hear? They heard. Did the people change? They did not. “But the people refused to listen to the voice of Samuel” (1 Samuel 8:19).

And so the three results the lesson names came true, one after another.

First, the nation was divided. After Solomon died, his son Rehoboam chose to rule the people with a heavier yoke, and ten tribes abandoned the house of David, saying, “To your tents, Israel!” (1 Kings 12:16) One kingdom split into two, north and south.

Second, spiritual corruption. The northern kingdom of Israel had nineteen kings in all, and Scripture’s verdict on every one of them is the same: none was good; all did what was evil in Yahweh’s sight.

Third, the road to destruction. In 722 BC the northern kingdom was destroyed by Assyria; in 586 BC Jerusalem, in the southern kingdom, fell to Babylon, and the temple was burned.

Brothers and sisters, between that phrase “like all the nations” in 1 Samuel 8 and the fall of Jerusalem’s walls lie more than four hundred years. One wrong choice affected a whole generation.

That is why the lesson is called “Care About Every Choice.” Because at the moment of choosing, you often cannot see where it ends.

sections.heading: 5. Two Kinds of Wisdom Establish Two Kinds of System
sections.html:
At this point the lesson quotes James 3:14-18. Let’s read the whole passage through once:

“But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your heart, don’t boast and don’t lie against the truth. This wisdom is not that which comes down from above, but is earthly, sensual, and demonic. For where jealousy and selfish ambition are, there is confusion and every evil deed. But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy. Now the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.” (James 3:14-18)

Scripture tells us plainly here: there are two kinds of wisdom.

(1) Worldly wisdom is the wisdom of the self-centred life

James says this wisdom “is earthly, sensual, and demonic.” The three words in the original descend in stages. “Earthly” is ἐπίγειος (epigeios): its vision reaches no further than the horizon. “Sensual” is ψυχικός (psychikos), literally “of the soul,” driven by human emotion, will and desire. “Demonic” is δαιμονιώδης (daimoniōdēs): its source, astonishingly, is the power of darkness. Brothers and sisters, this is a staircase going down: first the vision grows short, then the soul takes charge, and finally Satan makes use of it.

The lesson lists four fruits of this wisdom: jealousy, selfish ambition, selfishness and confusion.

“Jealousy” is ζῆλος (zēlos) in the original. The word is neutral in itself — “zeal” — but once it centres on “self,” zeal turns into being unable to bear seeing others do well. “Selfish ambition” is ἐριθεία (eritheia), a word that originally described the mindset of a hired hand working for his wages, and came to mean “forming factions for one’s own advantage.” Notice that there is nothing in this word about “contending for the truth”; there is only “I want to win.”

And the result? James says, “For where jealousy and selfish ambition are, there is confusion and every evil deed.” (James 3:16) “Confusion” is ἀκαταστασία (akatastasia) in the original: turmoil, disorder, an inability to settle.

Brothers and sisters, isn’t this exactly what 321 says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose. When a self-centred person meets a self-centred person, it is like two stones striking each other — what comes off is not sparks, but chips.

Professor John Gottman of the University of Washington, a leading authority on marriage research, found in a longitudinal study carried out with Robert Levenson in 1992 that the most accurate predictor of whether a couple would divorce was not whether they argued but how they argued. He called criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling the “Four Horsemen” of marriage, and the most destructive of them is contempt. In his long-term samples, by watching just a few minutes of a couple’s interaction, he could predict with roughly ninety per cent accuracy whether they would later divorce.

What is contempt? Contempt is “I am above you.” Contempt is the self-centred life at its most naked.

(2) The wisdom from above is the wisdom of selflessness

“But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.” (James 3:17)

The lesson lists the qualities of this wisdom as purity, peace, gentleness, yieldedness, mercy and abundant fruit. Here we need to match the wording precisely. Where the Chinese Union Version has a single phrase for “gentle and yielding,” the original has two words: ἐπιεικής (epieikēs), meaning forbearing, not insisting on one’s own rights; and εὐπειθής (eupeithēs), meaning easily persuaded, willing to listen to counsel. And where the Chinese Union Version says “abundant in good fruit,” it is not a vague “bearing much fruit” but bearing fruit that is good.

Notice James’s order: “first pure, then peaceful.” Purity comes first, peace after. Because peace without purity is only compromise, only papering over the cracks. Only when we are first pure before God can there be true peace with others.

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed? “Not insisting on one’s own rights” and “willing to listen to counsel” — these two are exactly what 321 calls selflessness. 321 says: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. ἐπιεικής is laying down our rights; εὐπειθής is returning to our originally intended position.

And the result? The lesson says: peace, the fruit of righteousness, growth in life. James says, “Now the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.” (James 3:18)

This is a farmer’s picture. The fruit of righteousness is not argued into being; it is sown and grown. And the seed that is sown has a name: peace. Whatever seed you scatter in a home or in a church, that is what you will reap.

So the lesson sums it up in one sentence: whichever wisdom you use, that is the system you establish.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly where 321’s 920 practice comes in. Everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; before them we practise living out the “0,” the selfless life; and what grows from it is the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22-23)

You see, the list in James 3:17 and the list in Galatians 5:22 are scenery along the same road. For the wisdom from above is, in the end, the wisdom of the Holy Spirit.

sections.heading: 6. The Way You Lead Determines the System You Establish
sections.html:
Here the lesson asks three very concrete and very piercing questions:

In the family — is it control, or love?

In the church — is it power, or service?

In relationships — is it demanding, or building others up?

Brothers and sisters, please don’t rush to answer. First, think back to last night.

The Lord Jesus himself laid out these two roads with perfect clarity: “But Jesus summoned them, and said, ‘You know that the rulers of the nations lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. It shall not be so among you, but whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant. Whoever desires to be first among you shall be your bondservant, even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.’” (Matthew 20:25-28)

“It shall not be so among you.” Those few words are the watershed between the two systems.

Peter learned this lesson too. In his old age he wrote to the elders: “Shepherd the flock of God which is among you, exercising the oversight, not under compulsion, but voluntarily, not for dishonest gain, but willingly; not as lording it over those entrusted to you, but making yourselves examples to the flock.” (1 Peter 5:2-3)

Not lording it over them, but being an example. This is the first of 321’s Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model. And we ourselves are to become a role model for others.

The lesson says: every choice is establishing an environment.

Kurt Lewin, the father of social psychology, carried out a classic study in 1939 with Ronald Lippitt and Ralph White. They divided boys of about ten years old into several groups doing handicrafts, and gave them adult leaders of three different styles: autocratic, democratic and laissez-faire. The results were very clear. The autocratic groups’ output was not low, but the groups were full of hostility and aggression, and as soon as the leader left the room, work stopped at once. The democratic groups were friendly and cooperative, and even when the leader was absent the boys kept on working.

Brothers and sisters, pay special attention to that detail: what happens once the leader leaves the room.

That is the system you have really established.

Control establishes an environment where people “only move when someone is watching”; love establishes an environment where people “are willing even when no one is watching.” Power establishes a church that “is afraid of you”; service establishes a church that “becomes like you.” Demanding establishes a group of people who “don’t dare make a mistake”; building others up establishes a group of people who “dare to grow up.”

The organisational psychologist Edgar Schein, in Organizational Culture and Leadership (first edition 1985), wrote a much-quoted line: culture and leadership are two sides of the same coin. In his view, the most important work of leaders is to create and manage culture.

The lesson says that over time this forms a culture, an atmosphere, a system.

Brothers and sisters, culture is not a slogan on the wall; culture is “the way we usually do things around here.” When someone in your family makes a mistake, do they usually hide first, or come to you first? When someone in your small group is struggling, do they usually put on a mask, or tell the truth? That “usually” is the system you have established.

And how was it established? Not through one special conference, but through your choices, made again and again. Just like that path on the mountainside.

321 says: people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things; life first, then relationships, then ministry. When we lead by control, power and demands, we are putting tasks ahead of people; only when we lead by love, service and building others up are we putting people ahead of tasks.

Paul says, “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself” (Philippians 2:3). Brothers and sisters, if this one verse were truly lived out in a home, that home would become God’s system.

Let’s turn the lesson’s three questions into three very concrete scenes for you to take home.

The first scene is at home. Your child brings home a report card, and it isn’t good. The controlling response is: “See? I told you so, and you wouldn’t listen.” The loving response is: “Let’s look at it together and see where you got stuck.” Both are concern, both are for the child’s good; but the first response establishes a home of “I don’t dare let you know,” and the second establishes a home of “when something happens, I’ll tell you first.” Ten years from now, how far apart will those two homes be?

The second scene is at church. A young co-worker has made a mess of a task. The response of power is: “Don’t give him this job again.” The response of service is: “I’ll go through it with him one more time.” Both are being responsible; but the first response establishes a team where “only a handful of people dare to lift a finger,” and the second establishes a team where “new people keep growing up.”

The third scene is in relationships. Your spiritual companion has a gift that is stronger than yours. The demanding response is: “Why isn’t he helping more?” The response that builds up is: “I want to find a way to give his gift a stage.” In Ephesians 4:11-12 Paul says that the fivefold ministry the Lord gave is “for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ.” Building people up is the very purpose for which God established those ministries.

sections.heading: 7. Don’t Bring the World’s System into God’s Kingdom
sections.html:
Here the lesson says something that cuts deep: very often the problem is not that we aren’t serving, but that we are serving in “the world’s way.”

Brothers and sisters, listen to that once more. The problem is not that there is no service; the problem is the way we serve.

The lesson gives three examples: competition in place of building others up, control in place of leading, performance in place of life.

None of these three substitutions involves not working; on the contrary, they often involve working very hard. The most dangerous thing in a church has never been laziness; it is doing God’s work with worldly drive.

Paul puts it with absolute firmness: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2)

The word “world” in Greek is κόσμος (kosmos). Its original meaning is “an ordered arrangement, a system,” the opposite of chaos. Brothers and sisters, do you see it? The very word Scripture uses for “the world” means “a system.” The world is not a heap of loose sand; the world is a system that runs with great precision and great allure.

The apostle John names the three pillars of this system: “For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s.” (1 John 2:16)

The lust of the flesh is “I want to feel good”; the lust of the eyes is “I want to possess”; the pride of life is “I want to be seen.”

Brothers and sisters, “I want to be seen” is precisely the root of “performance in place of life.”

Psychology has observed this very clearly. In 1971 the psychologist Edward Deci found that when people are doing something out of their own interest, once they start doing it for an external reward, the reward actually erodes their inner motivation. In 1973 Mark Lepper, David Greene and Richard Nisbett ran a well-known experiment at Stanford University. They took young children who already liked drawing, and told one group in advance, “When you finish your drawing you’ll get a certificate.” The result: the group that expected a reward spent noticeably less time drawing of their own accord during later free play. This phenomenon came to be known as the “overjustification effect.”

Brothers and sisters, this gives us a sober warning: when service begins to be for applause, the heart of service begins to die. The busier things are on the outside, the drier they are within.

The lesson says: this is bringing Babylon into the church.

In Scripture, Babylon has never been just a city. From the Tower of Babel in Genesis 11 — “Come, let’s build ourselves a city, and a tower whose top reaches to the sky, and let’s make a name for ourselves, lest we be scattered abroad on the surface of the whole earth” (Genesis 11:4) — the spirit of Babylon was set: man climbing upward by his own strength, man making a name for himself. By the time we reach Revelation, God issues a call to his people: “Come out of her, my people, that you have no participation in her sins, and that you don’t receive of her plagues” (Revelation 18:4).

The lesson says the result is: busy on the outside, dry within.

Scripture really does describe such a church. The Lord said to the church in Sardis, “I know your works, that you have a reputation of being alive, but you are dead.” (Revelation 3:1)

A reputation of being alive, but dead. Brothers and sisters, what a fearful sentence that is.

321 says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you are glad, rely on the brain and you are troubled. 321 also says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. When we shift our focus from Jesus to what people think of us, we are already building God’s temple the Babylonian way.

Paul reminds us, “But let each man be careful how he builds on it.” (1 Corinthians 3:10) He does not say “whether to build”; he says “how to build.” Because “if anyone builds on the foundation with gold, silver, costly stones, wood, hay, or stubble, each man’s work will be revealed. For the Day will declare it, because it is revealed in fire; and the fire itself will test what sort of work each man’s work is” (1 Corinthians 3:12-13).

sections.heading: 8. The Key to Establishing God’s System: 321
sections.html:
The lesson puts it beautifully: establishing God’s system does not depend on methods; it means going back to the foundation.

Paul says, “For no one can lay any other foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ.” (1 Corinthians 3:11)

The foundation is not ours to lay; the foundation has already been laid. What we have to do is go back and build on that foundation.

The lesson divides this foundation into five practical realities.

The Three Foundations

First, Jesus is my role model. When I don’t know what to do, I ask: what would Jesus do? On the night of his greatest authority, what he picked up was a towel for washing feet — he “arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist. Then he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet” (John 13:4-5).

Second, the Bible is my standard. Not my feelings, not majority opinion, not the way the wind of this age is blowing. “Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.” (Psalm 119:105)

Third, the Holy Spirit is my guide. Not cleverness, not experience. “‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says Yahweh of Armies.” (Zechariah 4:6)

The Two Core Values

First, let Jesus be King. This is the very opposite of 1 Samuel 8. Israel said, “We want a king, like all the nations”; we are to say, “Lord, you are my King.”

Second, let Jesus receive the glory. Not me receiving the glory, not my ministry receiving the glory, not my family or my church receiving the glory. “For of him, and through him, and to him are all things. To him be the glory for ever! Amen.” (Romans 11:36)

The lesson says: when these five realities are lived out, God’s system is being established.

Brothers and sisters, notice the words “lived out.” The lesson’s last sentence carries great weight: not slogans, but every choice.

Slogans hang on the wall; choices are walked out underfoot.

We can also see it along 321’s Path of Serving: Spirit — the Holy Spirit is my guide; Understanding — the Bible is my standard; Life — Jesus is my role model; Service — let Jesus be King; God — let Jesus receive all the glory. The end of that path is exactly the Goal of 321: establish God’s system.

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed? The Goal of 321 is exactly the subject of today’s lesson. The Three Foundations plus the Two Core Values are not five nice-sounding sentences; they are five realities that must be cashed out in every single choice.

There is a little mathematical calculation that shows the weight of “every choice” very well. If a person improves by just one per cent a day, after three hundred and sixty-five days they are at 1.01 to the power of 365 — about 37.8 times where they began. Conversely, if they slip back one per cent a day, after a year they are left with 0.99 to the power of 365 — about 0.03, almost nothing. The same one per cent, in different directions, and after a year the difference is more than a thousandfold.

This is not motivational talk; this is the truth about “every choice.” A system grows exactly like this, one day at a time.

sections.heading: 9. Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s walk today’s road once more and string the 321 vision together.

First, the Goal: establish God’s system. This is where all of 321’s practice is headed, and it is the theme of today’s lesson. We do not pursue selflessness to make ourselves better; we pursue it so that God’s kingdom may be established on earth. The Lord taught us to pray, “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:10)

Second, the self-centred life and selflessness. “Like all the nations” in 1 Samuel 8 is the self-centred life; the “gentle, reasonable” of James 3 is selflessness. The self-centred life builds Babylon; selflessness builds Jerusalem. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out — “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

Third, humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. When Israel wanted a king, they were reaching to seize a visible power; when Rehoboam chose the heavier yoke, he too was seizing power. “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6) Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

Fourth, the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. This is exactly the order of the lesson’s conclusion. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry. A system is what these five changes add up to.

Fifth, life first, then relationships, then ministry. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. What points four and five of the lesson expose is that we so often turn this order upside down — grabbing at ministry first, managing relationships second, and only thinking of life last. Turn the order upside down, and the system is bent out of shape.

Sixth, the change of perspective: from man’s to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. First Samuel 8 is those four turns in reverse; today we are to turn each of them back again.

Seventh, the 920 practice and 235 relationships. In the family, in the small group, at work — everyone you have a relationship with is your “2”; before them you live out the “0” and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions, and this is the smallest and truest unit of God’s system. Going further, you become a “2,” a spiritual companion, with a selfless person; you form the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children; you become part of the “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades — and so God’s system grows, ring by ring.

sections.heading: 10. Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. Let’s take them deeper one at a time, using 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: Examine the system I am establishing

Ask yourself honestly: my present daily living, my family, my service — are they God’s system or the Worldly system?

Information: Today you have heard the two lists of the two kinds of wisdom. Copy out James 3:17 and stick it somewhere you’ll see it every day.

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light. Don’t ask, “Have I committed any big sins?” Ask, “What atmosphere is growing in my home and in my service?”

Conviction: Admit that I really am building something. If I don’t admit it, I will never check whether I am building it right.

Implementation: Tonight, take a sheet of paper and draw two columns. On the left, write “the three moods that come up most often in my home”; on the right, write the qualities listed in James 3:17; then compare them.

Evaluation: This week, on which day did I respond to someone in an earthly, soulish way?

Correction: Say to the person I affected: “I’m sorry; my attitude that day was wrong.”

Repetition: Examine yourself regularly, every Sunday evening; don’t do it just once and call it done.

Multiplication: Take this self-examination into your small group, and bring one person to do it with you.

Practice 2: Choose the wisdom that comes from heaven

In conflicts and decisions, don’t follow emotion and instinct; choose a response of peace, gentleness and humility.

Information: Remember James’s order — first pure, then peaceful. That order cannot be reversed.

Revelation: In the moment of conflict, ask the Holy Spirit to remind you: what is stirring in me right now — jealousy, or peace?

Conviction: Believe that the Lord Jesus’ way really is right, even when in the moment it looks like losing out.

Implementation: Set a concrete rule, for example: when emotions rise, stay quiet for sixty seconds before you speak.

Evaluation: Was there anything I said today that my emotions said, not the Holy Spirit?

Correction: Turn back straight away, take those words back, and say it more gently than the first time.

Repetition: Once a day, seven times a week, three hundred and sixty-five times a year. Remember that 1.01 calculation.

Multiplication: When someone at home asks you, “Why have you changed?”, tell them about the wisdom from above.

Practice 3: Change your environment, starting with yourself

Don’t wait for your environment to change; start by living out 321 yourself, so that God’s system spreads outward from you.

Information: “Unless Yahweh builds the house, they who build it labor in vain.” (Psalm 127:1)

Revelation: See that God has already placed a “seed of God’s system” within you.

Conviction: From today on, stop saying, “Let the others change first.”

Implementation: This week, choose one of your “2”s — a family member, a co-worker — and in a concrete way live out one of the nine graces towards that person.

Evaluation: This week, did I slip back again into the mindset of “waiting for my environment to change”?

Correction: Change every sentence that runs “He ought to do this and that” into “Lord, change me first.”

Repetition: Keep it up for four weeks; don’t do it only once.

Multiplication: Bring one person to walk with you and become your spiritual companion — this is the beginning of a 235 relationship.

sections.heading: 11. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the lesson’s conclusion says: a system is not established in a day; it is the result of countless choices added together.

Then it gives us a very clear road: when one person changes, a family changes; when a family changes, a church changes; when a church changes, a generation changes.

Look where that road begins — with “one person.”

And that one person is sitting right here this morning, listening to this lesson.

Let’s go back to the grassy slope where we started. You don’t have to wait for someone to come and build a highway; you only have to walk it once more today. Walk in the right direction, walk across, and walk it again tomorrow. A year from now, the path will be there; ten years from now, your children will be walking that path; a hundred years from now, perhaps someone you have never met will walk the path your feet wore down, and it will bring them into the presence of God.

At the end of his life Joshua stood at Shechem and said to all Israel, “If it seems evil to you to serve Yahweh, choose today whom you will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell; but as for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh.” (Joshua 24:15)

“As for me and my house” — Joshua didn’t wait for anyone else. He began with himself, with his own household.

Brothers and sisters, starting today: in every choice, let Jesus be King, and let God’s system be established on earth.

Not for our name, but for his name. Not that I receive the glory, but that Jesus receives all the glory.

keyVerses: James 3:17-18

“But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy. Now the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.” (James 3:17-18)
1 Samuel 8:5
“They said to him, ‘Behold, you are old, and your sons don’t walk in your ways. Now make us a king to judge us like all the nations.’” (1 Samuel 8:5)
1 Corinthians 3:11
“For no one can lay any other foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ.” (1 Corinthians 3:11)
declarations: The lesson leaves us with a short but powerful sentence:
You are not just “living your life”; you are “establishing a system.”

Brothers and sisters, keep this sentence in your heart. The glass of water you poured this morning, the sentence you spoke today, the message you held back from answering today — they look like nothing more than daily life, but in fact they are bricks.
Then let us make this declaration of faith together:
Lord, I am willing to begin with myself, to bring every choice back into you, to establish God’s system, and to let your kingdom reign in my life!
practices: Examine the system I am establishing
Choose the wisdom that comes from heaven
Change my environment, starting with myself
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

This morning you have shown us that we are not just living our lives; we are establishing a system. The way we live each day, our habits every time we make a decision, our attitude every time we respond to something — all of these are wearing a path in our families, our churches and our generation.

Lord, forgive us. So often, like Israel, we want to be “like all the nations”; so often we handle relationships with earthly, soulish wisdom — competition in place of building others up, control in place of leading, performance in place of life — and we bring Babylon into your house.

Lord, wash us clean with your precious blood, and give us the wisdom that is from above — first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.

Help us, starting with the very first choice of today: to let Jesus be my role model, to let the Bible be my standard, to let the Holy Spirit be my guide, to let Jesus be King, and to let Jesus receive all the glory.
Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Think back to one small choice you made this week (a sentence, a message, an attitude). If that choice were repeated for a year, what kind of culture would it establish in your home? Compare it with James 3:17: “But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.”

In your present service, is there anything that you are “doing,” but doing in the world’s way? Compare it with Romans 12:2: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” How do you plan to hand it back to the Lord and let Jesus be King?

blocks.x: You’re Not Just Living Your Life — You’re Establishing a System
Morning Devotion 321 · Lesson 110 · Blog Post

On a mountainside there is a slope covered in wild grass. The first person walks across it, and the grass is pressed down only a little; the next day it springs back up. A second person crosses too, then a third, a tenth, a hundredth.

Six months later a faint pale line appears there; a year later that pale line has become a firm little path; three years later, whoever comes that way doesn’t have to think at all — their feet simply take them onto that path.
So let me ask: on what day was that path made?
On no day at all. Nobody held a meeting to decide on it, nobody drew up plans, nobody turned a single spadeful of earth. That path was made by “countless footsteps passing over it.”
1. A System Isn’t Something Big — It’s Small Choices

We often think of a “system” as something very large, as though only churches, nations and institutions deserve to be called systems. But in fact, the way you live each day, your habits in making decisions, and your attitude in responding to things are establishing a system.

What is the first thing you do when you wake up in the morning? Where do you put your time? When you stand at a fork in the road, do you first ask, “Do I like it?” or do you first ask, “Lord, what do you want me to do?” When someone bumps into you, what is the very first reaction that comes out of you?
These look like nothing more than daily life, but in fact they are bricks. And this system affects not only you; it affects your family, your church, even a whole generation.
The Lord Jesus said: “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much.” (Luke 16:10)
2. Two Kinds of Wisdom Grow Two Kinds of Environment
The Bible tells us there are two kinds of wisdom — and whichever wisdom we use, that is the system we establish.

One is worldly wisdom. James says it “is earthly, sensual, and demonic,” and the fruit it bears is jealousy, selfish ambition, selfishness and confusion: “For where jealousy and selfish ambition are, there is confusion and every evil deed.” (James 3:16)

The other is the wisdom from above: “But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.” (James 3:17)
Notice the order: first pure, then peaceful. Purity comes first, peace after. Peace without purity is only papering over the cracks.

In a 1992 longitudinal study, the marriage researcher John Gottman found that the most accurate predictor of whether a couple would divorce was not whether they argued but how they argued — and the single most destructive element was contempt. What is contempt? Contempt is “I am above you.”
3. Don’t Bring the World’s Ways into God’s House

Very often the problem is not that we aren’t serving, but that we are serving in the world’s way: competition in place of building others up, control in place of leading, performance in place of life.

In a classic 1939 study, the psychologist Kurt Lewin found that in groups with an autocratic leader, work stopped the moment the leader left the room; in groups with a democratic leader, the children carried on cooperating even when the leader wasn’t there.
What things look like once the leader has left is the system you have really established.
Control establishes an environment where people “only move when someone is watching”; love establishes an environment where people “are willing even when no one is watching.”
4. It Starts with One Person

Establishing God’s system doesn’t depend on methods; it means going back to the foundation: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide; let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.
When these five realities are lived out, God’s system is being established. Not slogans, but every choice.

A system is not established in a day; it is the result of countless choices added together. When one person changes, a family changes; when a family changes, a church changes; when a church changes, a generation changes.
The starting point is always “one person.” Joshua said: “But as for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh.” (Joshua 24:15) He didn’t wait for anyone else.
You don’t have to wait for someone to come and build a highway; you only have to walk it once more today, and once more tomorrow. A year from now, the path will be there.
Question for Reflection
If the reaction that came out of you most often this week were repeated for a whole year, what kind of culture would it establish in your home?

brief12.title: Caring About Every Choice
notes: Slide text:
A Change of Choices (8): Establishing a System
“But the wisdom that is from above
is first pure, then peaceful.”
(James 3:17)
Key points:
1. The title and subtitle come from the lesson: A Change of Choices (8): Establishing a System.
2. Key verses James 3:17–18: read the full passage first and let everyone settle into quiet.
3. State the main thread: a system isn’t established in a day; it is the sum of countless choices.
4. Preview the six points, from “the individual” all the way to “321”.

brief12.title: You’re Not Just Living Your Life
notes: Slide text:
The path worn across a grassy slope
Nobody designed it, yet it’s real
Lifestyle, decision habits, responses
These three are establishing a system
Key points:
1. Open with the path across the grassy slope: the path wasn’t built; it was walked into being.
2. Bring in the three phrases of the lesson’s introduction: the way you live, your habits in making decisions, your attitude in responding.
3. Quote Luke 16:10: “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much.”
4. Stress: the system affects not only you, but your family, your church and a whole generation.

brief12.title: Key Verses and Background
notes: Slide text:
1 Sam 8: Israel wants to be like the nations
James 3: two wisdoms, two outcomes
“The foundation which has been laid,
which is Jesus Christ.” (1 Cor 3:11)
Key points:
1. 1 Samuel 8: around 1050 BC, at Ramah; Israel had been a theocracy.
2. The author of James is the Lord Jesus’ brother in the flesh, writing around AD 45–49.
3. Faced with strife in the church, James didn’t revise the structure first; he went to the source of wisdom (James 3:13).
4. One passage is a negative warning, the other a positive standard; the foundation is 1 Corinthians 3:11.

brief12.title: 1. A System Begins with the Individual
notes: Slide text:
Levels: individual, family, church, nation
The larger the system, the greater its influence
A fish in a tank, a fish in the ocean
But it all begins with “the individual”
Key points:
1. Bronfenbrenner’s ecological systems theory, The Ecology of Human Development (1979): layer upon layer of concentric circles.
2. Ichthyology: goldfish and koi are indeterminate growers — the bigger the body of water, the bigger they grow.
3. Scripture’s order: Acts 16:31, “you will be saved, you and your household.”
4. Psalm 127:1: “Unless Yahweh builds the house, they who build it labor in vain.”
5. 321: life first, then relationships, then ministry; the first brick is laid on yourself.

brief12.title: 2. One Wrong Choice
notes: Slide text:
“Now make us a king to judge us
like all the nations.” (1 Sam 8:5)
From God’s rule to man’s, godly to worldly
Division, corruption, destruction
Key points:
1. 1 Samuel 8:7: God says they have rejected me as king over them.
2. “Rejected” is the Hebrew ma’as: to refuse, cast away, regard as useless.
3. Asch’s 1951 conformity experiments: about three-quarters conformed at least once.
4. Consequences: the kingdom divided (1 Kings 12:16); the north fell in 722 BC, the south in 586 BC.
5. 321: the shift of perspective run in reverse — God’s exchanged for man’s, the eternal for the temporary.

brief12.title: 3. Two Wisdoms, Two Systems
notes: Slide text:
Self-centred: jealousy, ambition, selfishness, confusion
Result: confusion and every evil deed
Selfless: pure, peaceful, gentle, reasonable
Result: the fruit of righteousness sown in peace
Key points:
1. Read the whole of James 3:14–18, noting the wording “selfish ambition”, “gentle, reasonable” and “full of… good fruits”.
2. Original language: earthly (epigeios), soulish (psychikos), demonic (daimoniōdēs) — a staircase going down.
3. Gottman’s 1992 study: contempt is the strongest predictor of divorce.
4. “First pure, then peaceful” — the order cannot be reversed.
5. 321: the 920 practice — live out the “0” before every “2” and bear the ninefold fruit.

brief12.title: 4. How Do You Lead?
notes: Slide text:
Family: control, or love?
Church: power, or service?
Relationships: demanding, or building up?
“It shall not be so among you” (Matt 20:26)
Key points:
1. Matthew 20:25–28: the Lord says, “It shall not be so among you.”
2. 1 Peter 5:2–3: “not as lording it over those entrusted to you, but making yourselves examples to the flock.”
3. Lewin’s 1939 leadership-style study: once the leader left, the autocratic groups stopped working.
4. Schein, Organizational Culture and Leadership: culture and leadership are two sides of the same coin.
5. 321: people matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

brief12.title: 5. Don’t Bring the World into God’s Kingdom
notes: Slide text:
Not a lack of service, but the wrong way
Competition for building up, control for leading
Performance for life — Babylon in the church
Result: busy outside, dry within
Key points:
1. Romans 12:2: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind.”
2. “World” in Greek is kosmos, originally an ordered arrangement — a system.
3. 1 John 2:16, three pillars: the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, the pride of life.
4. Deci (1971) and Lepper et al. (1973): external rewards erode inner motivation.
5. Revelation 3:1: “you have a reputation of being alive, but you are dead.”

brief12.title: 6. The Key Is 321
notes: Slide text:
Three Foundations: model, standard, guide
Two Core Values: King, glory
Live out these five, and the system is built
Not slogans, but every choice
Key points:
1. 1 Corinthians 3:11: the foundation has already been laid — Jesus Christ.
2. A verse for each foundation: John 13:4–5, Psalm 119:105, Zechariah 4:6.
3. The Two Core Values: letting Jesus be King is the very opposite of 1 Samuel 8; Romans 11:36.
4. 1.01 to the power of 365 is about 37.8; 0.99 to the power of 365 is about 0.03 — every choice counts.
5. The Goal of 321 is to establish God’s system.

brief12.title: Practice for Daily Living
notes: Slide text:
Examine the system I am establishing
Choose the wisdom that comes from heaven
Change my environment, starting with myself
Deepened through the eight stages
Key points:
1. Practice one: draw two columns on a sheet of paper and compare with the qualities in James 3:17.
2. Practice two: when emotions rise, stay quiet for sixty seconds before speaking.
3. Practice three: this week, choose one of your “2”s and live out one of the nine graces towards them.
4. The eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

brief12.title: Closing and Call
notes: Slide text:
A system isn’t established in a day
It’s the sum of countless choices
One person, one family, one generation changes
From today, let Jesus be King
Key points:
1. Back to the grassy slope: you only have to walk it once more today, and once more tomorrow.
2. Joshua 24:15: “as for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh.”
3. The call always starts with “one person” — and that person is here right now.
4. Point to the Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

brief12.title: Prayer of Response and Blessing
notes: Slide text:
Lord, I am willing to begin with myself
to bring every choice back into you
to establish God’s system
and let your kingdom reign in my life
Key points:
1. Lead everyone in speaking the lesson’s declaration of faith together.
2. Intercede for the systems of our families, churches and generation.
3. Close with Matthew 6:10: “Let your Kingdom come.”
4. Blessing: may the Lord’s peace be with you all.

brief21.title: Caring About Every Choice
notes: Slide text:
A Change of Choices (8): Establishing a System
“But the wisdom that is from above
is first pure, then peaceful.”
(James 3:17)
Key points:
1. The title and subtitle come from the lesson: A Change of Choices (8): Establishing a System.
2. Key verses James 3:17–18: read the full passage first.
3. State the main thread: a system is the sum of countless choices.
4. Preview the six points and three practices.

brief21.title: The Path Across the Grassy Slope
notes: Slide text:
One person crosses; the grass springs back
A hundred cross; it becomes a path
No one designed it, no one dug it
The path was walked into being
Key points:
1. Open with the picture of the grassy slope; slow your pace so everyone can see it.
2. Key question: on what day was that path made?
3. Answer: on no day at all — it was made by countless footsteps passing over it.
4. This is how a system is formed.

brief21.title: You’re Not Just Living Your Life
notes: Slide text:
The way you live each day
Your habits in making decisions
Your attitude in responding
These three are establishing a system
Key points:
1. Unpack the three phrases of the lesson’s introduction one by one, each with a question from daily life.
2. The way you live: where does your time go, where does your money flow?
3. Decision habits: do you first ask “Do I like it?” or “Lord, what do you want me to do?”
