Or: in today’s meeting there’s a suggestion I really want to make; I let others finish first — I even let someone else say it and get the credit. Or: today my wife says something that isn’t very pleasant to hear; I don’t answer back; I go and pour her a glass of water.

The second practice: when you fall, choose again at once.

The lesson says: when you find you’ve slipped back into the self-centred life, don’t blame yourself; turn back at once and choose selflessness again.

Notice the words “don’t blame yourself.” Self-reproach looks very spiritual, but it is still the self-centred life — the focus is still on me. “God is light, and in him is no darkness at all” (1 John 1:5); his light exposes our sin in order to forgive, not to humiliate. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9)

So practise a “ten-second turnaround”: notice it, confess it, receive forgiveness, and choose again straight away. Don’t spend ten minutes stewing over it; ten minutes is long enough to do it three more times.

The third practice: declare every day, “Christ lives in me.”

The lesson says: through prayer and declaration, let “I have already” move from mindset into life, so that selflessness becomes something lived out naturally.

Declaring is not shouting slogans; declaring is putting God’s word back into your own heart. Every morning, say this once to your own heart: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20)

Now let’s use the eight stages to walk these three practices out solidly.

Stage one, Information. Today you have received a whole new set of information: selflessness is not hard, you’re just not used to it yet; Jesus does the hard part, we do the simple part. Write those two sentences down and put them where you can see them.

Stage two, Revelation. Information goes into the head; revelation goes into the heart. Ask the Holy Spirit today to shine his light on you in one specific situation: at that moment, how did your “self” climb onto the throne? Without revelation, information is just notes.

Stage three, Conviction. Conviction is your heart truly yielding, saying: Lord, you are right. Not a grudging admission, but a willing surrender.

Stage four, Implementation. Choose one small thing today; don’t wait. Settle it in your heart: today I will be selfless in this one thing.

Stage five, Evaluation. Tonight, spend three minutes looking back: at what moment was I selfless? At what moment was I self-centred again? Just record it; don’t condemn.

Stage six, Correction. For the moment you failed, think of a better way. For example: next time she says that, I’ll take a deep breath for three seconds before I speak.

Stage seven, Repetition. This is the most crucial stage, and the one nobody loves. Remember Dr Lally’s research — an average of sixty-six days, and missing one day won’t ruin everything. Give yourself sixty-six days, not six.

Stage eight, Multiplication. When this habit has grown, pass it on. Find a spiritual companion, tell them your experience, and walk alongside them for a while. The mark of mature life is that it can reproduce. “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” (2 Timothy 2:2)

Brothers and sisters, the lesson ends by giving us a gentle reminder; please take it home with you:

It’s not that you can’t — it’s that you’re not used to it yet.

sections.heading: 11. Closing and Call: Let Every Choice Become an Opportunity to Cultivate the Life of Christ
sections.html:
The lesson’s conclusion is beautifully put: selflessness is not some unattainable plane; it is a choice you can live out every day.

One choice shows no change; choices sustained become life.

Brothers and sisters, this is a great comfort, and also a great challenge.

The comfort is this: today you don’t have to become a completely selfless person. Today God only asks you to choose once, in one small thing.

The challenge is this: you can’t choose only once. A single choice is like one footstep on the grass — by the next day the grass has sprung back up; but a thousand choices wear a path.

So today I want to issue this call to you, brothers and sisters.

First, let Jesus be King. Not your feelings as king, not your face as king, not your arguments as king. This morning, in your heart, hand the throne back to him and say: Lord Jesus, come and be King.

Second, let Jesus receive all the glory. When you have been selfless in some small thing, and the relationship has eased, and the matter has passed, don’t quietly make a note in your heart: “That was my self-discipline.” Give it back to him: Lord, that was you living it out in me.

Brothers and sisters, starting today, let every choice become an opportunity to cultivate the life of Christ.

Your first thought in the morning is an opportunity.

The words you say before you leave the house are an opportunity.

That unfairness at the office is an opportunity.

That silence at the dinner table is an opportunity.

Time after time, the Lord’s likeness will show in you. And one day you will suddenly find that the thing you once had to grit your teeth to do now comes as naturally as walking down the stairs in your own home.

Then you will understand — selflessness really isn’t hard after all.

“The thief only comes to steal, kill, and destroy. I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.” (John 10:10)
Matthew 5:48

practices: Remind yourself each day: I no longer need to prove myself; I simply let Jesus live.
When your rights are infringed, choose not to grasp them; follow the Lord who emptied himself.

prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,

We thank you. You said you came that the sheep may have life, and may have it abundantly. This morning we place a long-held misunderstanding in your hands: we always thought selflessness was hard, when really we just weren’t used to it yet.

Lord, thank you that you have already done the hard part. The cross dealt with our self-centred life; the resurrection gave us the selfless life. We are not striving to become selfless people; we are living out the life you have already given us.

Forgive us; we are in the habit of thinking of ourselves, fighting for ourselves and living by our own feelings. May your Spirit shine on us today, so that we see that moment, that remark, that thought.

Lord, we are willing. We are willing to begin with small things — setting aside our opinions, setting aside our face, setting aside our insistence. When we fall, help us not to blame ourselves, but to turn back at once and choose again. We are willing to declare every day: I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.
Lord Jesus, come and be King. Be King over my tongue, King over my emotions, King in my home. May all the goodness that shows in us bring glory to you, and not to us.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: The lesson says, “The problem is not that selflessness is hard, but that we’re not used to it yet.” Share something you have gone through “from not being used to it to being used to it” (for example, learning to drive, learning a language, getting up early). What does that experience remind you of as you practise selflessness today? “who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil.” (Hebrews 5:14)

The lesson says, “The key is not ‘Can I do it?’ but ‘Am I willing to let him live?’” Say specifically: in what small thing will you practise selflessness this coming week? Which spiritual companion do you need to walk these sixty-six days with you? “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20)

blog.title: Selflessness Is Not Hard

blocks.x: It’s Not That You Can’t — You’re Just Not Used to It Yet
Morning Devotion 321 · Lesson 111 · Blog Post

The stairs in your home — you’ve walked them thousands of times. Each morning as you come down, do you have to look down and count the steps? No, you don’t. You can come down the stairs while thinking about what groceries to buy today.

But suppose today you were put on an unfamiliar spiral staircase, with steps that are narrow and high and open in between. You would certainly grip the handrail, look down, take it one step at a time, and breathe a sigh of relief when you got to the bottom.
Both are stairs — so why is one as easy as breathing, and the other as hard as an exam?
Walking down stairs hasn’t suddenly become difficult; you just “aren’t used to that staircase yet.”
1. Where Does Selflessness Get Stuck?
In church we have all heard the word “selflessness,” and we all nod. But many people actually carry a wrong mindset about it in their hearts: it sounds wonderful, but it’s very hard to do.

Because it feels hard, selflessness ends up stuck in three places — stuck in the vision, as a beautiful piece of doctrine; stuck in the slogans, as a resounding line in our meetings; stuck in our hopes, as a longing for “some day, I hope.”
But it never gets into three other places: it never gets into our life, never gets into our habits, never gets into our actual daily living.

Perhaps you have had a moment like this: during morning devotions you say through your tears, “Lord, I am willing to be selfless,” and less than five minutes after you get home, your husband kicks his shoes off anywhere, and that “self” inside you climbs straight back onto the throne. So you wonder: maybe I’m just not cut out for this?
No. The truth is this — selflessness is not hard at all; in fact it is the lightest road there is.
This is not a pep talk; these are the Lord’s own words: “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” (Matthew 11:30)
What is truly heavy has never been “selflessness”; it is the “self-centred life.”
2. Jesus Does the Hard Part; We Do the Simple Part
Why do we find selflessness hard? Because we are used to the “self-centred life” — in the habit of thinking of ourselves, fighting for ourselves, living by our own feelings.

The psychological data are very honest. Research in 2002 by Professor Wendy Wood of the University of Southern California and her colleagues showed that about forty-three per cent of people’s everyday behaviour is habit, repeated automatically in the same settings. In other words, nearly half of life is not decided; it plays on autoplay.
So the problem is not that “selflessness is hard” but that “we’re not used to it yet.”

The difference between those two sentences is the difference between heaven and earth. “Selflessness is hard” describes the nature of the thing; once you define it like that, all that’s left is to give up. “I’m not used to it yet” describes the stage I’m at — and stages pass.
Better news still: the hardest stretch, Jesus has already done for us.

The cross dealt with the “self-centred life” — “our old man was crucified with him, that the body of sin might be done away with” (Romans 6:6). The resurrection gave us the “selfless” life — “if the Spirit of him who raised up Jesus from the dead dwells in you” (Romans 8:11).

It’s like getting to the twentieth floor. You can take the stairs, panting as you climb floor by floor; or you can step into the lift, stand steady, and press the button. What lifts your whole self sixty metres straight up is the steel cables and the motor; all you do are three simple things: step in, stand steady, press the button.
So it is not “striving to become selfless”; it is “living out the life you have already been given.”
3. When You Fall, Get Up and Choose Again

A study by Professor Karen Adolph of New York University and her colleagues, published in 2012 in the journal Psychological Science, found that toddlers who have just learned to walk take on average about 2,368 steps and fall about seventeen times every hour.
Seventeen falls an hour. If that child thought with our adult logic, he would have given up long ago: I’ve tried; I’m not suited to walking; I’ll stick to crawling.
But the child doesn’t think like that. He cries for a moment, grabs the coffee table and stands up again.
And us? We choose selflessness, fail three times, and start drawing conclusions: I can’t do it.

Scripture says, “for a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again” (Proverbs 24:16). Notice that the verse does not say the righteous “don’t fall”; it says the righteous fall and “rise up again.” The difference between the righteous and the wicked lies not in whether they fall, but in whether they get up.

Research in 2010 by Dr Phillippa Lally of University College London found that it takes an average of sixty-six days for a new behaviour to become automatic. And one finding is especially comforting: missing the occasional day had no significant effect on the whole process of forming the habit.
Missing one day won’t ruin everything. What really ruins everything is lying on the ground after you fall, refusing to get up, and berating yourself all the while.

So starting today, you can do three very small things: first, practise selflessness in small things — set aside your opinions, your face, your insistence; second, when you fall, choose again at once, without blaming yourself; third, declare every day, “Christ lives in me.”
Selflessness is not some unattainable plane; it is a choice you can live out every day. One choice shows no change; choices sustained become life.
A single choice is like one footstep on the grass — by the next day the grass has sprung back up. But a thousand choices wear a path.
One day you will suddenly find that the thing you once had to grit your teeth to do now comes as naturally as walking down the stairs in your own home.
Then you will understand — selflessness really isn’t hard after all.
Reflection question: this week, in what one “small thing” will you practise setting yourself aside?

3. Ask the Holy Spirit to shine on specific situations, so we see the “self” in that moment.
4. Declare Galatians 2:20, so that “I have already” enters our life.
5. Blessing: may the Lord give you victory in small things, and a life that is light, joyful and victorious.

brief21.title: Theme Verse and Background

John wrote in Ephesus, around AD 80
Following chapter 9: the blind man thrown out

The good shepherd lays down his life (John 10:11)

brief21.title: Cultivation, Not a Switch

Selflessness is not an instant change

2. Correct the wrong expectation: selflessness is not a switch but a seedling.

brief21.title: Three Levels of Cultivation
notes: Slide text:
A change of mindset: “I have already”
A change of choice: denying of self
A change of habit: living out selflessness
Only repeated choice becomes life
Key points:
1. Three levels: mindset (“I have already”), choice (denying of self), habit (living out selflessness).
2. Galatians 2:20 “I have been crucified” is a Greek perfect: completed in the past, effect continuing.
3. Luke 9:23 “deny himself” is the same word as Peter “denying” the Lord; only Luke adds “daily.”
4. Example: learning a foreign language — grammar is mindset, speaking up is choice, no longer translating is habit.
5. Research from 1998 onward by Ann Graybiel of MIT: habit is the brain’s chunking.

brief21.title: Because We’re Used to Self
notes: Slide text:
The habit of thinking of ourselves
The habit of fighting for ourselves
The habit of living by our own feelings
So selflessness feels unnatural
Key points:
1. Lesson point 2: because we are used to the self-centred life.
2. Three habits: thinking of ourselves, fighting for ourselves, living by our own feelings.
3. Ask the congregation to be still for three seconds and count how many thoughts this morning circled around “me.”
4. 321: pride is leaving our originally intended position and grasping power; pride provokes pride, and both sides lose.

brief21.title: Not Hard — Just Not Used to It
notes: Slide text:
“For desire is present with me, but I don’t
find it doing that which is good.” (Romans 7:18)
About 43% of daily behaviour is habit
Water flowing long enough cuts a riverbed
Key points:

2. Data: Wendy Wood and colleagues, 2002 — about 43% of daily behaviour is habitual.
3. Illustration: the riverbed cut deeper and deeper; physics: static friction exceeds kinetic friction — starting is hardest.
4. Experiment: a right-hander writing their name left-handed — not unable, just not used to it.
5. Key line: the problem is not that selflessness is hard but that we’re not used to it yet.

brief21.title: Two Things Jesus Has Done

The cross — dealing with the self-centred life

4. The resurrection gives life: Romans 6:4; 8:11; 2 Corinthians 5:17, a new creation.

brief21.title: Jesus Does the Hard Part; We Do the Simple Part

Twenty floors: the stairs or the lift
Cables and motor lift you sixty metres
Our part: believe, choose, practise
Not striving to be selfless — living out his life

2. Illustration: to reach the twentieth floor, the stairs are effort, the lift is grace.
3. Ephesians 2:8-9 and Philippians 2:13: even the willing is God at work within us.
4. Believe, choose, practise correspond to Romans 6:6 knowing, 6:11 considering, 6:13 presenting.
5. Example: Hudson Taylor’s breakthrough in 1869 — not working up faith, but looking to the trustworthy Lord.

brief21.title: The Child Learning to Walk

About 2,368 steps an hour
About 17 falls an hour

2. Data: Karen Adolph, 2012, Psychological Science — toddlers take about 2,368 steps and fall 17 times an hour.

brief21.title: When You Fall, Get Up and Choose Again
notes: Slide text:
“A righteous man falls seven times and rises up again”
(Proverbs 24:16)
A new habit takes 66 days on average
Missing one day won’t ruin everything
Key points:

2. Science: myelination raises conduction from about 1 metre per second to over 100 metres per second.
3. Data: Phillippa Lally, 2010 — 66 days on average to form a habit; missing a day has no significant effect.
4. Hebrews 5:14 “exercised” and 1 Timothy 4:7 “exercise”: Greek gymnazō, the root of “gymnasium.”
5. Galatians 5:1: selflessness is not pressure but freedom; tell the yoke of bondage from the Lord’s yoke.

brief21.title: Perfection: Revelation, Not Demand
notes: Slide text:
“You shall be perfect, just as your Father
in heaven is perfect.” (Matthew 5:48)
Greek teleios: grown into what one should be
Not flawless, but whole and mature
Key points:
1. Lesson point 5: Matthew 5:48 is not a demand but a revelation.
2. Greek teleios comes from telos (purpose): mature and whole, not flawless.
3. Illustration: an unripe fruit isn’t bad, just not ripe yet; once ripe and able to feed people, it is teleios.

brief21.title: Because Christ Is in You

“Christ in you, the hope

Declare daily: Christ lives in me

brief21.title: The 3-2-1 Vision in Summary

brief21.title: Closing and Call

4. Declare Galatians 2:20, so that “I have already” enters our life.
