script12.title: Selflessness Is Not Hard
script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we read Lesson 111 together: “Selflessness Is Not Hard,” subtitled “A Change of Habits (Part 1).” Our theme verse is John 10:10: “The thief only comes to steal, kill, and destroy. I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.”

script12.title: Not That You Can’t — Just Not Used to It
script: Brothers and sisters, on the stairs in your home, do you have to look down and count the steps? No, you don’t. But put you on an unfamiliar spiral staircase, and you’ll grip the handrail and take it one step at a time with total concentration. Both are stairs — so why is one easy and the other hard? Walking down stairs hasn’t become difficult; you just aren’t used to it yet.

That is exactly our misunderstanding about selflessness: it sounds wonderful, but it’s very hard to do. So selflessness gets stuck in the vision, in the slogans, in our hopes, and never gets into our life, our habits, our actual daily living.
But the truth is this: selflessness is not hard at all; in fact it is the lightest road there is. The Lord himself said, “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” (Matthew 11:30)

script12.title: Theme Verse and Background
script: John’s Gospel was written in Ephesus around AD 80 to 90. Chapter 10 follows on from chapter 9: the man born blind is healed, yet the Pharisees throw him out of the synagogue. Far from feeding the sheep, the shepherds drove a sheep out.

It is right here that the Lord speaks our theme verse. The word for “thief” means a sneak-thief; he doesn’t rob openly — he just whispers in your ear, “You need to think of yourself, you know.” But the Lord says, I came that they may have life. The word “abundantly” means overflowing, more than enough — like a cup filled to the top and still spilling over.

In the next verse the Lord says, “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.” (John 10:11) Brothers and sisters, the selfless life is not a diminished life; it is an overflowing life.

script12.title: Selflessness Is the Cultivation of Life
script: The lesson’s first point says: selflessness is not an instant change; it is a process of cultivation.

This process has three levels. First, a change of mindset — “I have already.” Paul says, “I have been crucified with Christ.” (Galatians 2:20) In the original it is a perfect tense: completed in the past, with its effect continuing to this day.

Second, a change of choice — denying of self. The Lord said, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.” (Luke 9:23) The original word for “deny himself” is the very same word as Peter “denying” the Lord. Denying of self means disowning yourself.
Third, a change of habit — living out selflessness. Having the mindset isn’t enough; making the choice isn’t enough either. The choice must be repeated, become a habit, and finally become life.

script12.title: Why Selflessness Feels Hard
script: Why do we find selflessness hard? Because we are used to the self-centred life — in the habit of thinking of ourselves, in the habit of fighting for ourselves, in the habit of living by our own feelings.

A 2002 study by Professor Wendy Wood of the University of Southern California found that about forty-three per cent of people’s everyday behaviour is habit, repeated automatically in the same settings. Brothers and sisters, nearly half of life is not decided; it plays on autoplay — and what plays was recorded slowly over decades, every time we thought of ourselves. It’s like water cutting a riverbed: the longer it flows, the deeper it cuts.

But the lesson reminds us of one crucial sentence: the problem is not that selflessness is hard, but that we’re not used to it yet. If you’re right-handed, writing your name with your left hand will look ugly — but it’s not that you can’t; you’re just not used to it.

script12.title: Selflessness Is the Easiest Road
script: Brothers and sisters, giving the sheep life — is that something the sheep do, or the shepherd? The shepherd.

Jesus has already done two crucial things. The cross dealt with the self-centred life — “our old man was crucified with him” (Romans 6:6). The resurrection gave us the selfless life (Romans 8:11). So the principle is simple: Jesus does the hard part; we do the simple part.
It’s like getting to the twentieth floor. What lifts your whole self sixty metres is the steel cables and the motor; all you do is step into the lift, stand steady and press the button.
The three things we do are: believe, choose, practise. It is not striving to become selfless; it is living out the life he has already given you.

script12.title: The Power of Habit
script: The lesson uses an example we have all lived through — learning to walk.

A 2012 study by Professor Karen Adolph of New York University found that toddlers who are just learning to walk take on average about 2,368 steps and fall about seventeen times every hour. Seventeen falls an hour, and yet the child never says, “I’m not suited to walking”; he cries for a moment, grabs the coffee table and stands up again.

Scripture says, “for a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again” (Proverbs 24:16). The difference between the righteous and the wicked lies not in whether they fall, but in whether they get up.

A 2010 study by Dr Phillippa Lally of University College London found that forming a new habit takes sixty-six days on average — and missing the occasional day doesn’t affect the whole process. Brothers and sisters, falling once doesn’t mean you’ve lost it all.

script12.title: You Already Have the Selfless Life
script: “Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect.” (Matthew 5:48)

The lesson says this is not a demand but a revelation. The root of the original word for “perfect” means “purpose”; it means grown into what one should be, not flawless. Why can we be perfect? Because the life of Christ is in you. “Christ in you, the hope of glory.” (Colossians 1:27)
Brothers and sisters, an acorn doesn’t need to strive to become an oak tree; it already holds the blueprint of the whole tree. All it has to do is put down roots and reach up to the light.
So the key is not “Can I do it?” but “Am I willing to let him live?” The first question only makes you smaller the more you ask it; the second you can answer today.

script12.title: The More You Practise, the Lighter It Gets
script: The lesson says that when you begin to cultivate the habit of selflessness, you will become more and more at ease, more and more joyful, more and more free. Why? Because you no longer live under the heavy burden of “self”: no longer needing to prove yourself, no longer needing to hold on to your rights, no longer needing to control everything.

The Lord is our role model: he “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7). The original word for “emptied himself” literally means he poured himself out. He had the right; he chose not to grasp it.

Brothers and sisters, it’s like crossing the sea. You can row for all you’re worth and make ten kilometres a day; or you can spread a sail and make a hundred kilometres a day. The sail produces no power; it simply doesn’t block the wind. And that wind is the Holy Spirit.

script12.title: Putting It into Practice
script: The lesson gives us three practices.

First, practise selflessness in small things: set aside your opinions, set aside your face, set aside your insistence. When you eat out today, let someone else choose the restaurant; in today’s meeting, let others finish speaking first.
Second, when you fall, choose again at once. Notice the words “don’t blame yourself,” because self-reproach still keeps the focus on me. Notice it, confess it, and choose again.
Third, declare every day, “Christ lives in me.”

321 says there are eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Brothers and sisters, please especially remember stage seven — Repetition. Without repetition, the six stages before it are only a one-off moment of being moved.

script12.title: Closing and Call
script: The lesson’s conclusion says: selflessness is not some unattainable plane; it is a choice you can live out every day. One choice shows no change; choices sustained become life.
A single choice is like one footstep on the grass — by the next day the grass has sprung back up; but a thousand choices wear a path.
So today, first, let Jesus be King — hand the throne back to him. Second, let Jesus receive all the glory — don’t quietly make a note that says, “That was my self-discipline.”
Starting today, let every choice become an opportunity to cultivate the life of Christ.

script12.title: Prayer of Response and Blessing
script: Let us pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, thank you — you have already done the hard part. The cross dealt with our self-centred life; the resurrection gave us the selfless life.

Forgive us for being in the habit of thinking of ourselves and fighting for ourselves. Lord, we are willing to begin with small things; when we fall, help us not to blame ourselves, but to choose again at once.

We declare: I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. Lord Jesus, come and be King; may the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
Brothers and sisters, may the Lord bless you. Please remember this one line: it’s not that you can’t — you’re just not used to it yet.

script21.title: Selflessness Is Not Hard
script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we read Lesson 111 together: “Selflessness Is Not Hard,” subtitled “A Change of Habits (Part 1).”
Our theme verse is John 10:10: “The thief only comes to steal, kill, and destroy. I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.”
Please keep this verse in your heart. The whole lesson today walks around this one sentence.

script21.title: A Very Ordinary Question
script: Before we come to the lesson, let me ask you a very homely question.

Brothers and sisters, you have walked the stairs in your home thousands of times — do you have to look down and count the steps each time you come down? No, you don’t. But put you on an unfamiliar spiral staircase, narrow and high and open in between, and you’ll grip the handrail, take it one step at a time, and breathe a sigh of relief when you get to the bottom.
Both are stairs — so why is one as easy as breathing, and the other as hard as an exam? Notice: walking down stairs hasn’t suddenly become difficult; you just aren’t used to that staircase yet.

script21.title: Where Does Selflessness Get Stuck?
script: Brothers and sisters, that is what today is about.
The lesson is very honest right at the start: many people have a wrong mindset about “selflessness” — it sounds wonderful, but it’s very hard to do.
Because it feels hard, selflessness gets stuck in the vision, the slogans and our hopes, and never gets into our life, our habits, our actual daily living.

But the truth is this: selflessness is not hard at all; in fact it is the lightest road there is. This is not a pep talk; these are the Lord’s words: “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” (Matthew 11:30)

script21.title: Theme Verse and Background
script: Let’s first stand at the scene of our theme verse.

The author of John’s Gospel is John, the disciple whom the Lord loved; it is generally thought to have been written in Ephesus around AD 80 to 90. Chapter 10 follows on from chapter 9: the man born blind is healed, yet the Pharisees throw him out of the synagogue. Far from feeding the sheep, the shepherds drove a sheep out.

It is against this background that the Lord speaks our theme verse. The word for “thief” means a sneak-thief who strikes when no one is looking. That is exactly Satan’s method: he rarely announces loudly, “I’m coming to destroy you”; he just whispers softly, “You need to think of yourself, you know.” But the Lord says, I came that they may have life. The word “abundantly” means overflowing, more than enough — like a glass of water filled to the top and still spilling over.

In the next verse the Lord says, “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.” (John 10:11) And later he says, “I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again.” (John 10:18) Laying it down is the cross; taking it again is the resurrection. Today’s message is built on these two things.

script21.title: Cultivation, Not a Switch
script: The lesson’s first point says: selflessness is not an instant change; it is a process of cultivation.

Many people are disappointed not because the teaching is wrong but because their expectation is wrong. We think selflessness is a switch: flick it, and from then on all is peace. Then we press it with no response, and conclude that the switch is broken — or that we are.

No. Selflessness is not a switch; it is a seedling. Paul says, “that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man … and put on the new man.” (Ephesians 4:22, 24) Putting on clothes is not something you do once and never have to do again; it is something you do every morning.

script21.title: Three Levels of Cultivation
script: The lesson says this process has three levels.

First, a change of mindset — “I have already.” “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) In Greek, “I have been crucified” is a perfect tense: completed in the past, with its effect continuing to this day.

Second, a change of choice — denying of self. “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.” (Luke 9:23) The original word for “deny himself” is the very same word as Peter “denying” the Lord. Denying of self means disowning yourself. And Luke especially adds one word — “daily.”
Third, a change of habit — living out selflessness. Having the mindset isn’t enough; making the choice isn’t enough either. The choice must be repeated, become a habit, and finally become life.

Research from 1998 onward by Professor Ann Graybiel of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology shows that when actions are performed over and over, the brain packages them into a single unit that runs automatically. The essence of a habit is transferring something from “I have to think hard about it” to “I can do it without thinking.”

script21.title: Because We’re Used to Self
script: The lesson’s second point asks: why do we find selflessness hard? The answer comes down to one thing: because we are used to the self-centred life.
The lesson lists three habits: the habit of thinking of ourselves, the habit of fighting for ourselves, the habit of living by our own feelings.

Brothers and sisters, please be still for three seconds and honestly ask yourself: from this morning until now, how many of your thoughts have circled around “me”? 321 says pride is leaving our originally intended position, grasping power and wanting to take God’s place. The habit of thinking of ourselves is putting ourselves at the centre — and that is God’s place.

script21.title: Not Hard — Just Not Used to It
script: Paul puts it with great honesty: “For desire is present with me, but I don’t find it doing that which is good.” (Romans 7:18) It isn’t that Paul was unwilling; he desired it. The problem was not in the will but in the inertia.

A 2002 study by Professor Wendy Wood of the University of Southern California showed that about forty-three per cent of people’s everyday behaviour is habit, repeated automatically in the same settings. Nearly half of life is not decided; it plays on autoplay.
Who recorded what’s playing? Think of rain: at first the water spreads everywhere, but over time it cuts a channel; the deeper the channel, the more naturally the next rain runs into it.

So the lesson reminds us of one crucial sentence: the problem is not that “selflessness is hard” but that “we’re not used to it yet.” If you’re right-handed, writing your name with your left hand will come out crooked and ugly — but it’s not that you can’t; you’re just not used to it. Brothers and sisters, selflessness is exactly the same.

script21.title: Two Things Jesus Has Done
script: The lesson’s third point is the turning point of the whole lesson: selflessness is actually the easiest road.
Let me ask: giving the sheep life — is that something the sheep do, or the shepherd? The sheep only have to follow.

Jesus has already done two crucial things. The first: the cross — dealing with the self-centred life. “Our old man was crucified with him, that the body of sin might be done away with.” (Romans 6:6) The old self is not bad behaviour; it is the very life that has itself at the centre. God’s way is not repair but execution. You can polish the leaves of a bitter tree one by one, and the fruit will still be bitter.

The second: the resurrection — giving the selfless life. “But if the Spirit of him who raised up Jesus from the dead dwells in you … he will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you.” (Romans 8:11) God did not give us an improved version of the old self; he gave us a brand-new life.

script21.title: Jesus Does the Hard Part; We Do the Simple Part
script: So the lesson draws out a wonderfully liberating principle: Jesus does the hard part; we do the simple part.

I often use a lift as an illustration. In a twenty-storey building you can climb the stairs, or you can step into the lift, stand steady and press the button. What lifts your whole self sixty metres straight up is the steel cables and the motor; all you do are three simple things.
Sanctification works the same way: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure.” (Philippians 2:13) Even the willing is God at work within us.

So what is our part? The lesson names three things: believe, choose, practise. They correspond exactly to Romans 6 — believing is “knowing” (6:6), choosing is “consider yourselves to be dead to sin” (6:11), practising is “present yourselves to God” (6:13). It is not striving to become selfless; it is living out the life you have already been given.

script21.title: The Child Learning to Walk
script: The lesson’s fourth point uses an example we have all lived through yet none of us remembers — learning to walk.
At first it is hard; we fall often; we are very unsteady. So why does it become easy later? Because it becomes a habit.

A study by Professor Karen Adolph of New York University, published in 2012 in the journal Psychological Science, found that children aged twelve to nineteen months take on average about 2,368 steps and fall about seventeen times every hour.

Brothers and sisters, seventeen falls an hour. If the child thought with our adult logic, he would have given up long ago: I’m not suited to walking; I’ll stick to crawling. But he cries for a moment, grabs the coffee table and stands up again. And us? We fail three times and conclude: I can’t do it.

script21.title: When You Fall, Get Up and Choose Again
script: Scripture said it long ago: “for a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again” (Proverbs 24:16). The verse does not say the righteous don’t fall; it says they fall and rise up again. The difference between the righteous and the wicked lies not in whether they fall, but in whether they get up.

The psalmist also says, “Though he stumble, he shall not fall, for Yahweh holds him up with his hand.” (Psalm 37:24) You think you’re practising getting up; in fact, there has been a hand under your arm all along.

What does repetition do in us? Neuroscience says that nerve fibres used again and again get wrapped in myelin, like putting insulation on an electric wire, and conduction speed rises from about one metre per second to more than a hundred metres per second. You don’t turn into a different person; that road gets paved into a motorway.

A 2010 study by Dr Phillippa Lally of University College London found that it takes an average of sixty-six days for a new behaviour to become automatic — and missing the occasional day has no significant effect. Brothers and sisters, missing one day won’t ruin everything; what really ruins everything is lying on the ground after you fall, refusing to get up, and berating yourself all the while.

script21.title: Perfection: Revelation, Not Demand
script: The lesson’s fifth point: you already have the selfless life. The verse is: “Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect.” (Matthew 5:48)
The lesson says: this verse is not a demand but a revelation.

The Greek root of “perfect” means “purpose, end, goal”; it does not mean flawless but grown into what one should be. A green, unripe fruit is not bad; it simply isn’t ripe yet. When it has ripened and can feed people, it is perfect. The context is the Lord speaking about loving our enemies: “For he makes his sun to rise on the evil and the good.” (Matthew 5:45) The Father’s love makes no distinction; he wants us to be like him, to love without gaps.

script21.title: Because Christ Is in You
script: Why can we be perfect? Because the life of Christ is in you. “Christ in you, the hope of glory.” (Colossians 1:27)
Brothers and sisters, it is not that God gives you a manual and tells you to imitate him; it is that God puts his own life inside you.

I think of an acorn. It doesn’t need to strive to become an oak tree — it already holds the blueprint of the whole tree; it only has to put down roots and reach up to the light. The Lord says, “He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit.” (John 15:5) The Lord does not require the branches to try hard to produce grapes; he requires only that they remain in him.

So the lesson swaps the whole question out. The key is not “Can I do it?” but “Am I willing to let him live?” The first question puts the focus on me and only makes you smaller the more you ask it; the second puts the focus on him, and you can answer it today.

The self-determination theory developed from 1985 onward by Edward Deci and Richard Ryan of the University of Rochester shows that change driven by autonomous motivation lasts longer than change driven by outside pressure. Brothers and sisters, God never forces us. He asks just one question: are you willing?

script21.title: Putting Down Three Heavy Bags
script: The lesson’s sixth point: the more you practise, the lighter it gets. Why? Because you no longer live under the heavy burden of “self.”
We often think “self” is our asset; in fact “self” is our luggage. The lesson lists the three heaviest pieces.

The first: no longer needing to prove yourself. How exhausting is proving yourself? You have to keep comparing, keep calculating what others think of you. Paul says, “Or am I striving to please men?” (Galatians 1:10)

The second: no longer needing to hold on to your rights. The role model is the Lord himself: “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” (Philippians 2:6-7) The original word for “emptied himself” literally means he poured himself out. He had the right; he chose not to grasp it. Brothers and sisters, when your hand is gripping something, it can’t do anything else.

The third: no longer needing to control everything. “Casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.” (1 Peter 5:7) “Casting” in the original means throwing with force — heaving the bundle off your shoulders onto someone else’s back. It is an action, not a feeling.

script21.title: Ship the Oars, Raise the Sail
script: The lesson says: you simply let Jesus live. This is the lightest life, the most abundant life.

Let me use a boat as an illustration. You have to cross the same stretch of sea. You can row for all you’re worth, until your palms blister, and make ten kilometres a day; or you can raise a sail, hold the tiller, and make a hundred kilometres a day. The self-centred life is rowing for all you’re worth; selflessness is spreading the sail. The sail itself produces not one ounce of power; it does only one thing — it doesn’t block the wind, and it lets itself be filled by the wind.
And that wind is the Holy Spirit. 321 says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you are glad, rely on the brain and you are troubled.

When the sail is spread, “the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22-23) Notice: it is “fruit,” not “product.” Products are churned out in factories; fruit grows out of life.
This is the 920 practice: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2,” and before them we live out the selfless “0.” The person beside you today is the training ground God has given you.

script21.title: Putting It into Practice (1)
script: The lesson gives us three practices for daily living.
The first: begin practising selflessness in small things — set aside your opinions, set aside your face, set aside your insistence.

Notice the words “small things.” Many people talk straight away about laying down their lives for the Lord, yet go red in the face at the dinner table over a single remark. Habits are never formed in the big things; they are formed in the small things. Make it one concrete thing: today when you eat out, someone else chooses the restaurant; in today’s meeting, I let others finish speaking first; today my wife says something that isn’t pleasant to hear, and I don’t answer back — I go and pour her a glass of water.

The second: when you fall, choose again at once, without blaming yourself. Self-reproach looks very spiritual, but it is still the self-centred life — the focus is still on me. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins.” (1 John 1:9) Practise a “ten-second turnaround”: notice it, confess it, and choose again. Don’t spend ten minutes stewing over it; ten minutes is long enough to do it three more times.

script21.title: Putting It into Practice (2)
script: The third: declare every day, “Christ lives in me.” Declaring is not shouting slogans; it is putting God’s word back into your own heart. Every morning, say this once to your own heart: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20)
Now let’s use 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset to walk these three practices out solidly.
Information: today you have received two new sentences — selflessness isn’t hard; you’re just not used to it yet.
Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light on you today in one specific situation.
Conviction: let your heart truly yield and say, Lord, you are right.
Implementation: choose one small thing today; don’t wait.
Evaluation: tonight, spend three minutes looking back — just record it; don’t condemn.
Correction: think of a better way — for example, next time take a deep breath for three seconds first.
Repetition: remember the sixty-six days — and missing one day won’t ruin everything.
Multiplication: when the habit has grown, walk alongside a brother or sister for a while.

script21.title: The 3-2-1 Vision in Summary
script: Brothers and sisters, let’s place today’s message within the whole picture of 321.

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — he emptied himself, he laid down his life, he went ahead of us. The Bible is my standard — when my feelings say “I can’t do it,” the Bible says “I have been crucified with Christ,” and I do my reckoning by the Bible. The Holy Spirit is my guide — it is not me squeezing out fruit; it is the Holy Spirit bearing fruit.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — the lesson’s question, “Am I willing to let him live?”, is precisely about this; there is only one throne, and either Jesus sits on it or “self” does. Let Jesus receive all the glory — what people see is no longer our self-discipline but his beauty. The Goal: establish God’s system; this system is not piled up out of structures but put together by a company of selfless people.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into fullness without limit. A drop of water in the palm of your hand soon dries up; but if that drop falls into the ocean, it no longer has a shape of its own — yet it possesses the vastness of the whole ocean.

Last of all, 235 relationships. The road of selflessness is not walked alone. If you can find a “2,” and each week ask each other, “In what small thing were you selfless this week?”, your sixty-six days will be far steadier.

script21.title: Closing and Call
script: The lesson’s conclusion is beautifully put: selflessness is not some unattainable plane; it is a choice you can live out every day. One choice shows no change; choices sustained become life.

The comfort is this: today God only asks you to choose once, in one small thing. The challenge is this: you can’t choose only once. A single choice is like one footstep on the grass — by the next day the grass has sprung back up; but a thousand choices wear a path.

So today there are two calls. First, let Jesus be King: not your feelings as king, not your face as king — in your heart, hand the throne back to him. Second, let Jesus receive all the glory; don’t quietly make a note that says, “That was my self-discipline.”

Starting today, let every choice become an opportunity to cultivate the life of Christ. Your first thought in the morning is an opportunity; the words you say before you leave the house are an opportunity; that unfairness at the office is an opportunity too.

One day you will suddenly find that the thing you once had to grit your teeth to do now comes as naturally as walking down the stairs in your own home. Then you will understand — selflessness really isn’t hard after all.

script21.title: Prayer of Response and Blessing
script: Let us bow our heads and pray together.

Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you. You said you came that the sheep may have life, and may have it abundantly. This morning we place a long-held misunderstanding in your hands: we always thought selflessness was hard, when really we just weren’t used to it yet.

Lord, thank you that you have already done the hard part. The cross dealt with our self-centred life; the resurrection gave us the selfless life. Forgive us for being in the habit of thinking of ourselves, fighting for ourselves and living by our own feelings; may your Spirit shine on us today, so that we see that moment, that remark, that thought.

Lord, we are willing. We are willing to begin with small things — setting aside our opinions, setting aside our face, setting aside our insistence. When we fall, help us not to blame ourselves, but to turn back at once and choose again.

We declare: I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. Lord Jesus, come and be King; may all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

Brothers and sisters, may the Lord bless you and keep you. May he give you victory today in one small thing. Please take this one line home with you: it’s not that you can’t — you’re just not used to it yet.

sections.heading: Introduction: Why Does Trying Harder Only Make Us Fail More?
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we’re going to face together a struggle that almost everyone who earnestly loves the Lord has been through.

There was a sister who had believed in the Lord for more than ten years. She loved the Lord, she served, she gave — in every way she kept up with the best of them. But she carried a deep pain: her temper. Every time she finished shouting at her children at home, she would hide in her room and weep. Again and again she resolved: “Next time I will never lose my temper.” She wrote “I WILL BE GENTLE” in big letters in a notebook and stuck it on the fridge, on her dressing-table mirror, beside the steering wheel of her car. And the result? She told me, “Pastor, the more I remind myself not to lose my temper, the more easily I lose it. I stare at those words, and all the while my heart keeps saying: I’ve failed again.”

Her predicament isn’t hers alone. It’s a dead end that countless Christians walk down every single day: straining to “deal with themselves” without ever “cultivating life”. The result is that the harder they try, the more they fail; the more they struggle, the more they hurt.

Psychology, in fact, discovered this phenomenon long ago. In 1987 the American psychologist Daniel Wegner, then at Trinity University in San Antonio (he later moved to Harvard), and his team carried out a famous experiment, published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. He sat his participants down and gave them just one instruction: “For the next five minutes, please don’t think of a white bear.” Every single participant failed. What’s more, once the experiment was over, this group thought of white bears more often than the group that had never been asked to suppress the thought at all. Wegner called it the “rebound effect”, and it later grew into his “ironic process theory”.

That experiment tells us something that cuts close to the bone: the harder you push “don’t”, the more your heart fills up with “that very thing”. Because when you say “don’t think of a white bear”, your mind first has to summon the white bear in order to know what it’s fighting. And so the white bear moves in.

Brothers and sisters, that is exactly why so many people’s spiritual lives stay stuck. We pour all our strength into staring at our sins, staring at our weaknesses, staring at our self-centred life; and because we call that self-centred life out to look at it every day and feed it our attention every day, it just keeps growing bigger.

But God’s way is not like that. God doesn’t want you to combat the self-centred life; he wants you to cultivate selflessness. That is the heart of today’s lesson. In the last lesson we saw that changing a habit is a matter of life; in this lesson we will see that habits are changed not by combating, but by cultivating.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Two Letters, Two Angles, One Truth
sections.html:
Today’s key passages come from two apostles and two letters written into very different situations, yet they point to the same truth.

Second Corinthians is the letter the apostle Paul wrote from Macedonia to the church in Corinth, somewhere between AD 55 and 57. Corinth was then the capital of the province of Achaia, a great port city — commercially booming, ideologically mixed and morally loose. The Corinthian church was one Paul had planted with his own hands, and yet it was the church that grieved him most: they split into factions, tolerated sexual immorality and looked down on Paul’s apostleship. Second Corinthians is the most personal and emotionally intense of all Paul’s letters; in it he defends his ministry and also lays his own weakness open before them.

The context of 2 Corinthians 5:17 matters enormously. Verse 14 says, “For the love of Christ constrains us; because we judge thus, that one died for all, therefore all died.” Verse 15 says, “He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again.” Notice the logic of these two verses: one died for all, therefore all died — that is the end of the self-centred life; no longer living to themselves but to the Lord — that is the beginning of selflessness. So the “new creation” of verse 17 is not a motivational slogan. Paul is speaking of a fact that has already happened, a fact legally accomplished.

“New creation” in the original is kainē ktisis. Greek has two words for “new”: neos means new in time, brand new off the production line; kainos means new in kind, never seen before. Paul uses kainos. In other words, when you believed, it wasn’t that the old you was repaired, refurbished and polished up; an “essentially brand-new creature” came into being. The twentieth-century apologist C. S. Lewis put it very clearly in Mere Christianity: God became man not to turn the old kind of man into a better man, but to produce a new kind of man.

First John, for its part, was written by the apostle John somewhere between AD 80 and 95, from the region around Ephesus, to the churches of Asia Minor. At the time an early form of Gnosticism was beginning to seep into the church, with some claiming that spiritual people could sin freely and that whatever the body did made no difference. Against this error John lists, one by one, the marks of true believers in a string of statements about “whoever is born of God”. The “doesn’t commit sin” of 3:9 is in the Greek present tense: it expresses an ongoing state, a habitual way of life. It isn’t saying that a believer will never stumble even once — because the same letter says in 1:8, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” What John means is this: the life that is born of God does not by nature make sin its normal state, because God’s word abides in him.

Notice that word “word”. The Chinese Union Version has very honestly added a small-print note: in the original it is “seed” — Greek sperma, a seed. What does a seed do? A seed grows. So John’s point is not “You must strain with all your might not to sin”, but “A seed of God has already been placed inside you — let it grow.”

Two letters, two apostles, two situations — yet with one voice they proclaim one thing: a Christian’s victory comes not by repairing the old, but by cultivating the new.

sections.heading: 1. You Are Already a New Creation
sections.html:
“Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” (2 Corinthians 5:17)

Brothers and sisters, notice the tense of this verse. Paul didn’t say, “You will become a new creation”, nor did he say, “If you try hard enough you’ll become a new creation.” He said: he is a new creation. Already.

The moment you believed, two things happened at once: your identity was changed, and your life was renewed. You are no longer a person in Adam; you are a person in Christ. Colossians 1:13 says that God is the one “who delivered us out of the power of darkness, and translated us into the Kingdom of the Son of his love”. The word “translated” in the original was the term used when ancient empires moved whole populations — your household registration has been transferred. You are not a temporary resident; your registration has been moved.

So in the language of 321 we can put it like this: selflessness has already been accomplished in our standing. It is an established fact, not a goal. In Galatians 2:20 Paul says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” “I have been crucified with Christ” is in the perfect tense — the thing has been done and settled.

So where is the problem? The problem is this: our daily living hasn’t caught up yet.

And so an awkward situation appears in us: our identity is new, but our habits are old.

I often use an illustration. A man moves from the countryside into a new house in the city. The house is new, the address is new, the keys are new; but the habits he built up over twenty years are still there — he doesn’t take his shoes off at the door, he drops rubbish wherever he is, and at three in the morning he’s still out in the yard talking at the top of his voice. The house has changed; his living hasn’t. It isn’t that he’s “not the owner” — he is the owner. He just hasn’t yet learned how to live in his new house.

Brothers and sisters, your struggle doesn’t mean you aren’t a new creation. Your struggle is precisely the proof that you are. A fish on the bank thrashes in agony, because it belongs in the water; put a stone on the bank and it feels nothing at all. You grieve over your sin because there is already a new life inside you, protesting. People who haven’t been saved don’t feel heartache over sin; they only feel heartache over getting caught.

That is where the struggle comes from — and it is also a sign of hope.

From the 321 perspective, this is exactly the starting point of the “fivefold change”: mindset → life → daily living → relationships → ministry. Many people want to jump straight to “daily living”, to get rid of some bad habit right away; but God’s order is to change the mindset first. If you still believe “I’m a terrible, failing person who keeps on sinning”, your daily living will never turn around, because daily living flows out of life, and life is steered by mindset. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living.

This morning, the first mindset that has to go is this one: I am not “a sinner trying hard to be better”. I am “a child who has already been made new and is learning to grow up”.

sections.heading: 2. Two Lives at Work Within
sections.html:
In Romans 7 Paul describes this war in vivid, unsparing detail:

“For I don’t know what I am doing. For I don’t practice what I desire to do; but what I hate, that I do.” (Romans 7:15)

“For the good which I desire, I don’t do; but the evil which I don’t desire, that I practice.” (Romans 7:19)

“I find then the law that, to me, while I desire to do good, evil is present.” (Romans 7:21)

“But I see a different law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me into captivity under the law of sin which is in my members. What a wretched man I am! Who will deliver me out of the body of this death?” (Romans 7:23–24)

Brothers and sisters, did you hear that? These are the words of the apostle Paul. Not a new believer, not a Christian in name only — this is Paul, who wrote the greater part of the New Testament. If even Paul could say “What a wretched man I am!”, then your struggle this morning is nothing strange.

Paul uses a key word: “law”, Greek nomos. Here it doesn’t mean the written commandments of Moses; it means a principle that operates consistently, an inevitable regularity — like gravity. There are two “laws” at work within us; that is, two lives at work within us.

The first is the self-centred life, the old life. Its traits are these: it sins, it likes to have its own way, it is pulled along by sin. This isn’t an occasional slip; it is its nature. Paul says, “For I know that in me, that is, in my flesh, dwells no good thing. For desire is present with me, but I don’t find it doing that which is good.” (Romans 7:18) Notice: the resolving you can manage; the doing you can’t. That is the limit of the old life.

The second is the selfless life, the new life. Its traits are these: it comes from God, it does not sin, it delights in God’s will. Paul says, “For I delight in God’s law after the inward man.” (Romans 7:22)

When two lives exist at the same time, there is a tug of war. Galatians 5:17 puts it even more bluntly: “For the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; and these are contrary to one another, that you may not do the things that you desire.”

Here I want to point out something very important: the tug of war is not itself sin; the tug of war is the battlefield. A nation without an army has no wars; a person without new life has no struggle. When you hear that voice inside you saying “Don’t do this”, that isn’t your own self-reproach — that is the Holy Spirit.

Physiology offers a fascinating parallel. In the human heart there is a cluster of special cells called the sinoatrial node. It generates its own electrical signal, sixty to a hundred times a minute, and for your whole life it never needs reminding and never needs your effort — it simply beats. That is what we call “the nature of life”. You don’t have to get up every morning and resolve, “Today I will make my heart beat.” In the same way, the new life has the nature of the new life: of itself it longs for God, it loves people, it hates sin. Your task is not to beat for it, but not to strangle it.

Here the 321 vision gives us a crucial sentence: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite — “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. So selflessness is not hollowing yourself out into a zero; it is letting the infinite Lord take first place within you.

sections.heading: 3. The Wrong Method: Combating the Self-Centred Life
sections.html:
Once they know there are two lives inside, many people immediately adopt a method that looks very spiritual but leads absolutely nowhere: combating the self-centred life.

Their approach is this: suppress hard, restrain with all their might, and try to make themselves stop sinning.

And so come all kinds of spiritual effort: resolution charts, fasting charts, check-in charts, confession lists, self-punishment, berating themselves a hundred times over in their hearts. On the surface it looks very devout; the result is more exhaustion, more failure, more discouragement.

Why? The answer is so simple it’s hard to believe: because the life of sin sins by nature.

The lesson uses a wonderfully vivid picture: a duck swims naturally; a chicken swimming is pure misery. Throw a chicken into the water and it isn’t that it doesn’t try — it flaps for all it’s worth — but it isn’t built for water. A duck has waterproof feathers, webbed feet and a thick layer of fat; a chicken has none of these. The problem isn’t effort; the problem is nature.

So listen carefully: you cannot turn the self-centred life into selflessness. You can train a chicken to run faster and crow louder, but you can never train it to become a duck. That road goes nowhere.

In Colossians 2:23 Paul passes a very stern verdict on this kind of religious effort: “These things indeed appear like wisdom in self-imposed worship, humility, and severity to the body; but aren’t of any value against the indulgence of the flesh.” Those words, “not of any value”, wipe out thousands of years of human moral effort at a stroke.

Go back to Wegner’s white bear experiment from the introduction. When that sister stuck “I WILL BE GENTLE” on her fridge, she thought she was cultivating gentleness; in fact, twenty times a day she was reminding herself, “I lose my temper easily.” What she was feeding wasn’t the new life; it was the old life’s sense of its own presence. That is the rebound effect of suppression: the harder you press down, the harder it springs back; the more it springs back, the more worn out you get.

Ancient China has a saying, “pulling up the sprouts to help them grow”, from the Mencius (Gongsun Chou, Part One). A farmer in the state of Song thought his rice shoots were growing too slowly, so he pulled each one up a little higher, then went home and said, “I’m worn out today — I’ve helped the shoots grow taller.” His son ran out to the field to look, and every shoot had withered. Brothers and sisters, the spiritual life is the same — life can only be cultivated; it cannot be yanked. The harder you combat, the faster the shoots die.

321 says: pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. The deepest problem with “combating the self-centred life” isn’t the method; it’s the position. It is me snatching God’s work away from him and setting myself up as the lord who changes lives. And there has only ever been One who can change a life.

sections.heading: 4. The Key to the Truth: Not Combating, but Cultivating
sections.html:
“Whoever is born of God doesn’t commit sin, because his seed remains in him, and he can’t sin, because he is born of God.” (1 John 3:9)

Brothers and sisters, the key is not making the self-centred life better; it is letting selflessness grow up.

John uses an agricultural picture: a seed. A seed doesn’t need to be persuaded, doesn’t need to be whipped along, doesn’t need a pep talk. A seed needs only three things: soil, water and light. Give it those three and it grows by itself. That is the law of life.

The Lord Jesus himself used the same picture. Mark 4:26–28: “God’s Kingdom is as if a man should cast seed on the earth, and should sleep and rise night and day, and the seed should spring up and grow, though he doesn’t know how. For the earth bears fruit: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear.” Look: “though he doesn’t know how.” The farmer doesn’t know how the seed grows, and he doesn’t need to know. His job is to sow, to water, to clear away whatever blocks the light; the growing is God’s work. First Corinthians 3:6 says, “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase.”

So God’s method can be said in a single sentence: not getting rid of the darkness, but turning on the light.

That is a physical fact and a spiritual truth. Darkness isn’t a substance; darkness is the absence of light. You can’t pour darkness into a bucket and carry it out, you can’t chase it away with a stick, you can’t suck it up with a vacuum cleaner. The strongest man in the world can’t shift a single cubic centimetre of darkness. But a candle, a torch — one click, and the darkness leaves the stage at once. The sun’s light travels a hundred and fifty million kilometres, taking about eight minutes and twenty seconds to reach the earth, and the moment it arrives, the night is over for half the planet. When the light comes, darkness simply leaves.

John 1:5 says, “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn’t overcome it.” The Lord Jesus said, “I am the light of the world. He who follows me will not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life.” (John 8:12)

The nineteenth-century Scottish minister Thomas Chalmers (1780–1847) preached a famous sermon called “The Expulsive Power of a New Affection”. He said that an old love in the human heart is not driven out by “not loving it”; it is pushed out by a new love that is greater, more beautiful and more true. If you want a child to let go of the toy in his hand, the most effective way isn’t to snatch it — it’s to give him something better.

Every parent understands this. A toddler grips a pair of scissors and won’t let go: the more you grab, the tighter he holds, screaming as he does. But put an ice cream in front of him, and his hand loosens all by itself. Brothers and sisters, this isn’t a technique; it’s the law of life.

Nature gives us a very beautiful example too. Oaks and beeches show a phenomenon called “marcescence”: their dead leaves don’t fall in late autumn but hang on the branches all winter, through wind and rain. When do they finally fall? Not until spring, at the moment the new bud pushes out from beneath the leaf stalk — then the old leaf drops to the ground. Brothers and sisters, those old habits you’ve been fighting for ten years and still can’t pull out — perhaps you aren’t meant to pull harder one more time, but to wait for the new life to grow and push them off.

So God’s method is: don’t combat the old life; cultivate the new life.

This is the very heart of 321: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. Notice, it isn’t “I overcome Satan”; it’s “selflessness overcomes Satan”. If you take on Satan with the self-centred life, you’re playing on his home ground; if you let Christ reign as King within you, it’s his ground of defeat.

sections.heading: 5. Why Is Combating the Self-Centred Life a Lie?
sections.html:
“As it is written, ‘There is no one righteous; no, not one.’” (Romans 3:10)

“Because by the works of the law, no flesh will be justified in his sight; for through the law comes the knowledge of sin.” (Romans 3:20)

Brothers and sisters, think about it with the simplest logic: if people could overcome sin by effort, Jesus wouldn’t have needed to come.

If moral self-cultivation could save people, the cross would be the greatest waste in history; if dealing with ourselves could make us holy, the sweat like great drops of blood in Gethsemane would mean nothing; if people could become good by themselves, then Paul’s words in Galatians 2:21 would hold: “I don’t reject the grace of God. For if righteousness is through the law, then Christ died for nothing!”

So we have to say something very weighty: “combating the self-centred life” is relying on ourselves; and relying on ourselves is going back to the self-centred life. That is precisely Satan’s trap.

See how cunning Satan’s trap is. He doesn’t need to tempt you into some great sin — that would be too obvious. All he needs is to get you doing something that looks very spiritual: working hard at dealing with yourself. And so you enter a loop: keep trying, keep failing, and finally give up. In the first stage you’re full of ambition; in the second you start to doubt; in the third you conclude, “This is just who I am. I can’t change.” The moment you say that sentence, Satan’s work is done. He hasn’t made you worse; he has made you despair.

Revelation 12:10 calls Satan the one “who accuses them before our God day and night”. His main weapon isn’t temptation; it’s accusation. Temptation makes you fall once; accusation keeps you lying on the ground and never getting up.

In Galatians 3:3 Paul fires a deafening question at the Galatians: “Are you so foolish? Having begun in the Spirit, are you now completed in the flesh?” When you were saved, it was by grace — and now that you’re being made holy, you want to rely on yourself? Logically, it makes no sense.

At the opening of Book One of his Confessions, Augustine wrote the prayer that has been repeated for sixteen hundred years: you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you. The emptiness inside a person can’t be filled by patching ourselves up; only God himself can fill it.

From the 321 perspective there is a crucial shift here: from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. Man’s perspective says, “I must try harder”; God’s perspective says, “I have already accomplished it for you; all you need to do is remain in me.” Man’s perspective sees my record of failure; God’s perspective sees Christ’s perfect record. Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.

321 has another very down-to-earth saying: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. Dealing with ourselves is the textbook case of “relying on the brain and ourselves” — analysing, reviewing, calculating, regretting, and the more we calculate, the more troubled we get. Cultivating Christ is “relying on the heart and the Holy Spirit” — looking up, obeying, drawing on his supply, giving thanks, and the further we go, the gladder we become.

sections.heading: 6. The Right Way: Cultivating the Selfless Life
sections.html:
So how exactly do we cultivate it?

The answer isn’t mysterious; it’s even a little ordinary: every time, choose selflessness; every time, obey the Holy Spirit; every time, live out Christ.

Not one earth-shattering act of consecration, but small choices, day by day, one at a time. Each time you choose selflessness once more, you live for yourself once less; and slowly selflessness grows stronger and the self-centred life grows weaker.

Remember this sentence: you don’t defeat it — you starve it.

There’s a widely told fable: an old man tells his grandson that two wolves are fighting inside every human heart, one evil and one good. The grandson asks, “Which one wins?” The old man says, “The one you feed.” Accounts of where the fable comes from vary widely, and we needn’t trace its origins, but it states a truth: whatever you feed grows.

Physiology gives us very reliable supporting evidence. A team led by Phillippa Lally at University College London published a study in the European Journal of Social Psychology in 2010 that followed ninety-six participants as they formed a new daily behaviour. They found that it took an average of sixty-six days for a behaviour to become automatic, with large individual differences, anywhere from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days. Even more important was another finding: missing a day now and then did not wreck the overall curve of habit formation. Brothers and sisters, did you hear that? Missing the odd day won’t ruin you. What really ruins you is giving up after you’ve missed one.

Brain science says the same thing. The principle the Canadian psychologist Donald Hebb set out in 1949 in his book The Organization of Behavior is usually summed up in one catchy line: neurons that fire together wire together. Every time you choose to obey, you walk that spiritual path one more time; walk it often enough and the grass is trampled flat and a path appears. Every time you choose to indulge, you also tread out a path — down the other way. Your life will grow into the shape of the path you walk every day.

So there are three very concrete channels for cultivating selflessness:

The first is prayer. Prayer isn’t persuading God; it’s handing ourselves over. The Lord Jesus’ prayer in Gethsemane is the supreme example: “nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.” (Matthew 26:39) Every time we pray like that, selflessness grows another inch.

The second is reading the Bible. “Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.” (Psalm 119:105) The Bible is my standard. Not my feelings, not other people’s opinions, not the mood of the times. First Peter 2:2 says, “as newborn babies, long for the pure milk of the Word, that with it you may grow.” A baby doesn’t drink milk to combat thinness; it drinks to grow.

The third is obeying the Holy Spirit. “But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh.” (Galatians 5:16) Notice the order of cause and effect in this verse: first walk by the Spirit, and then you won’t fulfil the lust of the flesh. It is not that you must first clean the lusts out completely before you can walk by the Spirit. Reverse that order and you’ll never get on the road in your whole life.

Here 321’s “920 practice” finds its footing: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; as we practise living out the selfless (0) life before them, we bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions. “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.” (Galatians 5:22–23) Notice: it’s “fruit”, not “product”. Products are manufactured; fruit grows. You have never seen an apple tree gritting its teeth in the night, straining to produce apples.

That sister who suffered over her temper later did something. She tore the words “I WILL BE GENTLE” off the fridge and put up a small card instead, which read: “Lord, right now I hand this child to you. Please let your gentleness flow through me.” She said, “Pastor, I still fail, but I no longer despair, because I know I’m not repairing myself; I’m inviting the Lord in.” Six months later her child said to her, “Mum, you’ve changed.” She hadn’t combated her temper away; she had cultivated Christ.

sections.heading: 7. The Real Key to Growth in Life
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, today’s last point gathers the six before it into one sentence: you are not “repairing yourself”; you are “cultivating Christ”.

The difference between the two is the difference between heaven and earth. In repairing yourself, the main character is me, the tool is my willpower, and success or failure depends on my performance. In cultivating Christ, the main character is him, the tool is his grace, and success or failure depends on his faithfulness.

The Lord Jesus said, “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5) A branch’s job isn’t to bear fruit; a branch’s job is to “remain”. Fruit is the by-product of being connected.

As Christ grows more and more within you, three things happen: sin naturally loses its influence, the struggle naturally lessens, and life naturally overcomes.

Notice that word “naturally”. It doesn’t mean easily, or without cost; it means no longer twisted, no longer forced. It’s like a tree: once it grows tall, the weeds beneath it naturally thin out — not because you squat there pulling weeds every day, but because the canopy blocks the sunlight and the weeds can’t grow. In gardening this is called “shade suppression”, and it is a real ecological phenomenon. Your task isn’t to pull weeds; it’s to let the tree grow tall.

So victory is not the result of effort; it is the result of life.

Right after crying out “What a wretched man I am!” in Romans 7, Paul says at once in 7:25, “I thank God through Jesus Christ, our Lord!” And then 8:1–2 goes on: “There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus … For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus made me free from the law of sin and of death.”

Look at the logic here: the law of sin and of death hasn’t been abolished; it still exists. But a higher law — the law of the Spirit of life — has overcome it. It’s like gravity: gravity hasn’t been abolished, but once the lift of aerodynamics is at work, a four-hundred-tonne aeroplane can fly. The aeroplane doesn’t fly by “combating gravity”; it flies by a higher law. Cut the engines and it drops at once; start the engines and it rises naturally into the sky.

In 2001 the American psychologist Barbara Fredrickson put forward her “broaden-and-build theory” in the journal American Psychologist. Her research showed that negative emotions narrow a person’s attention, while positive emotions broaden the range of thoughts and actions open to us and, over time, build up resources such as psychological resilience. From a side angle, this confirms the Bible’s order exactly: condemnation narrows us; grace enlarges us. Condemn yourself every day and your life grows narrower and narrower; look to Christ every day and your life grows wider and wider.

Second Corinthians 3:18 describes the beauty of this process: “But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit.” Just keep looking at him, and you will become like him. This is the gentlest way of sanctification in the whole Bible.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: One Road from Combating to Cultivating
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, today’s lesson is really an exercise in the very core of the 321 vision.

The Three Foundations of 321 are: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. Notice that none of these three foundations is called “my willpower is my strength”. The three channels for cultivating selflessness — obedience, Bible reading and prayer — correspond exactly to these three foundations: Jesus is my role model, so in Gethsemane I follow him in saying “not what I desire”; the Bible is my standard, so I don’t live by feelings but by God’s word; the Holy Spirit is my guide, so I don’t rely on the brain and myself — I rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit.

The Two Core Values of 321 are: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. The deadliest thing about “combating the self-centred life” is that it puts “me” on the throne, judging myself with one hand and saving myself with the other. “Cultivating selflessness” hands the throne back to the Lord. There’s a very simple test here: if you succeeded by combating, who gets the glory? Your perseverance. If you overcame by cultivating, who gets the glory? The Christ who lives within you. The Goal is to establish God’s system — not to build my record, but to build his Kingdom.

321 says: the old self is self-centred, the new self is selfless; the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. Go back to Eden: what did the serpent say to Eve? “You will be like God, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:5) Humanity’s first sin was leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place. And today, when we grit our teeth and say, “I will beat this sin by myself if it kills me”, we are really doing the same thing in a more hidden way: taking God’s place. Pride has two faces. One says, “I’m so capable”; the other says, “How can I be so useless?” — and at the centre of both faces is “I”.

So 321 says: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. When you stop wrestling with your own sin and humbly hand yourself over to Christ, the battle you’ve fought for ten years and could never win is lifted off your shoulders.

321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Many people fail at changing their habits because they have the order upside down. They want to get the ministry right first, to prove their life is fine; or to fix their relationships first, to make themselves feel a little better inside. God’s order is always life first. When life is right, relationships naturally come right; when relationships are right, ministry naturally bears fruit. The priority of relationships works the same way: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. If you’re still at war with yourself, how could you possibly get on well with other people?

Here 321’s “235 relationships” are an extremely practical help: becoming a “2” with a selfless person means a spiritual companion; establishing the “3” means spiritual parents and spiritual children; becoming a “5” means a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Changing a habit is almost impossible to do alone. Ecclesiastes 4:9–10 says, “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.” You need a “2” — not to police you or catch you out, but to remind you, when you fall, that you are a new creation.

Finally, 321’s shift of perspective is especially crucial in this lesson: from man’s to God’s — don’t look at what I can do; look at what God has already done; from the earthly to the heavenly — don’t look at my performance today; look at my standing in Christ; from the temporary to the eternal — don’t look at this one fall; look at the direction of a whole life; from the worldly to the godly — don’t pursue “being a better person”; pursue “letting Christ be lived out”.

The Path of Serving is the same road: Spirit (the Holy Spirit is my guide) → Understanding (the Bible is my standard) → Life (Jesus is my role model) → Service (let Jesus be King) → God (let Jesus receive all the glory). You’ll find that from beginning to end not one step of this road is “combating”; every step is “cultivating”.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. Let’s use 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to drive them deep and make them solid.

Practice 1: Stop Combating Yourself; Start Cultivating Life

When you discover your own weakness, don’t condemn or suppress it any more; turn to Jesus instead and let his life work within you.

Information: Copy today’s four key verses onto the first page of your notebook — 2 Corinthians 5:17, 1 John 3:9, Romans 8:1 and Colossians 2:23.

Revelation: Be still for three minutes and ask the Holy Spirit to show you how you have been “dealing with yourself” all these years. Not to add one more item of self-blame, but so that you can see where that road ends.

Conviction: Confess to God: “Lord, I’ve kept doing what you never asked me to do. I thought dealing with myself was godliness; in fact it was unbelief.”

Implementation: This week, whenever the voice of condemnation speaks up, change your words immediately — swap “How could I do this again?” for “Lord, I hand this over to you; please live it out in me.”

Evaluation: Every night before you sleep, ask one question: today, was I repairing myself, or cultivating Christ?

Correction: If you find you’ve slipped back into dealing with yourself, there’s no need to be upset; just come straight back to the cross. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9)

Repetition: For forty days in a row, let this new response become a reflex. Lally’s team reminds us that a new behaviour takes an average of sixty-six days to become automatic, so don’t judge yourself a failure on day ten.

Multiplication: Find a brother or sister who is suffering over some habit, and share today’s lesson with them.

Practice 2: Deliberately Feed the Selfless Life

Through prayer, Bible reading and obeying the Holy Spirit, make one selfless choice every day, so that the new life is cultivated.

Information: Set one concrete, tiny, doable “selfless choice”. Don’t make it “I will love people more”; make it “Every day I will pray for one minute for the person I least want to pray for.”

Revelation: Ask God to show you which “2” in your life he wants you to love in a special way this season.

Conviction: Believe that this one minute of prayer has more power than a whole year of self-examination.

Implementation: A fixed time, a fixed place, a fixed scripture. Habits need anchors.

Evaluation: After a week, check: have my feelings towards that person changed? Which of the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit is starting to put out a tender shoot?

Correction: If this practice is too big to manage, shrink it until you can definitely do it. Better small and steady than big and broken off.

Repetition: Feed it, time after time, until the new response shows up faster than the old one.

Multiplication: Invite a spiritual companion to do it with you, so you become each other’s “2”.

Practice 3: Value Direction, Not Failure

When you fall, don’t lose heart; turn back at once, choose selflessness once more, and keep walking the road of growth in life.

Information: Memorise Proverbs 24:16: “for a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again; but the wicked are overthrown by calamity.”

Revelation: See that the difference between the righteous and the wicked isn’t whether they fall, but whether they get up.

Conviction: Accept a new measure — not “Was I perfect today?” but “Which way was my face turned today?”

Implementation: After a fall, give yourself a “sixty-second rule”: confess, give thanks, get up and move forward — no lying on the ground chewing it over and over.

Evaluation: This month, after I fell, how long on average did it take me to turn back?

Correction: Shorten the time it takes to turn back. The mark of maturity is turning back faster and faster.

Repetition: Until “turning back at once” becomes your instinct.

Multiplication: Tell the true story of how you fell and got up again; it will help people far more than a perfect image. “Forgetting the things which are behind, and stretching forward to the things which are before, I press on toward the goal.” (Philippians 3:13–14)

A Gentle Reminder

You don’t become good by trying hard; you let Christ be lived out.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, today’s closing word is just two sentences: combating yourself is a heavy burden; cultivating Christ is light.

The more you combat, the more you fail; the more you cultivate, the more you overcome.

The Lord Jesus told us long ago all there is to say about the difference between these two roads: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” (Matthew 11:28–30)

Notice that the Lord didn’t say, “You don’t need to carry a yoke.” He said, “Take my yoke.” Christians aren’t people without responsibilities; they are people who have changed yokes. The old yoke is “I must make myself good”, and that yoke rubs your shoulders raw; the new yoke is “I will let Christ live in me”, and that yoke is made to measure for you — it is light.

This morning I want to invite you to make a decision. Not another resolution, not signing another contract you can’t keep. Rather, take that list in your hands, filled with “I absolutely must”, lay it quietly at the Lord’s feet, and say to him: Lord, I’m done combating; I want to cultivate you.

No more combating the self-centred life; give yourself to cultivating selflessness; let Jesus live out his life within you.

May you live this day not to prove yourself, but so that Jesus may reign as King; and may all the glory for every bit of growth in your life go to him alone.

keyVerses: “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” (2 Corinthians 5:17)
“Whoever is born of God doesn’t commit sin, because his seed remains in him, and he can’t sin, because he is born of God.” (1 John 3:9)
declarations: Lord, I will no longer rely on myself to combat sin. I will cultivate your life within me, and let Christ live in me, living out a victorious, free and abundant life!
practices: Stop combating yourself; start cultivating life
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

Thank you that while we were still straining to deal with ourselves, you had long since accomplished everything for us on the cross. Thank you that we are not sinners trying hard to be better; we are new creations you have already made.

Lord, we confess to you: for far too many years we have walked a road you never asked us to walk. We thought gritting our teeth was godliness, self-blame was repentance and suppression was holiness. Please forgive us, and please set us free.

Turn our eyes from our own failures to your perfection; turn our strength from combating the old life to cultivating the new. May the Holy Spirit remind us every day to choose selflessness once more and live for ourselves once less.
Lord, grow within us. As you increase more and more within us, may our sin naturally lose its influence, our struggle naturally lessen, and our life naturally overcome.
Let Jesus reign as King within us; let Jesus receive all the glory.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Second Corinthians 5:17 says, “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” Looking back over this year, in what area have you kept on “dealing with yourself”? When you hear the words “You are already a new creation”, what is your heart’s honest reaction — comfort, or doubt? Why?

Galatians 5:16 says, “But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh.” This week, what concrete, tiny choice that you can make every day will you use to “feed” the new life? Whom are you willing to invite to be your “2”, to practise alongside you and support each other?
